Start a session

Adaptive Session is the recommended default: it interleaves domains and pulls in whatever's due for spaced review, which research finds builds more durable retention than working one topic at a time — even though blocked practice feels easier in the moment. Save Domain Drill for a topic that's still genuinely new to you.

Recommended · interleaved + spaced

Adaptive Session

15 questions selected live: mixed across domains (interleaving), weighted toward your weakest areas, and pulled only from what's new or due — you won't see a repeat until the full bank's been covered. "Due" works the same way as the flashcards: answer one right and it steps further away before it's due again; miss it and it comes right back.

How this is designed

not just quiz software — tap to expand ▾
The tutor can pointAsked to let the tutor highlight and direct you toward what it thinks you should do next. The tutor can now take you to a spot in the app and mark it with a pulsing outline and a short note, such as "Tutor: Start with the due reviews". It can do this when you ask to be shown something in chat, and its opening message on the Tutor tab has a Show me link that takes you straight to your next best step. The highlight clears when you tap anywhere, press a key, or after nine seconds. The tutor is told to use this once it has finished explaining, since it moves you away from the chat.
More flashcards for the thin spotsA second pass at the subtopics with the fewest flashcards: eldercare and Medicaid planning, choosing a business retirement plan, buy-sell agreements, risk exposures, insurer ratings and policy replacement, and everyday tax law such as the net investment income tax and above-the-line deductions. Added 22 cards, skipping five that already existed under the same name, for a total of 674.
A plan before each case studyThe session plan from your tutor now also opens each case study. It reminds you that the questions share one client situation, shows how you did last time and your best score on that case, and suggests skimming the scenario once for numbers, dates and ownership before returning to the part each question needs. It disappears once you answer.
A tutor that greets you like oneThe tutor tab opened with the same generic welcome whenever you visited. Now, before you type anything, its first message reflects where you actually are: how many days to your exam, whether you studied yesterday or have been away (with a nudge toward a short warm-up after a few days off), how your last session went, your weakest area, and the one thing it would do next, taken from the same recommendation the Study tab shows. Once you start a conversation it stops changing, so it never rewrites something you are reading.
Coaching in the formula practiceThe formula practice showed the working after each answer but never said what the pattern meant. Now a short coaching line appears only at moments that matter: after two misses in a row on the same formula (slow down, write the formula and the givens first), when you reach three in a row (practice will now lean toward your weaker formulas), and every eight problems with a quick summary that names the formula that gave you the most trouble. Nothing appears on ordinary answers, so it stays worth reading.
Checkpoints in the flashcardsFlashcards ran on forever with no moment to step back, which a human tutor would never allow. Every 12 cards the deck now pauses for a short checkpoint: how many you knew, which cards you missed, and a note on what comes next. When you continue, the missed cards go to the front of the deck, so what the checkpoint says is what actually happens. This relies on the same spacing idea as the rest of the flashcards, with a quick look back after a small batch rather than at the very end.
A tutor at the start of each sessionAsked to make the app feel like a guided tutor wherever that helps. The tutor already answered questions on its own tab, after each question and on the results screen, but nothing guided you before you began. Now an adaptive, drill or review session opens with a short plan from your tutor: what the set leans on, how many are reviews that are due or revisit a confident miss or test a pair you mix up, and your most common slip to watch for. It tucks itself away as soon as you answer, and exam-style modes never show it. Time-value-of-money questions also get a one-line HP 10bII+ setup check (clear, P/YR, END mode) that adds your own most frequent calculator slip. Both come from your own history, with no button to press and no AI call needed.
The 2026 charity rulesCFP Board tests the current year's tax law, and the exams from July 2026 use 2026 law. The new charitable-giving rules for 2026 were missing from the app. Added two flashcards, two practice questions and a key number: itemizers only deduct gifts above 0.5% of income, the benefit is capped at a 35% rate for top-bracket taxpayers, and people taking the standard deduction can now deduct up to $1,000 ($2,000 for couples) of cash gifts to qualifying charities.
Filling the thinnest topicsAsked to make sure everything is covered appropriately across the app. Counting questions and flashcards against each of the 70 official subtopics showed the overall balance across the eight domains matches the exam weights well, but about 40 subtopics had only a few questions or almost no flashcards, such as education funding, risk principles, retirement income strategies, money conflict and trust taxation. Added 29 questions and 36 flashcards aimed at exactly those gaps (every new question passed the same wording and answer-length checks as the rest), and removed one flashcard that duplicated an existing one.
Checking the wording against the factsAsked to make sure all the text is accurate and not overdone. Checked the exam-day screen against CFP Board's own page and fixed two things: the 40-minute break between sections is scheduled but you can skip it (it isn't mandatory), and you clear your own calculator's memory rather than the proctor doing it. Added a reminder to recheck P/YR (default 12) and END mode afterward. The formula practice card said fifteen formulas when there are over thirty, so it now counts them live. Also shortened the longest explanations in Settings, Reference and the study guide, and removed a claim about free API credits that couldn't be verified.
Every AI feature now knows you use an HP 10bII+Asked to make sure the tutor always remembers the calculator is an HP 10bII+. Some prompts already said so, but others (the tutor chat, the in-question chat, the memory tricks, the question generators) relied on the AI guessing. Now every request to the AI carries the same short calculator rule: no CPT or I/Y key, use N, I/YR, PV, PMT and FV, P/YR, BEG/END, C ALL and the cash-flow keys. If a reply still names another calculator's keys, the app quietly asks again with a correction before you ever see it, while still letting the tutor explain how the HP differs from other models.
Retrieval practiceEvery mode tests you instead of re-showing notes — actively recalling an answer builds stronger, more durable memory than rereading. Rated "high utility" by the largest review of learning techniques (Dunlosky et al., 2013).
Why every wrong choice gets its own explanationMultiple-choice questions produce a weaker testing effect than free recall when they let you just recognize the right answer without genuinely engaging the others — research on the testing effect ties this to how little retrieval effort recognition alone demands. But multiple-choice can be constructed to induce real retrieval about the wrong options too. That's why every question here explains all four choices, not only the correct one — working out why the other three are wrong is part of the retrieval itself, not something to skip once you've spotted the answer.
Spaced repetitionQuestions and flashcards run on a Leitner-style schedule: get something right and it's pushed further out; miss it and it comes right back. You'll never see a repeat while unseen or due material is still available — the full bank gets covered before anything repeats.
InterleavingAdaptive Session deliberately mixes domains instead of blocking by topic. It feels harder in the moment, but mixing related material tends to build better long-term discrimination between concepts than one-topic-at-a-time drilling.
Elaborative interrogationEvery answer reveal prompts you to explain, in your own words, why the wrong choices don't work — not just accept the right one.
Specific, not generic, positive feedbackWhen a session shows a real, sizable jump in a domain compared to your prior average there, this app calls it out specifically — the domain, the numbers, the comparison — rather than a generic "great job." This follows Mueller & Dweck's research finding that specific, process-focused feedback builds more durable motivation and resilience than generic or ability-focused praise, which can backfire by making people avoid challenges. That research base is strongest with children and early adolescents; it's a reasonable, evidence-informed default for adults too, but less rigorously tested at that age. No points, badges, or streak pressure here — deliberately: research on self-determination theory finds that using rewards as a controlling "do X to earn Y" mechanism can undermine the intrinsic motivation it's meant to build.
Light mode by defaultResearch on display polarity (reviewed by Nielsen Norman Group, drawing on Legge, Piepenbrock, and Buchner & Baumgartner) consistently finds dark-text-on-light produces better reading accuracy and detail perception than dark mode — the advantage grows for smaller text, which matters given how much explanatory text is here. Dark mode's real edge is comfort in dim rooms, not comprehension, so it's a toggle (top right), not forced.
No red for wrong answersElliot et al. (2007, J. Exp. Psych: General) found that briefly seeing red before a test measurably lowered subsequent scores — red in an achievement context reads as danger and triggers avoidance, not just "incorrect." Wrong answers to practice questions use amber instead. (The TVM calculator's setup-mistake feedback is a different context — closer to a real calculator's own error indicator than to being marked wrong on a test — so it intentionally keeps the red that a real HP 10bII+ would show.)
Difficulty that adapts to youAdaptive Session now leans questions toward your current level, tracked from your last 20 answers — harder material when you're doing well, foundational material when you're not, and a deliberate mix in between. This is the same idea behind Item Response Theory (used by real adaptive tests like the GRE): match item difficulty to estimated ability. A single learner's app can't calibrate item difficulty the way a population-scale exam can, so this uses each question's own characteristics as a proxy instead — it's a good-faith approximation, not true IRT. The "in between" zone deliberately keeps some real challenge rather than only easy wins, following Bjork & Bjork's research on "desirable difficulties" — the finding that comfortable repetition feels productive but a well-matched challenge is what actually builds durable retention. Before there's enough answer history to react to, the engine doesn't assume average ability — a genuinely blank slate defaults to easier material first, the same posture as someone who's shown they're struggling, so the very first questions you ever see are a real crawl-before-you-walk starting point rather than a coin flip on hard material. The same caution applies per domain: touching a topic you haven't tried yet stays gentler on difficulty even if you're doing well elsewhere overall, until that specific area has its own track record to go on.
Writing harder questions when you outgrow the easy onesThe difficulty engine above only ever reweighted which existing questions get shown more. Once your recent accuracy stays consistently high, this now goes a step further and has the AI write genuinely new, harder material in your strongest domain — multi-step application questions and scenarios, not more single-fact recall — rather than only recycling the existing hard-tier pool, which is naturally the smallest of the three. Same Vygotsky/Bjork reasoning as above, extended from selecting difficulty into creating it. Requires an AI connection (set up in Settings) to run.
Stepping down to rebuild, then back up — deliberatelyThe global difficulty engine above already eases up smoothly when you're struggling overall. This adds something more structured for a specific domain having a real, sustained rough patch: it holds that domain on foundational questions until you actually demonstrate a genuine mastery streak, then deliberately escalates back up — rather than a smooth, continuous reweight. This follows Bloom's mastery learning approach, validated in Kulik, Kulik & Bangert-Drowns' 1990 meta-analysis of 108 controlled studies, which found real gains from requiring genuine mastery before advancing — and notably, a larger effect for struggling students specifically than strong ones. The "then back up" half matters too: Bandura's self-efficacy research finds that mastery experiences — actually succeeding at something — are the strongest known source of confidence, stronger than encouragement alone, which is why this is designed to hand you real wins to build on rather than just staying easy indefinitely.
Rating your confidence, not just your answerIn Adaptive Session, Domain Drill, and Missed Review, you can mark how sure you feel before answering — no pill starts pre-selected, since a genuine calibration read requires the rating to come from an actual choice, not an assumption standing in for one. The point isn't the rating itself, it's what it reveals: metacognitive calibration research consistently finds that how confident someone feels and how often they're actually right can diverge, and that mismatch — not just raw knowledge gaps — is a real, documented source of exam-day mistakes, since a wrong answer you never thought to double-check is the one that costs you. The rating locks the moment you answer — it's already been recorded, so it shouldn't keep looking editable — and if you marked something confident but got it wrong, that specific mismatch gets called out right there, not just folded into an aggregate stat you might never look at. The Detailed Diagnosis card compares your confident-answer accuracy against your unsure-answer accuracy directly, once there's enough logged to say something real. Worth being honest about the limits here: this is a simple self-report, not a validated psychological instrument, and it's deliberately absent from Mock Exam and the full simulation — the real exam never asks how sure you are, and preserving that realistic pressure matters more there than gathering calibration data.
Being confidently wrong is a teachable moment, if it's followed up on quicklyResearch on the "hypercorrection effect" (Butterfield & Metcalfe) finds something counterintuitive: being confidently wrong and then corrected tends to produce stronger, more durable learning than an ordinary uncertain miss — but that effect depends on the correction landing reasonably soon, not whenever the general review queue happens to bring the question back around. So a question you marked confident and missed gets quietly flagged for guaranteed placement in your very next Adaptive Session — ahead of the normal weighted selection, though capped at three per session so it can't take over the whole thing if several pile up at once. The flag clears the moment you answer it correctly again; from there it returns to ordinary spaced-repetition scheduling like everything else.
Evening warm modeLate-evening blue light suppressing melatonin and disrupting sleep timing is well-established, and sleep itself being important for learning is well-established. Whether dimming blue light specifically improves memory consolidation is less settled — the most rigorous recent sleep-lab study found no significant effect on consolidation itself, even though it confirmed melatonin suppression. So this is offered honestly as support for general sleep hygiene around a late session, not a claimed direct memory boost — the control for it lives in the Display card above.
A real calculator, not another multiple-choice questionThe TVM walkthrough tool doesn't ask you to recognize a right answer among four options — it makes you actually key N, I/YR, PV, and PMT in the order a real financial calculator expects, including getting sign convention right, then press the unknown variable's own key directly to compute it — no separate compute step, matching the HP 10bII+ and 12C rather than the TI BA II Plus's CPT key. Recognition and production are different skills, and the exam (and every calculation you'll ever do with a client) demands the second one. It runs its own adaptive difficulty ladder — two clean solves moves you up a tier, three-plus setup errors on one problem moves you back down — the same underlying logic as the difficulty engine above, applied to calculator methodology instead of question selection. There's also an optional two-part mode ("save, then spend it down") that chains an accumulation problem into a distribution problem, carrying your first answer forward as the starting point for the second — the same multi-step reasoning the real exam actually tests, not just isolated single calculations. This tier progression and multi-part mode are deliberately kept separate from the main question difficulty engine, so working through a hard calculator problem never quietly changes what questions you see next. Currently covers solving for N, FV, PV, and PMT, with lump-sum, ordinary-annuity, and annuity-due (BEGIN mode) problems; it doesn't yet handle solving for I/YR, which needs iteration rather than direct algebra — unlike N, which has a direct logarithmic solution.
Seeing the sign convention, not just reading about itEvery other explanation of TVM sign convention in this app is text: "money you put in is negative, money you get out is positive." Dual coding theory (Paivio) suggests pairing that kind of verbal rule with a visual representation builds a stronger, more retrievable memory than either alone — and sign convention is specifically where setup mistakes concentrate, per the TVM mistake-tracking above. So a simple cash-flow timeline now sits above the calculator itself: known values appear as arrows, pointing up for money received and down for money paid out, colored to match; whichever value you're actually solving for shows as a plain "?" instead, since its direction isn't known until you compute it. It updates with the problem, not with your keystrokes, so it shows the real setup immediately rather than only filling in as you type.
A coach that reacts to real progress, not just background tasksThe status line at the top of the Study tab used to only report on AI generation — starting, finishing, erroring. It now also watches for things actually worth saying: a genuine answer-count milestone, a domain crossing 80% mastery for the first time, a study streak hitting a real threshold — each tied to a specific, cited reason it matters, not generic praise. This is deliberately a different mechanism from the specific-feedback item above, which compares a single session's performance against your own prior average; this one tracks milestones across your whole history and won't re-announce the same one twice. When nothing genuinely new has happened, it rotates through short research notes on spacing, testing, and interleaving instead of going stale or repeating the same "ready" message indefinitely.
"Weakest" means struggling now, not just historicallyA domain you nailed early on can still develop a real recent rough patch, and a domain with a mediocre lifetime average can be one you've since gotten comfortable with — an all-time percentage blurs both of those together. Wherever this app picks out your weakest domain — the tutor's quick actions, the domain picker's default order, the reference tab's sort — a domain currently flagged as rebuilding fundamentals now takes priority over one with a merely lower historical average, since that status reflects what's actually happening in your last ten questions there, not a number that years-old easy answers can still be propping up.
Not every wrong answer is the same mistakePicking the exact same wrong choice on a question more than once — or making the same kind of setup error repeatedly in the TVM tool — is a meaningfully stronger signal than a typical miss. A one-off slip could be a careless moment; the same wrong answer twice usually means a specific, persistent misconception that a raw accuracy number won't surface on its own. This gets tracked separately and shown directly — in the Detailed Diagnosis card, the coach card, and the tutor's own context — so it's something concrete to work on rather than a vague "study more."
Refining "you'll never see a repeat" for struggling materialThe spaced repetition item above describes the intended behavior, but a missed question's schedule resets to due immediately, and missed material already gets extra selection priority — together, that could mean the same question resurfacing within a session or two of getting it wrong, even though "due" isn't the same as "should show again right now." Adaptive Session now excludes your most recently shown questions from the candidate pool outright rather than just down-weighting them, unless a domain's pool is genuinely too small to spare them — so even a domain you're actively struggling with gets real breathing room between repeats instead of cycling the same few questions back-to-back.
A repeat that doesn't look like oneSpacing solves timing, but not recognition — even with real distance between repeats, seeing the exact same wording again risks answering from memory of that specific question rather than genuinely re-deriving it from the underlying concept. When a question due for review has genuinely been seen before, Adaptive Session, Domain Drill, and Missed Review now quietly generate a fresh version of it — same concept and skill, different numbers, names, or framing — calibrated a notch easier or harder depending on your current standing in that domain. It still counts toward the same underlying question's progress, not a separate one, so spaced repetition keeps tracking correctly underneath it. Requires a connected API key; without one, or if generation fails, you simply see the original question exactly as before.
Turning a pattern into a one-tap questionThe recurring-mistake and TVM setup-mistake detection above already work passively — they show up in the Detailed Diagnosis card and the coach line whether or not you ever look. But noticing a pattern and acting on it are different things, so the Tutor tab also carries direct shortcuts for them: "Explain my recurring mistake" and "Explain my TVM setup mistake" only appear once you've genuinely earned them — the same threshold the diagnosis card uses — and send the tutor a specific, real message naming the actual question or mistake category, not a generic prompt. A button that's usually empty or irrelevant is worse than no button, so neither one exists until there's something real to say.
Letting the tutor actually do things, not just describe themAsking the tutor to "quiz me on tax planning" and getting back "go to the Study tab and tap Domain Drill" is a worse experience than the tutor just starting that drill directly — every extra step between intent and action is a chance to lose the thread. So when you ask for something concrete, the tutor can genuinely switch tabs, start a session, open the TVM tool, set your exam date, look up a term in the glossary, open your detailed progress breakdown, or generate fresh practice material on a domain — rather than only ever describing where to click. Each action shows a clear confirmation right in the chat, so what actually happened is never left ambiguous: asking it to generate more questions doesn't just say "done," it reports back exactly how many questions and flashcards were actually added. This isn't the tutor quietly changing things in the background, it's doing the specific thing you asked for, in the open.
A dumber explanation, on purposeThe rationale under each answer choice is written to be precise and complete, which is exactly what makes it unhelpful sometimes — a technically correct explanation someone doesn't yet have the footing to follow. "Explain this more simply," available after answering in Adaptive Session, Domain Drill, and Missed Review, asks for something deliberately different: plain language, a short analogy if one actually helps, and — when you got it wrong — specifically why your answer seemed reasonable rather than just re-explaining the correct one in isolation, since that's usually the actual gap. It's not a better explanation, just a different one for when the first didn't land; you can ask again for another attempt if it still doesn't click. Like the confidence rating, it's absent from Mock Exam and the full simulation on purpose. Its answer stays saved once generated, so seeing the same question again later shows the same explanation instantly instead of a new one — the point is a consistent thing to build on, not a fresh roll each time.
Explaining it back, before moving onReading someone else's explanation and being able to produce your own aren't the same skill — research on the "protégé effect" and self-explanation consistently finds that generating an explanation, even a rough one, forces a kind of processing that passive reading doesn't, and reliably surfaces gaps the reader didn't know were there. "Explain it back to me," sitting next to the simplify button, asks you to write a few sentences of your own before moving on, then gives feedback aimed at what you actually wrote — what's genuinely solid, what's missing or imprecise — rather than a generic "close enough." It's not a strict correctness grader and won't catch every subtlety; treat the feedback as a second opinion on your own reasoning, not a verdict.
A hook for facts that don't want to stickFlashcards work by brute-force repetition, but some term-definition pairs are arbitrary enough that repetition alone takes a long time to stick — the keyword mnemonic method (associating unfamiliar material with a vivid image, sound-alike, or wordplay hook) is well-established for exactly this kind of rote pairing. "Give me a memory trick for this," available after flipping a card, generates one specific to that exact term rather than a generic domain-level tip. Like the simplified explanations for questions, a card's memory trick is saved once generated, so it stays consistent instead of reshuffling into something different each time you flip back to it.
Generating an answer is a different skill than recognizing onePractice questions and flashcards both work by recognition — the answer is right there, waiting to be picked out or flipped to. Free recall (producing information from memory with no options in front of you at all) is a genuinely different, and research consistently finds a more durable, retrieval skill — Roediger and Karpicke's work on this is the reason "test yourself" and "reread your notes" aren't the same advice, even though both feel like studying. "Test your recall," on the Reference tab, asks you to write down everything you remember about a domain before ever looking at the official topic list — no hints, no options, no grading. Only once you've genuinely tried does the real list appear, so you can see for yourself what surfaced easily and what didn't.
Text written to be read isn't automatically clear when it's heardClaude's API can't generate audio at all — the actual voice behind every "read aloud" button is entirely the browser's own, built-in text-to-speech, which this app just picks the best-sounding option from. What Claude can genuinely do is rewrite the text itself before it's spoken: expanding an abbreviation like "RMD" into "required minimum distribution," breaking a long written sentence into shorter spoken ones, trading written-style phrasing for something that actually sounds natural out loud. That rewrite is optional (it needs an API key and adds a brief pause before speech starts, shown as a distinct "preparing" state on the button) and cached per card or question once generated, so it's asked for once and reused after that, not regenerated every time you tap the same speaker icon.
A second way to use the same terms, not a second set of themFlashcards are built for active recall — the definition is deliberately hidden until you flip, because the effort of trying to remember first is what makes it stick. That's exactly wrong for a different, equally real need: you're mid-question, you hit "GRAT" or "coinsurance clause," and you just want the answer, right now, with nothing to flip or rate. The glossary on this tab is that — every term visible at once, searchable by name or by anything in its definition. It reads from the exact same flashcard data (including anything the AI has generated for you), so the two never drift out of sync with each other — this is a different way of using the same terms, not a second, separate copy of them. It doesn't track anything new of its own, either; it just surfaces what's already known. The same weakness signal that reorders Key Numbers and the syllabus checklist marks matching terms with a small dot here too, and an optional toggle narrows the whole list down to just those domains in one tap — but the default view stays plain alphabetical, on purpose. A lookup tool that's fast specifically because you already know where "P" is shouldn't quietly reshuffle itself; showing you what's weak works better as something you can reach for, not something forced on you every time you're just trying to find a word.
Running low and actually weak in it are two different thingsNew flashcards get written for you automatically in the background as you study — no button required — but which domain gets the new material used to be decided purely by whichever one's card pool happened to run thin first. That's not the same as which domain you're actually struggling with: a domain you haven't touched in a while empties out regardless of whether you're strong or weak in it. Now pool size only decides which domains genuinely need fresh material at all — no point writing more for one that's still full of cards you haven't seen — and your actual quiz performance, the same signal that already targets weak spots for new practice questions, decides which of those to prioritize. The result lands specifically in whichever domain you're both running low on and genuinely performing worst in, and shows up here in the glossary the moment it's written, since it draws from the exact same data.
A definition tells you what something is; an example shows you what it doesThe short definition next to every glossary term is deliberately always visible — that's the entire point of a fast lookup, and it's still there, untouched, whether you tap anything or not. But a definition alone often isn't enough to see how a concept actually plays out with a real client and real numbers, and cramming that into every entry by default would turn a scannable list back into the wall of text a glossary is supposed to avoid. So tapping a term reveals a concrete, AI-generated example underneath — a specific scenario showing the concept in action, not the definition restated in different words — generated once and cached from then on, the same pattern already used for flashcard memory tricks. It needs an API key to generate; without one, tapping still shows you exactly why and how to add one, rather than just doing nothing.
A backup that doesn't wait for a second clickProgress lives in this browser's own storage, which isn't a permanent home — a refresh at the wrong moment, a browser update, low device storage, and it can quietly be gone. Tapping "Backup my progress" used to open a box with a download option inside it; now the download itself fires immediately, the moment you tap that first button, with the same box still opening right after so the copy-to-clipboard alternative is there too if you'd rather use that, or if the automatic download silently didn't work on your specific device. The file itself is named to be found later without guessing — "cfp-blueprint-backup-" followed by the actual date and time it was made, so if you've got several sitting in a downloads folder months from now, the most recent one is obvious at a glance, not just "backup (3).txt."
A drill that actually moves through the materialDomain Drill used to hand you the entire domain's question pool, shuffled, every single time — meaning drilling the same domain twice in a row genuinely showed the identical full set back, just in a different order, since nothing about it tracked what you'd already seen. Now it pulls a capped, 15-question set the same way spaced-repetition selection already works everywhere else in this app: never-seen questions first, then whatever's least recently seen, so a repeated drill on the same domain moves on to different material instead of replaying what you just did. Once you've genuinely worked through everything in a smaller domain, it starts back at the least-recently-seen end rather than repeating what you just answered, the same behavior Mock Exam already used.
Five problems, not one, on repeatThe TVM calculator's problems are grouped into small tiers — five or six at a time — and picking the next one used to be pure random chance, only ruling out whichever problem you'd just solved. Over a real working session that let the same problem or two turn up far more often than the rest, purely by chance, even though no two in a row were ever identical — the same underlying issue Domain Drill had, just at a smaller scale. It now tracks which problem in the tier has gone longest without appearing and picks that one, the same least-recently-seen principle used everywhere else selection happens in this app, so a real working session moves through the whole tier evenly instead of circling back to the same one or two problems by chance.
A blank answer isn't the same as no answerEvery AI-generated feature in this app — mnemonics, examples, generated practice material — asks the model for text and shows whatever comes back. A request can succeed at the network level with nothing genuinely wrong, and still occasionally come back with no usable text in it at all; that's rare, but it happens with any live API. That case used to be treated as a real answer rather than a failure, so it skipped the retry logic built for actual errors and went straight to "couldn't come up with one" on the very first, single attempt. It's now treated the same as any other failure, catching it in the same automatic retry-with-backoff already used for network issues and rate limits — so a blank response two seconds ago is now something this app quietly tries again on its own, not something you have to notice and ask for again yourself.
Written to be heard, not read and then convertedClaude can't generate audio directly — every voice in this app, including this one, is your device's own browser-native text-to-speech, the same voice the speaker buttons elsewhere already use. What makes this a genuine podcast rather than a definition read aloud is that the script is written for listening from the very first draft: short sentences, no bullet points or headers, a handful of concepts explained one at a time with a concrete example, the same shape a real spoken explanation actually takes. That's also why it skips the separate rewrite-for-speech step used elsewhere in this app — there's nothing to convert here, since it was never written as something to be read visually in the first place. Play, pause, and resume use the browser's own native controls, not just stop-and-restart, and each episode is written once and saved, so coming back to it later is instant.
The same tutor, in a different formatEvery domain overview episode is generic on purpose — it's built to work for anyone studying that topic. The "from your tutor" episode is the opposite: it's built specifically from this session's own progress data, using the exact same context the tutor already draws on for chat — readiness, weakest domain, recurring mistakes, confidence calibration — handed to the same underlying request as a spoken script instead of a written reply. Nothing new is tracked to make this possible; it's the tutor's own existing knowledge, just spoken instead of typed. Because that knowledge changes as you keep answering questions, this episode carries its own "written X ago" note the other two don't — a domain's core formulas don't go stale, but what you're actually weak in does, so this one is built to be regenerated as you go, not treated as a one-time listen.
Speech that pauses like a person, not a machineText-to-speech run on one long block of text tends to sound flat and rushed — no breath, no rhythm, every sentence blending into the next. This app now splits spoken text into sentences first, plays each one as its own short utterance, and puts a real, deliberate gap between them — a touch longer after a paragraph break than between two sentences in the same thought, since that's closer to how someone actually pauses when talking. Rate and pitch also shift slightly, sentence to sentence, within a narrow enough range that it reads as natural variation rather than a different voice altogether. Every speak button in this app — flashcards, question rationales, and every podcast episode — now goes through this same engine, and pause genuinely pauses the whole sequence, not just whatever single sentence happens to be mid-word when you tap it.
Following along, not just listeningReading along with audio while it plays — not before, not after, but genuinely at the same time — is a well-established way to strengthen how something sticks, since it engages the same content through two channels at once instead of one. The transcript now highlights whichever sentence is actually being spoken as it's spoken, tracking the exact same sentence boundaries the speech engine itself uses, so what's lit up on screen is never a beat off from what you're hearing. Playback speed is adjustable too, the same way any real podcast or audiobook app works — and speeding up genuinely means everything moves faster, not just the words with the same-length pauses now feeling stretched out between them; the gaps scale right along with the rate.
A domain episode that knows what you actually got wrongTwo of the three original episode types were the same for anyone studying that domain, and the third was personalized but covered your progress everywhere at once, not any one topic. This one sits in between: ask for a domain's common mistakes, and if you've genuinely missed real questions there, it's built from those exact questions and the real reasoning behind their correct answers, not a generic list of things people often get wrong. Haven't missed anything in that domain yet? It says so plainly and gives general guidance instead, rather than inventing a mistake pattern you don't actually have.
A transcript you can actually navigate, not just read along withTapping any sentence in the transcript jumps playback there directly, the same way a real podcast app's transcript works — and previous/next controls step through sentence by sentence, not by a fixed number of seconds, since that's the unit this app actually plays in. There's also a way to hear every domain back to back now, one continuous session instead of eight separate visits to the dropdown — and if one domain's episode fails to generate along the way, it's skipped rather than stopping the whole thing, so one bad moment doesn't cost you the rest.
Everything you've made, in one placeEvery episode already generated sits in a running list beneath the player — what domain, what kind, one tap to play it again — instead of needing to rebuild the exact domain-and-type combination through the dropdowns each time you want to hear something you already made. It only appears once there's genuinely something in it, and it updates itself the moment a new episode is written, so it never needs a separate action to stay current.
Duration isn't really the dial -- length isThere's no audio file being rendered here with a known runtime before it plays; a script gets written, then read aloud at whatever pace the moment calls for. So instead of asking for "5 minutes," this asks for a script written to roughly that length -- short, standard, or a full deep dive -- at a natural spoken pace of around 150 words a minute, and everything scales with it: fewer things covered in more depth for a short pass, more for a deep one, not just the same amount of material rushed or stretched to fit.
The same topic, pitched differently depending on where you actually standA domain overview used to be identical for everyone studying that domain, whether it was their first look or their fifth. Now, once there's real data -- a handful of answered questions in that specific domain -- it quietly adjusts: strong accuracy there skips the basics and goes straight at nuance and edge cases, weak accuracy builds from the ground up without assuming familiarity, and a recent confidence dip in that domain keeps things deliberately foundational. With nothing to go on yet, it stays honestly generic rather than pretending to know something it doesn't -- the personalization only speaks up once it has something real to say.
The headphones already worked -- the buttons on them didn'tAudio has always played through connected headphones automatically; that part is the operating system's job, not this app's. What genuinely wasn't wired up was the physical controls -- the play, pause, and skip buttons on a headset doing nothing for a page it didn't know was playing anything. Registering with the browser's media session changes that: those buttons now control this exact episode, and the lock screen shows what's actually playing instead of nothing.
A form of dropdowns, then a media playerThe podcast controls used to read as one long stack of identical-looking selectors and buttons, with the actual playback controls buried at the bottom in the same style as everything above them. Now the selectors and the player look like two different kinds of things, because they are -- choosing what to hear sits in one place, controlling something already playing sits in a visually distinct panel below it, with the same icon language the rest of the app already uses instead of a mix of text and raw keyboard symbols.
A tap that clearly landedWriting an episode takes a few real seconds, and the generate button used to sit there giving no sign anything had happened -- easy to tap again, thinking the first tap hadn't registered, which quietly kicked off a second, identical request in the background. The button now visibly disables and says "Writing…" the moment it's tapped, so a second tap can't fire, and switches back to a working state on its own whether the episode comes back successfully or the request fails.
A button sized for a finger, not a cursorThe stop button looked fine but measured smaller than every other tappable control in this player -- easy to miss, easy to catch the edge of something else instead. It now matches the same minimum touch size used everywhere else in this app, without changing how it looks.
A button that looked alive when it wasn'tPicking the personalized episode type left "play all domains" sitting there in its normal, fully-tappable color, but tapping it genuinely did nothing -- a per-domain queue doesn't mean anything for an episode that isn't about any one domain. It now visibly fades the moment that selection makes it inert, the same way every other unavailable button in this app already does, instead of quietly ignoring the tap.
A note that used to only tell half the truthAn episode built from real progress -- the personalized type, but also a domain overview pitched to actual accuracy, or a mistakes episode built from specific missed questions -- was only ever labeled as time-sensitive when it happened to be the personalized type specifically. The other three could just as easily go stale as real study continues, with nothing said about it. Now any episode genuinely built from real data carries the same honest note, whichever type it is.
Listening while doing something else, actuallyA podcast episode is meant to keep playing while attention moves elsewhere -- that's the entire premise of listening rather than reading. But switching to any other tab was quietly killing the audio, the same cleanup step that correctly clears a flashcard's old narration when a new card appears also firing on a podcast it had nothing to do with. Background playback now genuinely survives moving around the app, and still stops the instant something else asks to speak, or the person taps stop themselves.
One voice explaining, versus two people actually talkingA single voice reading a script -- however well-written -- still sounds like being read to. What research into how AI podcast tools actually work turned up is that the realism comes less from voice quality and more from structure: two hosts genuinely trading turns, one asking what the other explains, reacting instead of just narrating. Domain overviews, formulas, and mistakes episodes are now written as that kind of exchange and read aloud by two distinct voices when the device offers more than one, with the transcript itself showing who's talking. The personalized episode stays as it was, a tutor speaking directly to the student -- a different, equally deliberate kind of episode, not an oversight.
Saying "IRA" instead of spelling out an acronym that isn't a wordA device's built-in voice has never seen "QDRO" or "401(k)" and has no real way to know that one is said as a word and the other letter by letter -- left alone, it guesses, and the guess is often wrong in a way that's immediately, jarringly obvious. A running list of exactly how this domain's real acronyms are actually said out loud now gets applied right before anything is spoken, invisibly -- the transcript on screen still reads "QDRO," only the audio underneath changes.
Whoever's voice sounds best to you, not just to an algorithmVoice quality varies enormously by device, and what sounds natural to one person can grate on another -- there was never a way to do anything about that beyond hoping the automatic pick landed well. A Voice section in Settings now lists every voice actually available on this device, with a Preview button to hear each one before choosing, for the single narrator and separately for each of the two podcast hosts. Left alone, the automatic picks keep working exactly as before.
A question actually sounds like oneA device's built-in voice is a genuinely different, less expressive technology than a large voice model -- no amount of tuning turns one into the other, and being upfront about that matters more than pretending otherwise. But within what a single rate and pitch value per sentence can express, there was real room left unused: every sentence got the exact same flat treatment regardless of what it actually was. A question now lifts slightly in pitch, an exclamation gets a touch more energy, and a sentence trailing into "..." or a dash slows down instead of rushing to the next thought -- small, honest adjustments layered on top of the natural human variation already there, not a substitute for what a real neural voice does.
A preview that used to leave the podcast talking to no oneTrying out a voice in Settings while an episode was already playing in the background correctly interrupted the audio to speak the sample -- but the podcast's own controls never found out. The play button kept showing pause, the status kept saying "Playing..." forever, even though nothing of the episode would ever advance or finish again. Previewing a voice now properly tells the podcast it's stopped first, so its controls honestly reflect that instead of quietly lying about what's actually happening.
Reading a label even when it's not written exactly as expectedThe two-host format depends on the AI writing "HOST1:" and "HOST2:" at the start of each line, and it reliably does -- but "Host 1:" with a space is a perfectly reasonable thing for language model output to write too, and the original check for the label didn't recognize that variant at all, which risked a whole episode reading its own speaker labels aloud instead of splitting into a real back-and-forth. It now recognizes both forms the same way.
A dropdown that used to wait for nobodyA device's list of available voices doesn't always exist the instant a page loads -- some browsers hand it over gradually, after the fact. Opening Settings before that finished used to leave the voice pickers sitting there completely empty, with nothing to choose from, and no reason for them to ever change even once the real list showed up seconds later. The dropdowns now always show a working default immediately, and quietly fill themselves in the moment the device's actual voices become available, without needing the page closed and reopened.
One list, not three copies of the same listWhich domains the tutor is allowed to offer for a quiz, new practice material, or a podcast episode was written out by hand in three separate places, each one a small chance to drift out of sync with the real eight domains this app actually has, or with each other. All three now point at the same underlying list directly, so there's exactly one place that knows what the domains are.
Not leaving a stopped conversation's cast list lying aroundWhen a two-host episode stops, whether by finishing on its own or being told to stop, which two voices were reading it doesn't actually mean anything anymore. It was quietly being left behind anyway -- harmless today only because nothing happens to check it while nothing is playing, which is exactly the kind of leftover that turns into a real problem the next time this part of the code changes. It's now cleared out the moment playback genuinely ends, the same way everything else tied to that session already was.
Saying out loud that something changed, not just showing it"Playing...", "Paused.", "Written just now" -- these update visually the instant playback state changes, which is all a sighted person needs. Someone using a screen reader got none of that unless they happened to manually navigate back to check, since ordinary page text doesn't announce itself when it changes. Those two specific status messages now do, without touching the transcript itself -- a whole episode announcing itself sentence by sentence during playback would bury someone in noise rather than help them.
Getting rid of the one you don't want, not everything at onceAn episode you generated by accident, or one that's genuinely gone stale, used to have exactly one way out: wiping every saved episode along with it, or living with it forever. Each one in the library now has its own delete, with a confirmation first since regenerating it later means writing it again from scratch. Deleting the one currently playing stops it cleanly rather than leaving it running on borrowed time, and deleting whatever's currently selected on the main card correctly flips the button back to "Generate" instead of quietly offering to "regenerate" something that no longer exists.
Why you got it wrong, spelled out one keystroke at a timeGetting a math question wrong in an adaptive session used to leave the same kind of explanation as any other question -- a paragraph of reasoning, useful, but not the same as watching the actual keystrokes that get to the right number. The sixteen genuinely computational questions in the bank -- present value, future value, tax brackets, debt ratios, bond yields, and the rest -- now offer an exact, verified walkthrough on a wrong answer specifically: which numbers go where, which calculator keys to press for the ones that are true time-value-of-money problems, plain arithmetic steps for the ones that aren't. Scoped deliberately to adaptive sessions, where this was actually asked for.
A feature the tutor didn't know existedThe AI tutor already knew, in real detail, about the separate TVM calculator tool -- current tier, most common setup mistake, all of it. It had no idea the "Show calculator steps" button on regular math questions existed at all, so a student asking the tutor about a math question they'd just missed would have gotten a generic answer instead of being pointed at the exact, pre-verified walkthrough sitting right there in the app. The tutor now knows both exist and, deliberately, knows they're different things.
Not just the sixteen that happened to be written by handThe sixteen calculator-walkthrough questions were all hand-written into the original bank, but the AI question generator was already, separately, capable of writing genuinely computational questions of its own -- it just had no way to attach a walkthrough to one even when it wrote one. It now can: when a freshly generated question genuinely requires working through a calculation, the walkthrough comes back with it, checked the same way everything else the AI writes gets checked before it's trusted, so this isn't limited to a fixed set that stops growing.
Knowing which kind of "missed it again" this isThe tutor already sees when the same wrong answer gets picked on the same question more than once -- a real, specific misconception, not a one-off slip -- and it already knew the calculator-steps feature existed. What it couldn't do was connect the two: nothing told it that a particular recurring miss was on a genuine calculation with an exact walkthrough sitting right there, versus a conceptual question needing a different kind of explanation. It now knows which is which, for both a repeated miss and a single recent one.
One real calculator, not a generic stand-inThe four time-value-of-money walkthroughs were originally written the way calculator instructions get written by default -- a "compute" key pressed before the answer, "I/Y" for the interest key -- conventions that belong to a TI BA II Plus, not the HP 10bII+ this app and its tutor are actually built around. The HP 10bII+ has no separate compute key at all; you press the answer's own key directly. Its interest key is labeled I/YR. And it quietly defaults to 12 payments a year from the factory, which would give a genuinely wrong answer on every one of these annual-rate problems if left unchecked -- so each walkthrough now says so explicitly, rather than assuming it away.
Looking for an indicator that was never going to appearTwo of the four calculator walkthroughs are genuine annuities, and getting BEGIN versus END wrong there produces a different, wrong answer even with every other number entered correctly -- so each now says explicitly to confirm End mode, the setting an ordinary annuity actually requires. The genuinely easy way to get this wrong isn't picking the wrong mode -- it's not knowing there's no "END" to look for at all; only "BEGIN" ever shows on the display, and its absence is what End mode looks like. The other two walkthroughs are pure lump sums with no payment involved, where this setting does nothing at all -- so each says that plainly too, rather than leaving it an open question.
One clear action per step, not an outlier paragraphAdding the P/YR check and the End-mode confirmation to the two annuity walkthroughs, on top of everything already there, left one step doing three jobs at once -- explaining why there's no "END" indicator, giving the actual keystroke, and re-arguing why this problem needs that mode in the first place. Every other step in the sequence is one clear action in one sentence; that one had quietly become a paragraph. The reasoning now lives in the opening line that already introduces the problem, and the check itself is back to a single, scannable instruction like the eight steps around it.
A mistake the tool caught but never actually rememberedThe TVM walkthrough tool already knew, in the moment, when someone tried to solve a problem in the wrong BEGIN/END mode -- it blocked the answer and explained exactly what to fix. What it never did was count that as a setup mistake the way it counts mixing up a sign or entering a rate as a decimal, so it couldn't move someone's difficulty tier the way those do, and the tutor could never learn this was someone's actual recurring pattern. It's tracked the same way as the others now, automatically picked up by the same code that already reports whichever mistake shows up most.
Two explanations of the same calculation that could quietly disagreeAsking for a simpler explanation, or having an explanation graded through teaching it back, never told the AI what the verified calculator steps for that question actually were -- it worked from its own general knowledge instead. For most questions that's fine. For the sixteen genuine calculations, it meant the AI could describe the exact process differently than the walkthrough sitting right next to it, since a financial calculator question defaults to TI BA II Plus habits like a compute key that don't exist here. Both features now see the app's own verified steps directly, so a math explanation can't quietly contradict itself two features apart.
The same four-word instruction, spelled out three separate times"Every TVM key except the one being solved for" is a single idea, but it was written out as its own small piece of logic in three different places in the code -- once to check whether everything else was filled in, once to report how much progress had been made, once to validate the practice-problem data itself. None of the three ever disagreed with each other, but three separate copies of the same idea is three places a future change could quietly stop matching. It's one shared instruction now, used in all three places, so there's exactly one definition of "the other four keys" to ever update.
A list of what to actually do, not another summary of how it's goingThe detailed diagnosis already exists to answer "how am I doing" -- readiness, pacing, calibration, patterns, all synthesized into a few paragraphs meant to be read in the app. A study guide answers a genuinely different question: "what, specifically, do I do next?" So instead of another version of the same percentages, it names the actual unchecked subtopics in your weakest domains, the actual key numbers tied to them, the actual questions where you keep picking the same wrong answer, and the actual calculations you've missed -- built to print or save as a PDF and take somewhere the app isn't open. It stays quiet about domain weakness until there's enough real answers behind it to mean something; before that, "weakest domain" is just which domain counts most on the exam, not yet a real signal about you.
A page that existed, as far as the tutor was concerned, nowhereEvery other major tool in this app -- the podcast, the TVM calculator, starting a session -- has a direct way for the tutor to open it for you when you ask. The study guide launched without that, so asking the tutor for one would have gotten a shrug, not the guide. It's wired in now the same way as the others: ask for a study guide, or something concrete to review before exam day, and the tutor can open it directly instead of just describing what you could go find yourself.
The same six subtopics, forever, every time you opened itNothing in the guide's first version ever changed which specific items it showed -- the same starting slice of a static list, pulled the exact same way whether it was the first time or the fiftieth. Open it daily through a study period and it would have quietly gone stale, showing identical subtopics and numbers long after you'd already absorbed them. It now advances through the list by the calendar day -- stable if you open it twice in one sitting, genuinely different a week from now -- and trimmed each section down and cut long question text to an ellipsis, so a page meant to be scanned in a couple of minutes doesn't slowly turn into another full page of text. A single line at the top now also just says which one thing matters most today, rather than leaving that judgment to whoever's reading.
Reading the number again versus trying to remember it firstA 2021 meta-analysis spanning 242 studies and over 169,000 people found the same result an earlier landmark review had: testing yourself on something beats rereading it, by a wide margin -- and the techniques students actually reach for most, rereading and highlighting, are the ones the evidence rates weakest. Each key number in the guide is now written as a question first, with the answer a beat behind it, so the eye has to pause before it lands -- the same shape as a real flashcard, just on paper. Every number also carries a short memory hook, mostly built by tying it to another number already on the page (the family HSA limit is double the self-only one; the couple's estate exemption is exactly double the individual's) rather than invented wordplay, since anchoring new information to something already known is what actually makes an association stick.
A real answer, filed under the wrong kind of questionAsking the tutor to look something up only ever searched the glossary -- fine for a defined term, but the RMD age and the FDIC limit aren't glossary entries, they're figures in a separate reference list the search never touched. Two out of three specific numbers tested came back "nothing matched," even though the actual answer was sitting in the app the whole time. Looking something up now falls back to that same figures list when the glossary comes up empty, and hands back the number itself along with its memory hook directly -- not a redirect to go find it, an answer.
Seven shortcuts, and the newest tool wasn't one of themThe tutor tab lists exactly what it can do -- start a session, open the calculator, look something up, generate practice, set an exam date, make a podcast -- as a row of one-tap buttons, one for every major tool the tutor has. The study guide had existed as a real, working tool since the turn it was built, callable the moment someone typed the right words, but it was the one tool with no button in that row. It's genuinely just as capable of being asked for in a sentence as any of the others, but a feature only as discoverable as someone happening to phrase the request correctly isn't really discoverable at all.
Only one side of the pair knew there were two of them"Show me my weak spots" could genuinely mean either the progress breakdown or the study guide -- both are, in a real sense, about weak spots. The study guide's own description already explained how it differs from checking progress, but the progress tool's description never mentioned the study guide back -- so the distinction only existed from one direction, not both. Whichever one the tutor happens to consider first now correctly points to the other when the request sounds like it could mean either.
One door that was never told which calculator this house usesA full sweep for every remaining "CPT" or bare "I/Y" in the app turned up nothing wrong -- every calculator walkthrough, every AI-generation instruction, every tutor explanation already correctly said HP 10bII+. Only one place was never actually told: the spoken podcast episode about formulas, which asks for a worked example "the way you'd talk someone through it on a whiteboard" -- true, and mostly keeps things in plain math, but nothing stopped it from naturally reaching for "press CPT" the way most people describe a financial calculator, if a time-value problem came up. It's a low-odds gap, not a live one, but it's the one door in the entire app that was still unlocked after everything else got checked.
Being told which calculator to use didn't mean it always listenedEvery static walkthrough in this app was hand-verified against the HP 10bII+, and the AI question generator was explicitly instructed to follow the same conventions when it writes a new calculation question of its own. Instructed isn't the same as guaranteed -- a real, generated question surfaced with exactly the TI BA II Plus habits this whole effort was built to eliminate: a bare I/Y instead of I/YR, a compute step this calculator doesn't have. Worse, a generated question is saved once and reused rather than rewritten each time it comes up, so a bad one wouldn't just appear once -- it would stay wrong indefinitely. New calculation questions are now checked for these specific patterns before anything gets saved, and existing saved questions are checked and cleaned the same way the moment the app loads, so this doesn't require deleting the question and starting over -- just the walkthrough that was wrong.
The same mistake could happen anywhere an AI writes something and it gets savedThe real bug wasn't really about one question -- it was a pattern: telling an AI to follow a convention doesn't guarantee it will, and if that response gets cached instead of regenerated fresh each time, a slip becomes permanent. That pattern was checked everywhere it could plausibly repeat. The formulas podcast episode asks for a spoken example and, like the question generator, only gets told about calculator keys as a fallback -- its saved output is now checked the same way before anything is cached. Flashcards turned out to be safe by construction: a one-sentence, twenty-five-word definition has no room for a keystroke sequence to begin with. Teach-back never saves anything at all, so nothing there can get stuck regardless. The one other real gap was "explain this more simply," which saves its answer per question just like the podcast does -- now checked the same way, with a plain notice in its place if a bad one comes back, rather than silently keeping it forever.
A button offering to differ from an explanation that was never actually givenAfter the guard catches a bad response and replaces it with a plain notice, the button underneath it used to relabel itself "Try a different explanation" anyway -- the same label it earns after a real one succeeds. Nothing was technically broken, but the wording quietly implied a first explanation had already been delivered when what actually happened was closer to a do-over. It now stays "Explain this more simply" until an explanation genuinely goes through, so the label only ever offers something different from an explanation that was actually there.
The guard covered one episode type and missed the one right next to itThe formulas episode explicitly asks for a worked calculation, so that's where the calculator-convention guard went first. But the mistakes episode does something just as likely to reach for a calculator key without ever being asked to: when a student has genuinely missed one of the real calculation questions, it's told to explain "how to think about it correctly next time" -- reasonable instruction, and just as capable of drifting into calculator language as a formula walkthrough is, with nothing in place to catch it if it did. It's checked the same way now, only when a genuine calculation question is actually among what was missed, with the same guard against ever saving what comes back wrong.
A well-built engine nobody was ever shownUnderneath both flashcards and regular questions sits a genuine, correctly-built Leitner spaced-repetition system -- answer something right and it steps further away before showing up again (a day, then three, then a week, up to a month); miss it and it resets to due immediately. The code comment explaining it even cites the same research -- Cepeda et al., Dunlosky et al. -- that a real study guide should. None of that ever reached the actual screen: the flashcard tab said cards were "ordered by what you need most" and left it there, and the adaptive session said questions were pulled from "what's new or due" without ever explaining what due meant or why it mattered. Both now name the mechanism directly and explain the growing gap between repeats in plain terms, since the research is clear that people trust and stick with a system they actually understand, not just one that happens to work.
The exact moment a real effect was happening, and nothing said soBeing confidently wrong and then corrected produces unusually durable learning -- a genuinely well-documented finding -- but only if the correction happens again soon, which is exactly what quietly queuing that question for early re-placement was already doing. The one message that ever appears at this exact moment only said the confidence and the answer didn't match, true but incomplete: it never mentioned that this specific moment was about to be used to someone's advantage. It now says both -- what happened, and what the app is about to do about it -- verified against the actual, real placement in the very next session it produces, not just the message's own wording.
A good explanation that pushed the actual task off the screenExplaining the spaced-repetition system in full made the flashcard tab's opening text seven lines long -- accurate, worth knowing, and enough on a phone screen to push the card itself, the thing someone actually opened this tab to do, mostly out of view without scrolling. The explanation didn't get cut; it moved behind the same tap-to-expand pattern the app already uses for its detailed diagnosis, so the short version stays up front and the full one is still there the moment anyone wants it. The card that's flipped and rated dozens of times a session is back where it was -- immediately visible the instant the tab opens.
Two more techniques from the same research, checked against the full listDunlosky et al.'s 2013 review didn't rank ten study techniques evenly -- practice testing and spaced repetition topped the list, already built into how this guide works and rotates. Two more, rated moderate rather than top-tier but still genuinely worth using, hadn't been added yet: asking why a rule exists instead of just what it says, and deliberately mixing two domains together rather than drilling one at a time -- both now named directly in the guide rather than left implicit. Worth being honest about the other side of that same research too: arbitrary keyword mnemonics rated low utility, which is a different thing from what this guide's number hooks actually do -- tying a figure to another real, related number already on the page, not inventing an unrelated image to hang it on.
A citation list that already existed, just nowhere near the thing it was backing upThe app has carried a genuinely rigorous "How this is designed" section for a while -- Dunlosky et al. by name, Bjork & Bjork on desirable difficulties, Bandura on mastery experiences, Butterfield & Metcalfe on hypercorrection, real named studies, not vague appeals to "science says." The study guide kept applying that research without ever pointing to where it actually came from. Rather than copy that whole body of citations onto a page meant to be printed, the guide now has one real, working link: tap it and the guide closes, the app switches to where that documentation already lives, and opens it expanded. The evidence was always there -- it just wasn't reachable from the one page built to put it into practice.
A whole tracked system the guide never once looked at154 flashcards, each with their own real Leitner-tracked history of what's actually been marked known versus still learning, sat completely untouched by a page whose entire purpose is naming specific things worth reviewing. The guide pulled from questions, the syllabus, and key numbers, and never once asked the flashcard system what it already knew about where someone was genuinely struggling. It now does -- surfacing terms actually attempted and marked still learning, not just anything unseen, in the same weak domains the rest of the guide already focuses on, framed the same question-first way as everything else here. Checked afterward that a term someone's already gotten comfortable with correctly stays off the list, and that the page still holds to two printed pages with every section populated at once.
A page meant to travel alone that quietly assumed it wouldn'tPrinted the night before an exam, a page shouldn't need the app it came from. Two spots quietly did: the calculations section named a question and told you to go find "Show calculator steps" back where you'd printed this from, and the recurring-mistakes section gave the correct answer with no explanation of why it was correct, assuming that reasoning lived somewhere else. Both now carry everything themselves -- the full worked steps for each calculation printed right on the page, and the actual reasoning behind every correct answer -- and a line about "checking your notes" that quietly implied outside material got reworded to something that doesn't. Trimmed from three calculations to two to make room without pushing past two pages.
What the people who write official study guides for a living actually doPrinceton's own teaching center describes exam prep as rehearsal, not just review -- and specifically recommends periodically closing your cheat sheet and trying to reproduce it from memory, since the gap between what you can reconstruct and what's actually on the page is its own diagnostic. UNC's learning center teaches something similar for course content: outline everything you remember covering before you ever look at the syllabus again, top-down, then check what you missed. Neither was in this guide. Both are now, placed where they actually apply -- reconstructing a domain's subtopics before reading the list, and periodically trying to rebuild the whole page from memory across the repeated reviews this was built for.
Half a sentence, missing the half that made it mean anythingReal CFP prep providers specifically call out case-study questions as their own category worth separate practice -- several items bundled around one detailed client scenario, requiring a different mental approach than a standalone question. A recurring-mistake or missed-calculation question drawn from one of these never carried that scenario into the guide, just the bare question stem: "given Robert's 6-year retirement timeline," with no Robert, no timeline, no way to know what was actually being asked. Both sections now carry the scenario along with the question when one exists. Separately, cross-checking a university CFP program's own materials confirmed something worth knowing outright: instructors teach exclusively on the HP 10bII+ because it's the one calculator every major CFP textbook publisher gives full keystroke coverage for -- independent confirmation, from inside the industry, that this wasn't an arbitrary pick.
A description of the guide that stopped updating when the guide didn'tThe tutor decides whether to open the study guide based on one paragraph describing what it contains -- and that paragraph was written before the flashcard section, the inline calculator steps, and the scenario fix existed. It still only mentioned subtopics, numbers, and questions, so a student asking specifically about flashcard terms or a genuinely take-it-with-you page had no obvious signal pointing the tutor here. Updated to describe what the guide actually is now, not what it was when the tool was first wired up -- including the self-contained, no-need-to-reopen-the-app quality that's the whole reason a recent request asked for this in the first place.
One clock, timing everything from a one-line answer to a five-question batchEvery AI request in this app shared the same 45-second limit before it gave up and called it a timeout -- whether that request was a short "explain this more simply" or a full batch of five new questions, each with four rationales and possibly a full calculator walkthrough, a request that's grown substantially heavier over the course of this work as more was asked of it. Sized for the small ones, that limit was cutting off the large ones mid-generation -- not a network problem, a request that was still legitimately working when the clock ran out on it. The wait now scales with how much was actually asked for: the floor stays where it was for anything small, and a real question-generation batch gets genuinely enough room to finish, capped so a truly dead connection still fails visibly instead of hanging forever.
The same check written twice, and the same question shown twiceTwo kinds of duplication, found by actually looking for them rather than assuming there weren't any. The check for wrong calculator wording in AI-written prose was typed out identically in two separate places -- the podcast guard and the simplify guard -- rather than written once and shared, the same kind of drift a shared helper had already fixed elsewhere in this app. And a question that's both a repeated wrong-answer pattern and a currently-missed calculation could show up twice on the same printed page, its full stem appearing once under each heading. Fixed the first by consolidating both checks into one function. Fixed the second by merging the calculator steps directly into the recurring-mistake entry when a question qualifies for both, rather than either duplicating the question or dropping the steps -- confirmed the page still holds to two pages afterward, and actually got shorter since the duplicate stem is gone.
What "how many tokens do I have left" can honestly be answered withChecked this directly against Anthropic's own materials before building anything: there's no API that reports remaining account balance or credits -- a real, filed request for exactly this asked Anthropic to add one, and a direct attempt to query it returns a 404. The only place that number genuinely lives is the account's own billing page. What every response does honestly carry is how many tokens that single request used, so this app now keeps a running total of its own usage -- clearly labeled as tokens spent, not tokens remaining, with a direct link to the one place the real answer lives. Building this surfaced a genuine bug along the way: the running total was meant to survive a progress reset, since API usage and study progress are different things, but the code that would have actually preserved it had never been written -- caught by testing the claim directly instead of trusting the intention behind it.
Reading it fresh, instead of trusting that the last five fixes added upEvery change up to this point had made some individual piece of the guide better, and it still wasn't landing as valuable -- which meant the problem was never in any one piece. Reading the whole thing rendered, in order, the way someone actually would: nearly a third of it was explanation of how the guide works, repeated in full every single time it's opened, and one entire section was bare topic names with no information in them at all -- "Retirement Savings & Income Planning: Social Security and Medicare planning," and nothing else. That's not a small paper cut; on a page meant to be scanned in a couple of minutes, dead weight and empty labels were most of what was on it.
