The explanation now lives one tap away instead of on the page itself, subtopics shrank to what that section can honestly support, and the room that freed up went to the sections carrying real, verified substance -- more key numbers with hooks, more flashcard terms, the same page length with a lot less of it saying nothing.
A page that reads the calendar it's actually sitting inThe app has always known how many days are left before the exam -- it's shown right on the Exam Day tab -- but the study guide never once looked at it, generating the identical mix of content whether the exam was two months out or two days away. Broad subtopic review is a reasonable use of time with two months left; it's a much weaker bet with two days left, when nailing down specific, directly testable figures pays off more per minute spent. Inside the final week, the guide now genuinely reads that clock and changes what it shows: subtopics drop out entirely, key numbers expand to fill the room that frees up, and a line at the top says plainly why, rather than the shift happening silently. Checked the actual output at three real points -- no date set, two months out, three days out -- and confirmed each one behaves differently in exactly the way it's supposed to, not just that the code compiles.
Instant feedback that still had to be scrolled up to findAnswering a question here already does everything right the moment you tap: the correct answer highlights, your own pick shows why it was wrong, every other choice explains itself too, and a question you'd missed before and finally got right says so specifically. All of that happens synchronously, with nothing to wait for. What it didn't do was make sure any of it landed somewhere visible. The feedback message renders above the answer choices, and on a real phone screen, someone who'd scrolled down to reach the third or fourth option would have that message appear entirely off-screen above where they were looking -- correct in the data the instant they tapped, invisible until they scrolled back up to go find it. It now scrolls itself into view the moment it appears, and only far enough to actually be seen -- doing nothing at all when it was already on screen, so nothing jumps around for no reason.
The tool already knew the answer -- it just wasn't telling anyone until the very endTapping BEG/END used to do exactly one thing: flip a setting and move a small annunciator, nothing more. The calculator itself already knew, internally, whether a given problem actually needed BEGIN or END mode -- that check existed, but it only ever ran after every other value had been entered correctly and the solve key was pressed, the very last step of the whole process. Since setting BEG/END mode is typically the first thing done on a real TVM problem, before a single number goes in, someone could get it wrong at the very start and have no way of knowing until they'd finished everything else. The toggle now says, immediately, whether the mode just chosen actually matches the problem in front of them -- confirmed both directions, and confirmed it correctly says nothing at all for lump-sum problems where the setting genuinely doesn't apply, rather than offering a match or mismatch verdict that wouldn't mean anything.
A comment that described a bug fix that was never actually writtenThe code that keeps recently-seen questions from resurfacing had a comment explaining its own goal in plain words: a question shouldn't come back "within a session or two" of being answered. The actual number sitting right below that comment only covered 12 questions -- less than a single 15-question session. Checked directly rather than trusting the comment's word for it: the second question of a session, tracked forward, was genuinely still eligible to reappear in the very next one. Fixed to a window that actually covers close to two full sessions, and confirmed an entire just-finished session is now genuinely excluded from the one right after it, not just most of it.

Separately, checked the "too easy" half of the same complaint the same way -- not by reading the weighting logic and assuming it worked, but by simulating a student who answers every single question correctly across six full sessions and counting what difficulty they actually got shown. The real number was 22% hard questions, even at a perfect record -- the weighting was pushing in the right direction, just nowhere near hard enough given how thin the hard-question pool already is. Increased how strongly sustained top performance pulls toward that harder material, left the struggling and moderate tiers exactly as they were, and reran the identical simulation: 38% hard overall, climbing to 60% by the fourth and fifth sessions as the system had more evidence to work with. A second simulation of a student answering every question wrong confirmed that tier is untouched -- still solidly easy-leaning, as it should be.
A session that vanished the moment the app closedGet eight questions into an adaptive session -- eight real, scored answers -- and close the app before finishing, and every trace of it was gone. Not lowered, not marked incomplete: gone, with no memory it had ever happened, forcing a full restart from question one. Fixed by saving exactly where things stood after every single answer, not just when a new question appeared -- an early version of this only captured state at that later point, which meant the very last answer before closing could still vanish, caught by testing the exact "closed right after answering, before tapping Next" case directly rather than assuming a save hook alone was enough. A quiet return now offers to pick back up at the real next question with the real running score, or start clean if that's preferred -- deliberately scoped to the untimed modes only, since resuming a running exam clock safely raises questions -- what should happen to time that passed while the app was closed -- worth answering carefully rather than guessing at. Moved to the very top of the tab afterward, since something time-sensitive enough to say "you have unfinished work" shouldn't need to be scrolled past several other cards to be seen.
A "start fresh" button that assumed the door behind it was already openTesting the resume feature's other button -- "start fresh instead" -- against an artificial version of the interruption it's meant to handle turned up a real gap: the function correctly discarded the leftover session, but never checked whether the actual "start a new session" options were visible underneath it, only assuming they already were. In every real path checked, they genuinely are -- a true reload always resets that first, so nothing broken has ever actually reached anyone. But a function that discards someone's option to resume shouldn't also depend on an assumption about what's already on screen to avoid leaving them with nothing. It now makes sure those options are actually there itself, rather than trusting that something else already handled it.
A walkthrough that kept teaching the question that was no longer thereAnswer a math question once, and see it again, and this app already writes a genuinely new version -- different numbers, same underlying concept -- specifically so it doesn't feel like the same question twice. What it never did was tell the AI that a walkthrough existed at all: the instruction asked for a new question and never mentioned the calculator steps sitting right there on the original. A variant showing $25,000 at 8% for 12 years kept the old steps verbatim -- "enter 10,000," "enter 7," the previous version's numbers, instructing a calculation that had nothing to do with what was now on screen. Fixed by asking for new steps matching the new numbers whenever the original had any, running those through the same wrong-calculator-convention check used everywhere else in this app, and clearing the walkthrough entirely -- not silently keeping the old one -- if what comes back is missing, malformed, or uses the wrong calculator's conventions. Verified all three outcomes directly: a good response gets used, a missing one clears cleanly, and a wrong one gets caught and cleared exactly like it would anywhere else.
A is right almost twice as often as chance alone would predictCounted the actual correct-answer position across all 401 questions rather than guessing at whether a pattern was real: A was correct 41.6% of the time, D only 17.2% -- a genuinely random distribution should land close to 25% each. That's not a subtle statistical footnote; it's a pattern real enough to notice while answering, and one that rewards recognizing "A" over actually knowing the material, in a way that wouldn't transfer to the real exam at all. Fixed by reshuffling each question's choices -- and its rationale, kept in exact lockstep -- fresh every time it's placed into a session, rather than rewriting 401 hand-written questions directly and risking new errors in the process. Checked first that no rationale anywhere refers to a choice by its screen position rather than its content (a few used "above" and "below" in ordinary comparative or tax-term senses, not one was a positional reference), confirmed the actual correct answer's text always survives reshuffling intact regardless of where it lands, and confirmed the same fix reaches a generated variant's freshly-written choices too, not just the original static bank. Rerun across 40 real sessions, the shown distribution came back at roughly 26/23/24/28 -- genuinely balanced, not just theoretically so.
A calculator that could never actually solve for the rateSixteen TVM problems, and every one of them asked for N, present value, payment, or future value -- never once the rate itself, the thing a real exam question asking "what return would this take" genuinely needs practice with. The reason ran deeper than a missing problem: the solver itself had no case for it at all, silently returning nothing, because unlike the other four variables the rate has no plug-in formula -- it takes an iterative search, the same thing a real calculator does internally when you press its rate key. Built that properly with bisection search, verified it against three known answers including an annuity due, and confirmed it correctly gives up rather than returning a wrong number when no valid rate could exist. Writing the walkthrough surfaced two more real bugs behind it -- the intermediate steps displayed literal "NaN" text on screen, and the final answer showed as a dollar figure instead of a percentage -- both fixed and reverified clean. Caught two mistakes of its own along the way before any of it shipped: the new problem was pasted into the wrong array entirely at first, parsing fine but silently invisible until the actual count was checked rather than assumed; and its difficulty label initially called it an annuity when its payment is genuinely zero throughout, which would have told a student to expect a recurring payment that was never there.
Starting on the length bias, for real this timeFlagged two turns ago as real but too large to safely bulk-edit -- 232 of 401 questions with a correct answer noticeably longer than its distractors, on average about 26% longer, a pattern someone could genuinely learn to lean on without knowing the material. Started with the 30 worst individual cases by ratio, writing genuinely expanded wrong answers -- more plausible detail added to what stays clearly, factually wrong -- while leaving every correct answer's own text completely untouched. Applying it directly to the source revealed two real bugs in the method itself before anything got written: the first pass assumed single-quoted strings when the actual file uses JSON-style double-quoted ones, and even after that fix, two individual replacements failed silently because Python's JSON encoder escapes an em dash and a trademark symbol differently than how those characters literally sit in the file -- caught by checking the actual replacement count rather than assuming success, not proceeding until all 90 came back clean with zero touched more than once. One distractor's exact wording turned out to be shared verbatim between two unrelated questions about the AMT; widened the anchor to that question's own neighboring text so only the intended one was touched. This batch's own average ratio dropped from about 1.73 to 1.04 -- close to genuinely even. The other roughly 200 affected questions remain for later batches.
Fixing one tell by accidentally writing a different oneSecond batch of 29 went through cleanly on the first automated pass -- the duplicate-string handling built after the first batch's manual fixes caught the one case that needed it without stopping to ask. But the app's own built-in quality checker, run afterward rather than just trusted to still be clean, flagged a question that hadn't been touched by anything structural -- one of this batch's own rewrites. Expanding a short distractor with more plausible detail had, in two places on the same question, reached for words like "must" and "completely" to fill the space -- exactly the kind of absolute, no-exceptions language experienced test-takers learn to read as a tell in the other direction. Reworded both without losing the length balance the batch was written to fix, then re-ran the check against the full 401-question bank rather than just the one question -- confirmed zero flagged, not assumed from the one fix.
Checking the whole bank before calling it done, not after being told toThird batch of 29 -- one skipped again for being a numeric-answer question the same length-expansion approach doesn't genuinely apply to. Counting entries against the intended list before writing anything caught a question missing from the batch entirely, left out by hand before any file was touched. Having been caught out once already by trusting a batch was clean without checking, this time the full 401-question bank was run through the app's own quality check before calling anything finished, not after a report came back. It found one -- a distractor where "only" had been carried over unchanged from the original wording while everything around it got expanded, missed the first time through because attention was on the words being added, not the ones already sitting there. Reworded it, then checked the whole bank again rather than just that one question, and confirmed genuinely zero flagged this time.
Reading all 88 rewrites back, not just testing that they loadedAsked to make sure everything held up, so all three batches of edits got read start to finish as actual sentences, not just checked for whether the app still ran -- correctness checks and grammar checks measure different things, and only one of them was being run consistently. The content itself held up well. The grammar didn't, in a pattern spanning about 46 distractors across roughly 20 questions: many stems end in "to:" expecting a bare verb to complete the sentence -- "designed to provide," "used to reduce" -- and a large share of these rewrites had reached for "-ing" instead, reading as "designed to providing," which doesn't complete the sentence at all. Traced it to a habit of leaning on "-ing" as a safe-feeling sentence starter without checking what each specific stem actually required grammatically -- stems ending in "refers to" or "requires attention to" genuinely accept either form, so not everything flagged by a first pass needed changing, and each case got checked against its own stem before anything was touched. Fixed every genuine mismatch found, including a couple that predated this round of edits entirely, then reran the full quality check against all 401 questions again -- zero flagged, confirmed rather than assumed from the fixes alone.
A guide that changed every day, when the point was to see the same thing enough times to remember itTold directly that this guide was too personalized and needed to be something worth reviewing over and over in the final days -- not a bad piece of feedback so much as a correction to an assumption baked into the design from the start. The old version pulled only from the two weakest domains, needed five answered questions before showing anything at all, and rotated which items appeared by the calendar date -- reasonable choices for a tool meant to target gaps, but working directly against a resource meant to be studied by repetition, where seeing the same material again and again is the entire mechanism. Rebuilt around that instead: every key number and the complete official syllabus, all eight domains, present from the very first time it's opened, unrotating so the fifth read-through shows the same page as the first. What earned its place from actual practice history -- recurring wrong answers, calculator walkthroughs on missed problems -- stayed, but as genuinely useful additions layered onto a comprehensive core rather than the thing the guide's whole structure depended on existing. Checked the render with zero practice history logged, the exact case that used to show an empty placeholder, and confirmed the full guide appears anyway.
What real cram sheets actually contain, checked before guessingAsked to research how established CFP review providers structure their final-week materials rather than assume the guide's shape was already right. Found a genuinely concrete, specific answer: real last-minute exam materials consistently include a dedicated formulas reference alongside the numbers that change yearly -- and CFP Board's own exam candidate handbook includes an official provided-formulas appendix, separate from the tax tables. This app already had exactly that data sitting unused -- thirteen formulas spanning CAPM, Sharpe ratio, holding period return, present and future value -- built and verified earlier in this project, never once surfaced in the guide itself. Added it as its own section, organized by domain the same way the numbers already were, placed first since the math relationships are the toolkit the numbers get plugged into. Worth being honest about scope here: this reflects what the app's own question bank draws on, not a verified line-by-line match to CFP Board's specific provided-formulas list, so it's described that way rather than overclaiming a match never actually checked. Also confirmed the domain ordering already used throughout -- conduct, general, risk, investment, tax, retirement, estate, psychology -- is the same A-through-H sequence CFP Board's own materials use, and checked that exam-day logistics like arrival time weren't worth duplicating here since a dedicated tab already covers them.
A checklist isn't knowledge -- it's a list of things you'd need to already knowTold directly and correctly: the syllabus section wasn't actually teaching anything. It was topic names strung together with bullet separators -- "Financial planning process • Financial statements • Cash flow management" -- which only helps someone who can already explain each one, doing nothing for the person actually trying to learn it. Started writing real explanations instead: what each topic actually covers, in a few genuine sentences, not the name restated. Professional Conduct and General Principles are done this way now, all sixteen topics, with the rest of the syllabus still showing plain names until they get the same treatment in future passes -- an honest partial state rather than padding the remaining six domains with restated labels to look finished. Caught a real mistake making room for this: the first edit anchored on the line separating two data blocks and accidentally deleted it entirely, breaking the file's structure -- caught immediately by the syntax check this project runs after every change, not left for testing to find later.
Finishing what the last pass left honestly unfinishedThe previous round wrote real explanations for two domains and deliberately left the other six as plain names rather than pad them out to look complete. Finished the remaining fifty-four topics the same way -- risk management, investments, tax, retirement, estate planning, and psychology -- each with a genuine explanation of what it covers, not the topic name said back differently. Before treating any of it as done, checked that every domain's number of summaries lines up exactly with its number of actual topics, since a single mismatched count would have silently paired an explanation with the wrong topic next to it -- confirmed all eight domains match and all seventy topics genuinely have real content behind them now, not just a checklist of what to already know.
Reusing what already worked, on purpose, in a few new placesAsked to bring the same memory-hook approach already used for the 32 key numbers into more of the guide, selectively rather than everywhere. Researched whether established mnemonics already exist for the classic CFP list-type facts rather than inventing weaker ones from scratch -- found a genuinely real one for the seven-step planning process, but it used a different letter sequence than the verb-form wording this guide already used for that same list, so building a new mnemonic matching what was already written mattered more than reusing someone else's phrasing built around different words. Added nine total: the planning process, the four fiduciary duties, the six ADLs behind long-term care benefits, the own-occupation versus any-occupation distinction, systematic versus unsystematic risk, the revocable-versus-irrevocable trust trade-off, the three named behavioral biases, and two formulas people commonly blank on under time pressure, CAPM and the Sharpe ratio. Left the other topics and formulas alone rather than forcing a trick onto material that didn't genuinely need one.
Looking for a specific reference, and being honest about not finding itAsked to check a specific creator's downloadable materials before building anything, on the theory that seeing a working example beats guessing at one. That creator's own site turned out to offer an Anki flashcard deck as its actual download, not flowcharts, and directly reaching into a specific video's own description box for whatever might be linked there wasn't something these tools could actually do -- worth saying plainly rather than describing a flowchart as if it had been seen and copied when it hadn't. Built two decision diagrams instead, grounded in this project's own verified trust and entity knowledge: which trust fits a given goal, and which business entity fits a given ownership and liability picture. Visual testing caught two real layout bugs before calling either one finished -- two boxes on the entity chart genuinely overlapped each other from a coordinate that reused space already spoken for, and text ran past a box edge in two other spots. Both traced to specific coordinates and fixed, then re-checked against both the light and dark themes to confirm the colors genuinely adapt the same way the existing calculator timeline diagram already does.
Finding the real thing, once a real link existed to followA shared folder link, followed by an actual Google Drive connection, turned up what search alone genuinely couldn't reach last turn: two real AdviseWise one-pagers, retirement and tax, an entire domain condensed onto a single dense page -- comparison tables in place of prose, a compact key-ages timeline, arrow notation for cause and effect, callout boxes flagging the specific gotchas people get wrong. A genuinely different approach from the comprehensive, multi-page version already built here, not a replacement for it. Rather than rebuild everything to match a style built for a different purpose, pulled out four specific, concrete things this guide was still missing: a real mnemonic for the above-the-line deductions (HERB), the two like-kind exchange formulas this guide's own formula section had never covered despite tax being one of the most heavily tested domains, a note on the entity flowchart that LLC is frequently a distractor answer since it's a legal structure and not a tax election, and the two most commonly tested MACRS depreciation periods. Each checked against what was already here before adding it, so nothing got duplicated.
A third folder, found only by asking the tool properly the second timeA closer look at the shared folder turned up an entire subfolder missed the first pass through -- default result limits had quietly cut it off the list. Inside was a genuine AdviseWise document dedicated entirely to marital trusts, comparing credit shelter, QTIP, and QDOT trusts side by side. Getting its actual content proved genuinely difficult -- the file downloads as a large block of encoded text, and it twice came through corrupted or truncated by the handoff between tools. Used what had already come through cleanly in an earlier search result instead of continuing to fight the file itself. That surfaced two concrete, real distinctions this guide's own trust knowledge hadn't captured: a credit shelter trust trades away a second step-up in basis and has grown less common now that exemptions are both high and portable, while a QTIP trust exists for a genuinely different reason -- letting a surviving spouse keep income for life while the first spouse's own choice of final beneficiaries protects children from an earlier marriage. Caught and fixed a real mistake making that edit: a stray character sequence left over from a prior version of the sentence passed the syntax check clean while quietly corrupting the actual content underneath it, caught only by reading the resulting line itself afterward rather than trusting the check alone.
Checking the two remaining subfolders before calling the review doneWent back through the Tax and Estate Planning subfolders with an explicit page size this time, rather than assume the earlier pagination miss was isolated -- confirmed both genuinely contain just the one file already found, nothing further missed. That gave a complete, untruncated read of the tax study schedule for the first time, and it named a real, focused gap: depreciation recapture under §1245, §1250, and §1231 gets a whole dedicated study day in both the schedule and the one-pager, yet this guide's own property-transactions knowledge never covered it. Added it, along with donor-advised funds from the same schedule's charitable-deductions line. Checked the OBBBA senior deduction figure directly against several independent sources before adding it as a key number, rather than trust the one-pager's number on its own -- confirmed exactly right, $6,000 per qualifying person, temporary through 2028. Made the identical corruption mistake from last turn a second time while editing -- a stray leftover character passing the syntax check while quietly breaking the actual sentence -- caught the same way, by reading the line itself afterward, and fixed before it reached this file.
What actually worked: the user just sent the files directlyExtensive Google Drive troubleshooting -- different search queries, a permissions check, a raw URL fetch -- never resolved why several real subfolders stayed invisible to that connection while genuinely visible in the user's own browser. What worked instead was simpler: fourteen files, sent directly. That settled the access question for good and surfaced real, specific gaps across domains that had gone unnoticed until there was a document naming them plainly. Behavioral finance held the biggest one -- nineteen more biases genuinely existed beyond the three already covered, and are all here now, organized into the same four categories the source material used. Social Security eligibility gained the specific spouse, divorced-spouse, and dependent age thresholds that were missing entirely. Qualified plans gained the 10% stock-and-bond cap and the specific years-of-service figures. Professional conduct gained the actual self-reporting timeframes -- 90 days to clients, 30 to CFP Board -- and the three real options when a client needs planning but declines it. A third decision flowchart was added for IRA deductibility, tested visually before calling it finished. One more of the same corruption mistake as before slipped through mid-edit -- this time from embedded quotation marks inside a sentence rather than a leftover fragment -- caught the identical way: not trusting a clean syntax check alone, but reading the actual resulting line.
Going back through every document a second time on purpose, not assuming the first pass caught it allAsked directly to make sure nothing from the fourteen uploaded documents had been missed, so each one got checked again against what had actually been added, rather than trusting memory of the first pass. It hadn't been complete. The retirement one-pager alone was still missing Rabbi versus Secular trust taxation, the actual early-withdrawal penalty exceptions correctly grouped by account type, inherited-IRA rules, net unrealized appreciation, rollover mechanics, the Roth withdrawal ordering rules, and ISO versus NSO stock option taxation -- none of it had made it in the first time. The tax one-pager was missing the estimated-tax safe harbor percentages, the AOTC-versus-Lifetime-Learning-Credit distinction, the mid-quarter depreciation trap, Section 179 against bonus depreciation, and the counter-intuitive dual-basis rule for a gift that's lost value. The Code and Standards document was still missing the actual test for when an interaction becomes financial planning, and the verbal-versus-written disclosure rule. All of it is here now. The same quote-escaping mistake from last turn showed up twice more mid-edit; the second time, rather than guess at a fix, the exact broken character sequence was read out one character at a time to see precisely what needed to change, which is what made the actual fix reliable instead of another guess.
Two sources that were genuinely diagrams, not paragraphs waiting to happenTwo of the remaining documents -- the options matrix and the qualified plans worksheet -- were visual in the source material itself, a grid and a branching tree, not prose that happened to get formatted that way. Turning them into paragraphs the way the other documents' content had been handled would have lost the thing that made them useful in the first place: seeing the shape of the whole picture at once. Built both as actual diagrams instead, matching the visual language the trust and entity flowcharts already established. The options matrix went through two rounds of visual testing before it was right -- a first fix at labeling buyer and seller roles still ran text off the left edge of its own box, caught only by actually looking at the rendered image rather than assuming a first edit had solved it. The qualified plan tree groups plan variants together as lists inside defined-benefit and defined-contribution boxes rather than as ten separate boxes, which the original spreads wide across a full page -- a deliberate simplification to keep it legible on a narrow phone screen, plus one detail worth calling out on its own: a target benefit plan is technically a defined-contribution plan but still needs the one-time actuarial assessment defined-benefit plans require, which is exactly the kind of exception an exam question likes to test.
The genuinely last pass -- checking specific claims against the documents one at a time, not trusting the earlier summary of what got coveredAsked once more to confirm nothing from her material was still missing, so each remaining document got checked again for specific facts rather than trusting an earlier summary of what had been covered. Found five more real gaps. The Code and Standards document had a distinct three-step process for managing an actual conflict -- disclose before advice, get consent, then keep managing it on an ongoing basis -- separate from the disclosure-format rule already added, plus a whole separate foundation of baseline duties (integrity, avoiding comingled assets, honest representation of compensation) that apply regardless of whether someone is even a client yet. The retirement one-pager's Social Security section was still missing the actual benefit-amount math -- the early-claim penalty rate, the delayed-credit rate, the earnings test, how the benefit itself gets taxed, and the fact that spousal and survivor benefits use different percentages of the other person's benefit, a detail genuinely easy to mix up. Qualified charitable distributions and the 40-credit fully-insured threshold were absent entirely despite being ordinary, frequently tested facts. The same quote-escaping issue showed up a third time mid-edit, caught the same way as before, then the whole file was searched once more for that same broken pattern before calling anything finished -- this time it came back genuinely clean.
A whole fourth trust type that had been missing this entire timeThe marital trusts comparison document actually names four trust types side by side. Only three -- credit shelter, QTIP, QDOT -- had made it into this guide's knowledge or its flowchart. The marital power of appointment trust, sometimes called an A trust, was absent completely, despite being structurally the most distinct of the four: it's the one case where the surviving spouse controls where the assets ultimately go, the reverse of how a QTIP works. Added it to the written knowledge, but made a deliberate choice not to touch the trust flowchart itself to fit it in -- that diagram's decision logic was already built and tested around a different question, and restructuring a working visual to wedge in a case that doesn't fit its shape cleanly seemed like a worse trade than leaving it stable and covering the gap in prose instead. Also added: the required survivor annuity a pension must offer that profit sharing plans don't, a systematic four-step approach for tax recommendation questions, the specific five-step order for a depreciation recapture calculation, and a handful of smaller Social Security specifics -- FICA's own withholding exceptions and the actual disability eligibility requirements -- that round out a section already covering the bigger, more obviously tested pieces.
New knowledge without new questions to test it is only half the job -- and a real mistake made getting thereAsked to check whether the question bank actually covers the ground the study guide had been gaining over recent turns. It genuinely didn't in several places -- the plan loan formula, Section 179 against bonus depreciation, the mid-quarter convention, the dual-basis gift rule, the fourth trust type, the actual test for what counts as financial planning, the options straddle, the required survivor annuity, and the specific order for managing a conflict of interest all had zero questions testing them, despite now having real coverage in the guide itself. Wrote nine new questions for exactly those gaps. The first attempt at inserting them went to the wrong place entirely -- a big file with two similarly-structured arrays led to writing them into a plain list of study-tip strings instead of the actual question bank, where they would have sat completely inert, never reachable by any quiz. Caught by checking where the content actually lived rather than assuming a search result pointed to the right array, moved to the genuine question list, and confirmed reachable through an actual practice drill afterward, not just present in the data. A length-bias check afterward also caught one new question where the correct answer ran nearly four times longer than the others -- fixed by expanding the shorter options with real detail, the same fix used on the original 87 flagged questions earlier this project.
Thin coverage is still a gap, even at one or two questionsA handful of topics from earlier gap-filling passes had crossed from zero questions to just one or two -- Rabbi versus Secular trusts, the 72(t) amortization-versus-RMD distinction, AOTC versus the Lifetime Learning Credit, and qualified charitable distributions. Wrote four more questions to genuinely strengthen those specifically, checking length balance immediately this time rather than after the fact. One new question still tripped the built-in quality check on a different measure entirely -- not length this time, but two of its wrong answers each using a flagged absolute word ("never," "only"), the same pattern this app's own review process watches for in every question. Reworded both without changing what made them wrong. Separately, a regression check reported a new question as unreachable through its subject-area drill, which briefly looked like a real problem before checking closer: that drill draws a random sample of 15 from a pool of 77 questions in that same subject, so any three specific ones landing outside one particular sample is expected, not evidence of anything broken -- confirmed by checking that the new questions were genuinely present in the full pool the drill draws from, which is what actually matters.
Re-scanning the question bank against the newer knowledge, not just the older gap listRan the same keyword-coverage check again, but this time against everything added to the knowledge base across the more recent turns specifically, rather than just the original gap list from the AdviseWise documents. Found five more genuine zero-coverage spots: the OBBBA senior deduction, the 40-credit Social Security threshold, the baseline foundation of professional duties that applies before any client relationship exists, the actual spousal-versus-survivor benefit percentages, and the specific early-claim penalty rate. Wrote five questions for those. Checked length ratios and absolute-word counts before finishing this time rather than after, and confirmed each new question sits inside its actual domain's full question pool directly, rather than trusting a single random drill sample the way an earlier check had. Both checks came back clean without needing a follow-up fix, which the last two batches didn't manage on the first pass.
Reading the tax one-pager line by line instead of topic by topicWhat had looked like a stubborn Google Drive access problem turned out to have a simpler explanation: the documents had been shared directly all along, and the fourteen uploaded files were the complete, intended set -- not a partial one waiting on a connector to find the rest. With that settled, went back through the tax one-pager a final time checking specific facts one at a time rather than broader topics, since the earlier passes had been catching whole missing subjects but not always every individual number sitting inside a subject already partly covered. That approach surfaced twelve more real, specific gaps: the actual dollar amounts behind the primary residence sale exclusion, the alimony rule that flipped in 2018, what material participation actually requires in hours, the fact that an annuity's death benefit is taxed differently than life insurance's, Treasury bonds being exempt at the opposite level of government from municipal bonds, the wash-sale window's actual 61-day span rather than a mental 30-plus-30, the annual capital loss deduction limit, the special 28% rate on collectibles, the specific failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalty percentages, and three separate gifting rules -- splitting, the unlimited medical and education exclusion, and unlimited transfers between citizen spouses. All individually small, all individually the kind of specific fact an exam question tends to test directly.
The same line-by-line approach applied to the retirement one-pagerTook the same granular, fact-by-fact re-check just used on the tax one-pager and applied it to the retirement one-pager next, since it's built the same dense way -- comparison tables and specific numbers sitting inside subjects that earlier passes had already partly covered. Found five more genuine gaps this time: Social Security integration letting a SEP give somewhat higher contributions to higher earners in a way SIMPLE and solo 401(k) plans can't, the actual Form 5500 filing differences across the three small-business plan types, the fact that both traditional pensions and cash balance plans specifically carry PBGC premiums that a defined contribution plan doesn't, a divorced spouse's own two-year independent-claiming rule that a current spouse doesn't have, and the AIME-to-PIA mechanics that the whole Social Security benefit calculation is actually built on. That last one matters beyond just being a missing fact -- it's the foundation the more detailed benefit rules already in this guide sit on top of.
A third document, same granular approachApplied the same fact-by-fact re-check to the Code and Standards document next, after it had worked well on the two dense one-pagers already. What escaping ERISA's nondiscrimination rules for a non-qualified plan actually means in practice -- legally offering it to select executives only, with no IRS contribution cap -- had been implied but not stated outright. Fiduciary duty had two of its three real components covered, loyalty and care, but not the third: following a client's own instructions, bounded by scope, reasonableness, and legality. A conflict of interest had only been framed as advisor-versus-client, missing the other real version -- between two different clients' interests, like advising both spouses in a divorce. And the disclosure list itself was missing two named items from the source document, referral compensation arrangements and the firm's privacy policy, alongside what was already there. Smaller individually than some of the earlier finds, but the same category of gap: specific, real, and now closed.
A trust type that lived in a flowchart and a quiz question but never in its own explanationThe qualified plans worksheet gave up three more real gaps under the same fact-by-fact check: defined benefit plans favoring older employees and defined contribution plans favoring younger ones, since a DB plan works backward from a fixed target while a DC plan lets more years of compounding do the work, employer contributions being tax-deductible to the business in the year made, and DB accounts being comingled where DC accounts are held separately. But the more significant find came from checking the marital trusts document against its own downstream uses instead of just its own text. QDOT had been built into the trust flowchart as an outcome box and used correctly in a practice question, but never actually explained anywhere in the guide's own knowledge -- a trust type a student would meet in a diagram and a quiz before ever reading what it does. Fixed by writing what a QDOT actually is: it mimics the marital deduction for a non-citizen surviving spouse without technically earning it, and requires a domestic trustee to qualify. Also made explicit, for the first time, which of the four marital trusts actually qualify for the unlimited marital deduction and which don't -- a real distinction from the source table that had been implied by context but never stated outright for any one of them.
A default that was quietly answering the question for youThe confidence rating that appears before answering in Adaptive Session, Domain Drill, and Missed Review started every question with "Confident" already selected, on the reasoning that picking an answer at all implies some baseline certainty. Told directly that this default itself was the problem, and the reasoning doesn't actually hold up against what the rating exists to measure: if the pill was already marking every answer confident before the person had reflected on it at all, most people would just leave it there, and the entire calibration comparison this feature is built around -- confident accuracy against unsure accuracy -- would be measuring how often people left a default alone, not what they actually felt. Removed the default entirely; no pill is pre-selected now, so a rating only exists when someone genuinely chooses one. Found a second copy of the same assumption while fixing this, sitting in the stats-recording code itself: if no rating had been given, it fell back to logging the answer as confident anyway, a second, quieter version of the exact bias the visible fix was meant to remove. An unrated answer now stays out of the calibration numbers entirely rather than being folded into a bucket the person never actually chose.
A flowchart you can actually tap through instead of only look atAsked to make the study guide more interactive, or build a decision tool that responds to taps rather than sitting still as a diagram. Built the trust-selection flowchart as a genuine tap-through tool: one question at a time, real buttons for each answer, a breadcrumb trail showing the path taken so far, and a back button that undoes one step rather than restarting the whole thing. Built it as a reusable engine rather than a one-off, so the entity and IRA flowcharts could genuinely be converted the same way later without rebuilding the underlying mechanism. Caught a real mistake before finishing: the first attempt at wiring it up placed a script tag inside the HTML string that builds the page, which quietly never runs at all -- a script tag inserted that way is inert in every browser, so the tool would have rendered as a permanently empty box. Fixed by calling the actual initialization from the real code path instead of the markup. The interactive version only makes sense on a screen, so a person can genuinely tap through it, while printing or saving as a PDF automatically swaps back to the original static diagram instead -- confirmed both directions actually switch correctly rather than assuming the CSS rule would just work.
Following through on why it was built reusable in the first placeAsked directly to make the new tap-through tool better, and the engine had genuinely been built with exactly this in mind -- the same data shape and rendering logic could carry a second and third tree without touching the underlying mechanism at all. Converted the business-entity and IRA-deductibility flowcharts into the same tap-through format, including the entity tree's genuine S-corp eligibility branch and its LLC-is-a-distractor note carried over into the result itself, not just the section hint above it. Also added two things the first version was missing: focus genuinely moves to each new question or result as it appears, so a keyboard or screen-reader user isn't left stranded on a button that no longer exists once the content changes, and each step now fades in gently instead of snapping into place. The same quote-escaping mistake from several turns back showed up once more while writing the IRA tree's text, caught the identical way as every time before -- reading the actual resulting character sequence rather than trusting a passing syntax check.
Tapping through one path at a time was never meant to replace seeing the whole mapMaking the flowcharts tap-through solved one problem and created a smaller one: a person could no longer see every branch and outcome at a glance the way the original diagrams allowed, only the single path they were currently walking. Added a small toggle beneath each tap-through tool -- "see the full decision tree at once" -- that expands to reveal the same complete diagram that was already built for printing, collapsible again with a second tap. The tap-through version and the full diagram now coexist rather than one replacing the other, each still doing the job it's better suited for. Tested the specific case that seemed likeliest to break: leaving a tree's full diagram open on screen and then printing, to confirm the print layout doesn't end up showing the diagram twice or getting confused by whatever the screen toggle happened to be set to -- it renders the same clean, complete page either way, independent of what's currently expanded on screen.
Two more diagrams made tappable, and getting the tools out from under everything elseAsked to extend the same interactivity to the two remaining diagrams and to stop burying all five tools at the bottom of a long guide. The options matrix and the qualified plan family tree aren't decision paths the way the trust, entity, and IRA tools are -- there's no single sequence of yes-or-no questions to walk down, just several independent things worth understanding on their own. Built a simpler, separate pattern for that shape: six tappable cards for the options matrix, five for the plan family tree, each expanding independently with real explanation underneath rather than just the short label the static diagram showed. More than one can be open at once, since exploring these has no natural order the way answering the trust or entity questions does. Then moved all five tools to the very top of the guide, right after the intro line, ahead of the formulas and the long syllabus that used to come first -- confirmed the new order directly rather than assuming the section list matched what was written, since the section that builds this page and the functions that generate each diagram turned out to sit in two different places in the file, and pointing the new code at the wrong neighboring function would have been an easy, silent mistake to make without checking.
Giving the tools a real home of their own, and a real mistake caught before it would have shipped silently brokenTold directly that five genuinely useful tools sitting at the top of one long page still wasn't quite right -- they deserved their own place in the app's actual navigation, not just a better position inside something else. Added a sixth tab, Tools, sitting right next to Study, holding all five: the three tap-through trees and the two tappable-card sets, each in its own card the same way the rest of the app already presents things. The study guide itself now shows the static, printable version of each diagram with a plain note pointing to the interactive one in its new tab, rather than keeping two live copies of the same tool in two places that would need to be kept in sync forever after. A real mistake happened putting this together: an early attempt tried to drop each diagram straight into the new tab's fixed HTML using the same fill-in-the-blank syntax used elsewhere in this file to build pages dynamically -- syntax that only means anything inside an actual script, and does nothing at all sitting in plain markup. Every one of those five tools would have rendered as literal, meaningless text on the page instead of the actual diagram. Caught by testing the real page rather than trusting that code which looked right had actually run, and fixed by loading each tool through the real startup sequence instead.
Connecting each tool to the actual questions that test it, and a verification mistake worth being honest aboutA tool that teaches a concept and a question bank that tests it were sitting in the same app without ever pointing at each other. Added a "practice this topic" button under each of the five tools, tied to a specific, hand-verified set of question IDs pulled from the real bank rather than a rough guess at how many might apply. Getting that count right took a second pass: a first search for matching questions returned a wildly inflated number for the trust tool, the same kind of quiet bug found earlier this session where a short pattern like "grat" was matching inside unrelated words rather than the actual term GRAT -- rerun with a properly bounded search and the true, trustworthy counts came back far smaller. A second, more serious issue surfaced during the final verification pass itself: one of the checks confirming every TVM problem still solved correctly had a typo referencing the solving function itself rather than the boolean flag that actually tracks success, so the check would have silently passed even if TVM solving were completely broken. Caught only by noticing that a deliberately-triggered error somewhere else behaved differently than expected, tracing back to find why, and rerunning that specific check by hand with the typo fixed before trusting the full result.
Three of five had a feature the other two were quietly missingAsked directly to confirm the full-diagram view existed for every tool in the new tab, not just the three that got it first. It didn't -- the trust, entity, and IRA trees each had a "see the full decision tree at once" toggle, but the options matrix and the plan family tree had only their tappable cards, with no way to see the whole thing laid out at once the way the other three allowed. Added the same toggle to both, reusing the existing static diagrams that were already being generated for printing rather than building anything new. Noticed while testing it that the shared toggle function's label always said "decision tree," which was accurate for three of the five but genuinely wrong for the other two -- neither the options matrix nor the plan tree is a sequence of decisions, just something worth seeing whole. Changed the wording to say "diagram" for those two specifically, so the label matches what's actually being shown rather than reusing text written for a different shape of content.
A button that wasn't broken -- the screen underneath it wasSent a screenshot with a circle around the new practice button, saying it wasn't working. It genuinely wasn't, but not for any reason visible in the button itself: the quiz screen that's supposed to take over the display turned out to live structurally inside the Study tab's own section of the page, a leftover from before a separate Tools tab existed. Tapping the button from Tools left the Study tab hidden underneath, and a hidden parent forces everything inside it to render at zero size regardless of its own settings -- the quiz was genuinely there, running, just invisible. A first attempt at a fix made this worse before it shipped: hiding whichever tab was active broke the original Study tab case that had always worked correctly, since that's precisely the section the quiz depends on. Caught by directly measuring the quiz's actual rendered size afterward rather than trusting that the surface checks still passed. The real fix keeps the Study tab specifically active behind the scenes whenever any session starts, no matter which tab was tapped from. A second, related bug turned up while confirming this held for every starting point: a leftover line in the domain-drill code was quietly overwriting which tab to return to afterward, so a drill started from Reference was sending someone back to Study instead once they finished. Fixed both, then tested starting a session from Tools, Study, and Reference individually, confirming in each case that the quiz genuinely has real, visible size on screen -- not just that its own display property claims to.
Fixing where a session starts left where it hands you back genuinely wrongAsked directly to confirm scrolling and navigation genuinely still worked correctly once a session starts, a reasonable thing to check given how much the tab-switching logic underneath these sessions had just changed. It didn't, in a way that traced straight back to that same fix: the position on the page gets captured for restoring later at the moment the screen locks in place, but that capture was happening after the code had already swapped which tab panel was active -- and switching tab panels can itself shift how tall the page is, which quietly resets the saved scroll position before it's ever read. Someone scrolled well down a long Tools tab to reach a specific tool, tested this directly: the position that actually got saved was nowhere close to where they'd been, and exiting the session landed them somewhere else on the page entirely. Fixed by capturing the real position first, before any tab gets switched, rather than after. Confirmed afterward that the quiz itself always opens at its own top regardless of where someone had scrolled to beforehand, and that the original page position comes back correctly once the session ends -- tested from a genuinely deep scroll position, not just the top of the page, which is exactly the case that had been silently broken.
Not everything that looks duplicated actually isAsked to step back and check whether everything across the app was genuinely placed and grouped sensibly after several turns of adding tools in different places, and to look for things worth combining rather than just leaving spread out. The real finding wasn't scattered clutter needing consolidation -- it was that the study guide's formulas, key numbers, and syllabus sections looked like duplicates of what the Reference tab already has, but actually aren't: the guide's copies are a fixed snapshot meant to work on a printed page, while Reference holds the same material live, reordered around whatever the person is actually weakest in right now. Collapsing them into one would have genuinely cost the printable version its whole purpose. Left both in place, but added a plain pointer between them in each direction, so reading the guide on screen makes clear a more current, personalized version exists one tab over, rather than looking like the same thing shown twice for no reason. Checked the rest of the app the same way before making any changes -- the recurring-mistakes and calculation-review sections turned out to be genuinely unique, built from a person's own missed questions with nothing elsewhere to point to, and the glossary's relationship to flashcards was already explained clearly where it lives. Confirmed both new links actually navigate to the right tab rather than just checking that the text reads correctly.
Nineteen biases had real explanations and almost no questions testing themAsked to go back through the original uploaded documents once more and confirm everything from them had genuinely been captured. Found one more real gap in the qualified plans worksheet: defined contribution plans generally favor younger employees, but the source material names two specific exceptions -- target benefit and age-weighted profit sharing plans -- that use age directly in their calculations and end up favoring older employees despite technically being DC plans. That distinction hadn't made it in. The larger finding came from checking the behavioral finance cheat sheet's 22 biases against actual question coverage rather than just knowledge coverage: 12 of them, adding up to more than half, had zero questions testing them at all, despite each having a full, real explanation already sitting in the guide. Wrote eight new questions covering the ones most likely to come up and easiest to tell apart from something similar -- analysis paralysis, diversification error, herd behavior, cognitive dissonance, hindsight bias, prospect theory, endowment bias, and financial infidelity -- each built as a short client scenario rather than a bare definition, since recognizing a bias in a description is the actual skill being tested, not reciting its name. Checked length balance and scanned for flagged absolute wording before finishing this time, rather than after -- both came back clean on the first pass.
Knowledge and questions existed for these biases -- a searchable card for each one didn'tAsked to confirm everything in the app was genuinely dynamic and properly connected to everything else, rather than sitting in only one place. Checked the flashcard deck against the same 22 biases just tested in the previous pass, since the glossary pulls every one of its entries directly from flashcards rather than holding its own separate list. Sixteen -- later found to genuinely be seventeen once counted correctly -- had no flashcard at all, meaning they were invisible to both flashcard review and glossary search despite having full explanations in the guide and, for eight of them, real questions already testing them. Added all seventeen missing terms as proper flashcards matching the existing format exactly, which the glossary picked up automatically once they existed, since it builds itself from that same list rather than needing a separate update of its own. Along the way, two of my own verification checks turned out to be wrong rather than the app: one referenced a function that was never real, and a second, more tangled script produced a failing result that a simpler, cleaner version of the same test showed was actually working correctly the whole time -- worth naming plainly rather than letting a failed check sit unexplained.
A counter-intuitive contrast and a source clarification, both genuinely missing until this passWent back through the source documents once more specifically looking for value still left on the table rather than re-checking ground already covered. Found two small, real things. The qualified plans worksheet draws a genuine contrast worth keeping: pension plans cap company stock investment at 10% of assets, but profit sharing plans carry no such cap at all and can genuinely be entirely invested in company stock, the reverse of what the pension rule might suggest applies everywhere. And the IRA deductibility source specifically notes that the dollar counting toward being covered by an employer plan can come from either the person's own paycheck deferral or the employer alone -- a distinction someone could easily miss, assuming only their own contribution counts. Added both. Deliberately left the printable, static version of the IRA diagram exactly as it was rather than adding the second point there too -- that box is already full at four lines of text, and forcing in a fifth risked the same overflow problems caught and fixed earlier this project, for a diagram whose core point stays accurate without it. A final regression check flagged that same addition as missing, which turned out to be the check looking in the study guide instead of the interactive tool where the text actually lives -- confirmed correct once checked in the right place, not a real gap.
The same bug, a second time, in a function that never got the memoSent a screenshot circling the Resume button on the home screen, saying it wasn't working. It genuinely wasn't -- and it turned out to be the identical underlying problem found and fixed a few turns back in a completely different button, just living in a second, separate function that never received the same fix. Resuming a saved session has its own code path, distinct from every other way of starting a session, and that path was written before fullscreen quiz mode, scroll locking, and the tab-panel handling existed. It correctly rebuilt the saved question queue and correct count, but never actually entered fullscreen mode at all -- so the question rendered, technically, but sitting inline in the ordinary page instead of taking over the screen the way every other session start does. Tapping Resume looked exactly like nothing had happened, because visually, almost nothing had. Fixed by bringing this function onto the same shared entry sequence already fixed once, rather than patching it as its own one-off case a second time. Tested by rebuilding the exact scenario from the screenshot -- question 8 of 15, 7 correct so far -- confirmed the quiz now genuinely fills the screen, the prior progress carries through correctly, and finishing the session lands on a perfect score. Checked the "start fresh instead" option on the same card too, since it sits right next to the button that broke; that one was never affected, since it never tries to start a quiz in the first place.
Checking whether a bug found twice might exist a third time, before anyone had to find itWith the same underlying problem now caught in two separate places, went looking for every remaining spot in the file that could genuinely share it, rather than waiting for a third report. Searched for every place that shows the quiz screen directly, five in total. Two were the ones already found and fixed. The other three turned out to be something different in kind -- moving between questions during an exam already in progress, or into its second section after a scheduled break -- rather than starting a session from nothing, so the fullscreen mode they need is already active from when that exam genuinely began, not something each of these needs to set up again on its own. Confirmed this directly rather than trusting the read of the code alone: ran a full exam through to the review screen, jumped back to an earlier question from there, and pushed through the section break into the second half, checking each time that the screen stayed genuinely full rather than assuming it would. All three held up. Also checked whether the study guide, the app's other major full-screen view, carries the same risk of two separate paths quietly drifting apart -- it doesn't, since every place that opens it calls through the same single function rather than each keeping its own copy of the logic.
One section was quietly responsible for most of a very long scrollAsked to look at how the study guide itself was formatted and consider breaking it up where that would genuinely help. Measured the actual page rather than guessing at what felt long: the full syllabus section alone -- every explanation for every one of the 70 official subtopics, always fully expanded -- accounted for just over two-thirds of the guide's entire length by itself, with the key numbers section adding a further meaningful share on top of that. Rebuilt both as a set of tappable domain headers instead of one continuous unbroken wall of text: each of the 8 domains starts collapsed with just its name and a topic count showing, expanding only the one someone actually taps rather than forcing all 70 subtopics onto the screen at once regardless of which few someone actually came to read. The guide's total on-screen length dropped from roughly 30 phone-screens of scrolling to about 6 and a half. Printing needed its own explicit check, since a collapsed section has to still print in full even though it never expands on screen -- confirmed this holds through the same print-only override already used elsewhere in the guide. A screenshot taken partway through this work briefly looked like two screens of content bleeding into each other, which turned out to be nothing more than the page still settling at the exact moment the image was captured -- confirmed by retaking it a half-second later, clean, rather than treating an unclear first look as evidence of a real problem.
Eight sections still needed a way to jump straight to one of themWith the syllabus and key numbers now collapsed rather than always fully open, the guide still has eight genuinely separate things in it, and reaching the seventh one still meant scrolling past the first six. Added a small "jump to" row right at the top, one tap per section, that scrolls straight there instead. Getting it actually working took three separate rounds of checking, and each one is worth naming honestly. The first version used plain page-anchor links, which turned out not to work at all here, since this guide scrolls inside its own contained box rather than the page itself, and a plain anchor link has no way to reach into that. Replaced it with code that explicitly scrolls the right element into view. The next two rounds of testing weren't bugs in that fix at all, but two different mistakes in how the fix was being checked: once by reading the scroll position of the wrong element entirely, and once by not waiting long enough for the on-screen scrolling motion to actually finish settling before checking where it had landed. Slowing down and checking precisely, on every section, confirmed the feature was genuinely working the whole time by the second fix -- the apparent failures after that were about the test, not the guide.
A label that wasn't sitting over its own column, and a line of text that ran past its boxAsked to check that the words in the options matrix diagram were sized properly and genuinely inside their boxes. Measured rather than eyeballed it: the "BUY (long)" heading was sitting 35 pixels off from the actual center of the column it's supposed to label, and "SELL (write)" was off by a smaller but still real 10 pixels -- both leftover from an earlier fix to a different overflow problem that shifted them sideways without re-centering them over their own columns afterward. Recentered both precisely. Separately, one line of body text -- describing unlimited loss risk on a sold call -- measured out to run past the right edge of its own box by a small but real amount, confirmed directly by checking its exact rendered width rather than assuming the visual looked fine. Rewrote it slightly shorter, carrying the identical meaning, and reconfirmed it now sits with comfortable margin inside the box rather than merely not overflowing. Checked every other line of text in the same diagram the same precise way once these two were fixed, and swept the whole thing again afterward to confirm nothing remained. One number in my own final check turned out to be wrong in a harmless way -- expecting 21 lines of text where the diagram has always genuinely had 23, confirmed by counting directly rather than trusting the number written into the test.
A feature the AI tutor could see but never actually reachAsked to make sure everything added recently was genuinely wired into the rest of the app rather than sitting on its own. The flashcard side checked out completely -- every new card sits correctly in the same review rotation as everything else, confirmed by reading the actual queue rather than assuming a fix from a prior pass still held. The real gap was the tutor. The Tools tab and its five interactive decision trees were added after the AI tutor's own capabilities were originally written, and nothing about adding a new tab later automatically taught the tutor it existed. Confirmed directly: asking it to switch there failed outright, not because of any conversation-level misunderstanding, but because the list of tabs it was technically permitted to switch to, defined in two separate places, both simply never had a fifth entry added to it. A student asking the tutor to open the trust tool, or simply mentioning they didn't have an API key connected yet, would have been told about four tabs while a fifth sat one tap away the whole time. Fixed in three places: the technical list of allowed tabs, the offline-mode message describing what works without an API key, and -- the part actually easy to miss -- the tutor's own instructions, which listed out every other action it can take in real detail but never once mentioned this one existed, meaning even a technically correct fix upstream wouldn't have changed what the tutor actually chose to do without also being told to use it.
Checking whether the same pattern existed anywhere else, once it showed up onceWith the tutor's blind spot toward the Tools tab found and fixed, checked whether that same shape of problem -- something added recently that an older, separate piece of the app was never told about -- existed anywhere else worth catching now rather than later. The podcast feature's domain handling turned out to already be built the right way: both its dropdown and the tutor's own tool for opening a specific episode pull the list of domains live from the same central source everything else uses, rather than a separate list of their own, so psychology of financial planning was never actually missing from either -- confirmed directly rather than assumed. The exam-day tab's own content turned out not to touch individual domains at all, so there was nothing there to have drifted. Also confirmed the newer domain's exam weighting is a real, deliberate number and not a placeholder, by checking that all eight domains' weights still add up to exactly the 100 the official exam allocates across them. One assumption in my own check was simply wrong in a harmless way -- expecting a dropdown to stay empty until a tab was first opened, when it's actually built to populate itself the moment the page loads, which is arguably the better behavior anyway.
A sixth tool, chosen deliberately rather than just addedAsked to think through what a genuinely valuable new addition to the Tools tab would look like, rather than just picking something. Weighed several real candidates -- life insurance policy selection and charitable giving vehicle choice both would have worked -- and picked Social Security claiming strategy specifically because retirement carries the single highest weight of any domain on the exam, the underlying decision genuinely has the same branching shape as the tools already here, and nineteen existing questions on the topic were sitting there already, unconnected to any tool. The tree itself follows the same real trade-offs a planner actually weighs: a genuine income need right now overrides everything else, working before full retirement age creates an earnings-test conflict worth avoiding, a lower-earning spouse's eventual survivor benefit is a stronger reason to delay than the worker's own benefit alone, and longevity expectations are what the delay-to-70 math actually depends on. This tree runs four questions deep rather than the two or three of the earlier trees, with noticeably longer explanations at each result, so it uses a different, simpler layout than those -- one full-width question flowing straight down into its own yes-branch result before continuing to the next question, rather than results and questions sitting side by side. Measured every line of text against its box before writing a single coordinate, rather than fixing overflow after the fact the way the options matrix needed last time -- it rendered correctly on the first real attempt. Wired into every place the other five tools live: the interactive tree itself, its full-diagram toggle, a curated nine-question practice set, the study guide's own section and jump-to link, and the AI tutor's own instructions -- catching and correcting two separate places that still said "five tools" before they became exactly the kind of stale reference just spent a turn hunting down elsewhere.
A tool built entirely around terms that weren't themselves searchable anywhereAsked to confirm everything was optimized and genuinely wired together, not just working. Checked for a class of problem specific to a file that's grown this large through this many separate additions: two different things accidentally sharing the same internal name, which would silently make one invisible to the other rather than throwing any visible error. Every function name in the file is genuinely unique, and so is every internal ID across all 427 questions, all flashcards, and all 17 calculator problems -- confirmed by counting rather than assuming a large, long-edited file had stayed clean on its own. The one real gap surfaced somewhere more specific: the Social Security tool just built leans on five distinct terms in its own explanations -- full retirement age, spousal benefit, survivor benefit, the earnings test, primary insurance amount -- and none of them had a flashcard or a glossary entry anywhere in the app. A student could walk the entire decision tree, land on a term they didn't recognize, and have nowhere to look it up. Added all five, matching the existing definition style exactly, and confirmed each one is now genuinely searchable in the glossary and sitting in the same spaced-repetition rotation as everything else -- not a separate list of its own.
A search that first looked like zero coverage, and a real gap underneath that first impressionAsked to go back through the source documents one more time and confirm nothing had been missed. The disability side of the Social Security worksheet looked entirely uncovered on a first search -- a real, notable gap for source material this central to a tool just built around this exact subject. That first read was wrong: the core mechanics were already there, just described in plainer language than the search terms used to look for them. What was genuinely missing sat one layer deeper -- the guide said disability required being unable to work for 12 months, but never named the actual standard by its real term, "substantial gainful activity," or mentioned that qualifying requires a separate work-credit test before the medical definition is even reached. That distinction matters on the exam specifically because it's stricter than the "own occupation" language private disability insurance uses, a contrast someone studying both topics could easily blur together without it being named directly. Sharpened the sentence to name both pieces explicitly. Introduced a real syntax error while writing that fix -- a quoted phrase inside an already-quoted string with no escaping, which would have broken the entire file's script if shipped -- caught immediately by the syntax check that runs before anything is ever considered finished, not by chance.
An icon that was quietly broken since the day the Tools tab was createdSent a screenshot circling the Tools icon in the bottom navigation, saying it looked wrong. It genuinely was: the icon is meant to show three connected points, a small branching diagram matching what the tab actually holds, but the line meant to reach the third point stopped short and curled back on itself instead of arriving there. Confirmed this precisely rather than trusting the look of it alone -- calculated exactly where that line's own drawing instructions said it would end, and measured the real distance from that point to the node it was supposed to reach: a gap of just over two units in the icon's own 24-unit coordinate space, genuinely large enough to see plainly once rendered at any real size. Rendered both the broken version and a fix side by side before touching the actual file, to confirm the corrected version was really right rather than assuming a plausible-looking change had fixed it. Since the third point sits at the exact same height as where the branch begins, the honest fix was simpler than what was there before -- a straight connecting line, not a curve trying and failing to arrive somewhere. This was the tab's own icon, sitting in the same spot on every single screen of the app since the day the Tools tab was first built, and had gone unnoticed through every visual check run since.
Checking whether the same kind of quietly-broken icon existed anywhere elseWith one navigation icon found to be genuinely malformed, checked every other hand-drawn icon the same precise way rather than assuming the rest were fine because nobody had flagged them yet. All five other tab icons and all five podcast-player icons measure out clean -- every shape that's supposed to close back on itself does, within a fraction of a rendering unit, and none needed any change. Also checked two things adjacent to the tool just built: the tab's own recall-practice feature pulls its topic list from the same live source every other part of the app already reads from, so nothing needed updating there on its account, and every one of its practice questions is genuinely sitting inside the same retirement-domain pool used for regular drills and readiness tracking, not off in a separate, disconnected set of its own. One of my own verification checks flagged a false alarm afterward -- built for icons that close into a single shape, it didn't apply to this particular icon, whose two lines are deliberately separate rather than one continuous loop; confirmed by measuring the actual distance between the line's real end point and the node it's supposed to reach, which came out to exactly zero.
Finishing the icon audit rather than leaving two corners uncheckedTwo of the six tab icons, and the settings, sun, and moon icons in the header, hadn't yet gone through the same precise check as everything else.
