All five measure out correctly -- each closed shape returns to its exact starting point, and the calendar tab's small hanger marks and the sun's eight rays, each meant to be separate rather than joined, are exactly that on inspection rather than an assumption. Nothing here needed changing; the value was in actually finishing the check rather than treating the parts that hadn't caused a complaint yet as good enough to skip.
The tutor's own suggested questions never once mentioned the thing it had just learned to doWent through every screen in dark mode specifically, since nearly all of this session's checking had happened in light mode by default, and a theme swap can surface things a single-theme check wouldn't catch. The screens themselves held up cleanly. What turned up instead was the same shape of gap found twice already: the row of ready-made suggestions on the tutor's own opening screen -- the buttons meant to show someone what they can ask for without having to guess -- still had no button for the decision tools, even after the tutor itself had already been taught to navigate there. It's arguably the most visible version of this same oversight yet, since it's the very first thing anyone sees opening that tab. Added a ninth suggestion alongside the existing eight, confirmed it fires the same way every other one already does. Two other things looked like problems along the way and weren't: the light/dark toggle briefly appeared to show both its sun and moon icons visible at once, which turned out to be two icons stacked in the same place with one faded out rather than hidden, confirmed correct once actually reading the opacity instead of just whether each one existed on the page; and a moment later, the same icon looked like it had failed to switch at all, which was nothing more than checking it before its own quarter-second fade had finished playing out.
An odd number in a two-column rowAdding a ninth suggestion to an eight-item, two-column grid left it sitting alone with an empty gap beside it -- correct, but visibly unfinished. Had it span the full row instead of sitting in half of one, the standard fix for exactly this shape of layout problem, and confirmed its rendered width now genuinely matches the row rather than just looking close.
A guide telling people not to read it where they already wereAsked to make sure the study guide and its material didn't feel hidden. The card that opens it had its own line working directly against that: "meant to be printed or saved, not read in-app," sitting on a guide that has its own tap-to-expand sections and its own jump-to navigation -- features that only mean anything if someone's reading it right there in the app. Reworded it to invite both, rather than steering people away from the one way most people would actually first encounter it. Found a second, quieter version of the same problem: the guide's own copy points to the live formulas, numbers, and syllabus sitting in the Reference tab, but nothing pointed back the other way -- someone starting from Reference, never having scrolled far enough down Study to find the guide's own entry point, would have had no way to know it existed. Added the missing line in the other direction, on the three cards it's most relevant to, worth doing anyway since two of those three cards had no descriptive text of any kind before this.
A sentence written for someone who remembered where things used to beThe line pointing to the decision tools read "looking for X instead? those live in the Tools tab now" -- phrasing that made sense while that move was still recent, but reads as a small, pointless mystery to anyone opening the app fresh, who never knew there was anywhere else those tools could have been. Reworded to state plainly where they are, with nothing left implying a past they wouldn't recognize.
A question with no explanation to have led to itWent back through the qualified plans material once more looking for anything a question already tests but the guide itself never actually teaches. Found exactly that: a real practice question already exists on top-heavy plan status -- key employees holding more than 60% of total account balances, triggering a minimum contribution for everyone else -- but nothing in the guide's own explanations ever taught that rule in the first place. Someone missing that question would have had it flagged as worth reviewing, with nowhere in the guide that actually explains it. Added the explanation alongside the existing rules on nondiscrimination and vesting it's closely related to, and added a flashcard for the term itself, since it had none. A quick note on my own process: a check afterward briefly suggested the new explanation wasn't actually there, which turned out to be nothing more than checking the wrong position in a list of many separate topic summaries — confirmed genuinely present once looking in the right place.
A genuinely new source document, and a domain that had been thinner than the othersA new file arrived -- an investment planning one-pager from the same source as several documents already worked through. Its text layer held almost nothing usable despite having embedded fonts, a common trait of pages designed and exported visually rather than written as plain text, so reading it meant rendering the page as an image and reading it directly rather than extracting text that wasn't really there. What it held was substantial: portfolio theory lines rarely covered elsewhere (the security market line, capital market line, and efficient frontier, each distinct from the others despite sounding similar), the statistical building blocks behind them (covariance, correlation, R-squared, both flavors of mean return), the three forms of the efficient market hypothesis, a full page of investment strategy names, the fixed ordering of bond yields on a discount versus premium bond, and an entire real estate section -- cap rate, net operating income, passive losses -- that hadn't existed anywhere in the guide before. Investment planning had genuinely been a thinner domain than retirement, tax, or estate up to this point, each of which had already been through several dedicated passes; this one document closed a meaningful share of that gap in a single pass. Checked the newly-added terms against the flashcard system the same way as every other addition this session, and found the same pattern again -- fourteen of the most distinct new terms had no card at all. Added all fourteen, confirmed each one landed in the glossary and the review rotation the same as everything else.
Sixteen of twenty-one new concepts had never once been asked aboutWith the new investment material added to the guide and its terms added as flashcards, checked the same thing checked after every other major content addition this session: whether any of it was actually being tested. Sixteen of twenty-one concepts checked came back with zero questions anywhere in the bank -- the security market line, the capital market line, all three forms of the efficient market hypothesis, the fixed yield ordering on a discount bond, convexity, tax-equivalent yield, phantom income on a zero-coupon bond, and the entire real estate section among them. Wrote twelve new questions covering the ones most worth prioritizing, each built as a short scenario a planner would actually run into -- reading a security market line plot, comparing a taxable yield to a municipal one, sizing a cap rate from a property's own numbers -- rather than a bare definition to recall. Checked each one's own answer choices for balanced length and for absolute wording creeping into a correct answer before finishing this time, the same discipline established earlier this session, and found the choices needed real rebalancing on several of them before they were done -- one set of four numeric choices differed in length by nearly thirty times before being brought back in line with the others.
Adding value to a system that already had a great deal of itAsked to find genuine ways to make the adaptive session teach better, not just test better. Read through the actual selection engine before proposing anything, since it turned out to already be doing far more than expected -- spaced repetition, a research-backed priority for confidently-wrong answers that get corrected, a guaranteed floor across every domain so weaker ones never quietly vanish from a session, a cap on how often the same missed questions can resurface, and an AI-generated variant system that rewrites a question's surface details the second time it comes up specifically so the student is being tested on the concept rather than recognizing the wording. Several ideas worth trying turned out to already exist, in more sophisticated form than what would have been proposed. Two genuinely didn't: the selection logic has always known exactly why it picked each question, and never once showed that reasoning to the student, so a small label naming it now appears next to each question -- due for review, still working on this, revisiting a confident miss. And the results screen showed final numbers but never gave one last chance to retrieve the material itself, so missed questions now appear as a tap-to-reveal recap immediately afterward, prompting a genuine recall attempt before showing the answer, rather than ending on a static scorecard alone. Building the first feature surfaced a real bug: the reason a question was chosen was being attached to the session after the very first question had already rendered, so it silently never showed up on question one specifically until the assignment was moved earlier, before that first render happens rather than after. The same feature also revealed a layout problem once actual text landed in it -- the label describing a domain shared a row with the new badge in a way that split them into two misaligned columns instead of flowing together, fixed by letting that row wrap properly instead of forcing everything onto rigid, single-line tracks.
A feature that worked perfectly, until the app closed and reopened mid-sessionAsked to check that everything added recently was genuinely staying in sync with the rest of the app, rather than just working the moment it's first used. Saving a session partway through and picking it back up later already goes through its own separate rebuilding logic, distinct from a normal session start -- a real bug was found and fixed in that exact path earlier this session, and it was worth checking specifically whether the newest addition had inherited the same class of problem. It had: the data behind the new "why this question" label was never actually included in what gets saved when a session is paused, so resuming one didn't error, it just quietly went back to showing nothing at all -- confirmed directly by saving a session, genuinely reloading the page the way a person closing the app would, and resuming it. Fixed by adding that data to both sides of the round trip, saving it and restoring it, and reconfirmed the exact same scenario now carries it through correctly. The other new feature, the end-of-session recap, turned out not to share this problem -- it relies on data that was already part of the existing save path before either of these features existed, confirmed by running the identical save-and-resume test against it directly rather than assuming it was fine by association.
Confirming the fix didn't leave anything else nearby uncheckedWith that gap closed, checked the ground immediately around it rather than stopping at the one confirmed fix. A handful of other pieces of an in-progress session genuinely aren't part of that save-and-resume path at all -- checked that each one belongs only to the timed, one-sitting exam modes that were never resumable to begin with, so their absence there is correct by design rather than another instance of the same gap. Also confirmed starting a fresh session after finishing one correctly clears the prior session's recap rather than carrying a stale copy forward, and that the new label stays correct while moving back and forth through questions already on screen, not only on the very first one shown.
One more genuinely different shape of question to check againstA question can get its own text, choices, and explanation rewritten on the fly by the AI the second time it comes up, specifically so a student is tested on the underlying idea rather than recognizing familiar wording from before. That rewritten version is a different shape of data built somewhere else in the app entirely, so it was worth checking directly whether the new recap could handle one of those showing up missed, rather than assuming it would just because regular questions do. Built an example of exactly what that rewritten version looks like, put it in front of the recap the same way a real one would arrive, and missed it on purpose -- it displayed correctly, its own rewritten wording and explanation shown accurately with nothing broken or blank.
A message that said it once, for something that keeps being trueLooking for a genuinely different angle rather than re-checking the same two features again, found a system already quietly running underneath adaptive sessions: a domain that's shown real, sustained struggle gets deliberately eased toward simpler material until an actual mastery streak earns its way back to harder questions, grounded directly in established mastery-learning research. It already tells the student this is happening, through a coach message -- but only once, right at the moment it starts and the moment it ends. Someone several questions into that easier stretch has no ongoing reminder of why the material feels different, since that announcement already came and went. Extended the same "why this question" label from earlier to cover this specifically: a question drawn from a domain currently in that state now says so plainly, for as long as it stays true, not just at the single moment it began. Confirmed directly that it labels only the domain genuinely in that state and leaves every other domain's labels untouched, and that the original one-time coach announcement itself still fires correctly and independently of this.
Not all highlighting is created equal, so it mattered which kind this wasAsked to research whether highlighting key words once an answer is revealed could add value. The honest research picture has a real split in it: a student highlighting their own reading material, after the fact, is consistently rated one of the weaker study strategies in the literature -- it tends to create a feeling of having learned something without the deeper processing that actually produces it. But a different, more specific thing -- a system itself pointing to particular keywords as part of the feedback shown right after answering -- was tested directly in its own dedicated study and genuinely improved performance on related material afterward. That's the version worth building, and the distinction shaped the whole design: only a small, deliberate set of terms this app already treats as meaningful get marked, pulled from the same 191-term glossary built up over the course of this project, and only within the correct answer's own explanation rather than scattered everywhere. Checked how often this would actually fire across all 439 questions before writing a line of interface code -- the real number came back genuinely sparse, averaging well under one term per rationale and never more than three, confirming this wouldn't turn into the indiscriminate over-marking that makes the weaker version weak in the first place. Built it to read the full question bank dynamically rather than requiring any of those 439 questions to be hand-tagged, and made each marked term tappable, jumping straight to its full definition in the glossary. Tapping a term for a feature like this needed to reuse an existing, working path rather than invent a second lookup system, so it hands off directly to the glossary's own search box. A real bug surfaced immediately once this was actually tested rather than just reasoned through: the matching was quietly case-sensitive, so a glossary entry stored in title case never matched that same term appearing in a rationale's own ordinary lowercase prose, and nothing was being marked at all until that was caught and fixed. Working in that same stretch of code also surfaced an older, unrelated bug already sitting in the recap feature from earlier -- genuine question and answer text was being inserted without escaping it for HTML first, which a plain-text term like "S&P" would have quietly rendered incorrectly; fixed that at the same time, alongside the same escaping now protecting the new highlighted terms themselves.
Checking whether the glossary itself had room to grow, now that something depends on it directlyThe new highlighting only works for a term already sitting in the glossary, so its value is tied directly to how complete that glossary actually is. Read through every correct-answer explanation with no match at all, looking specifically for a real, nameable concept that simply had no entry yet, rather than assuming the absence meant nothing was there to find. Several genuinely were missing -- open-perils and named-perils coverage, informed consent, the elimination period on a long-term care policy, double taxation at the corporate level, a back-end ratio to pair with the existing front-end one, and future value and present value themselves, surprisingly absent given how central they are to everything the calculator teaches. Added all of those. Found a second, quieter kind of gap alongside it: two terms that already existed but were worded in a way that never actually matched how the concept shows up in a real sentence -- one stored with an extra descriptive word attached, the other missing a hyphen -- so they were technically covered while still never actually lighting up anywhere. Trimmed both to match natural usage, and lightly reworded three explanations that had split a key phrase apart with a parenthetical in the middle, in each case preserving the exact meaning while letting the phrase read as one contiguous piece. One honest note on process: a quick script written to measure this turned up a number that didn't match an earlier measurement from the exact same question set, which traced back to a classic, easy-to-miss JavaScript trap -- reusing one shared pattern object across many repeated checks, which quietly carries leftover position state from one check into the next and produces wrong answers on about half of them. The actual highlighting feature itself was never built that way and was never at risk; only that one disposable investigative script had the flaw, caught and corrected before trusting any of its output.
Technically fine isn't the same as actually fineTapping a highlighted term had been sending someone over to the Reference tab to look it up. Checked directly what that genuinely did to an in-progress quiz sitting underneath it, and the session itself turned out to survive completely intact -- same question, same place, nothing lost. But surviving in the data and feeling undisturbed to the person using it are two different things, and leaving the screen they were already on to go find an answer, then having to find their own way back, is a real interruption even when nothing was technically broken by it. Replaced it with a small card that opens right on top of the current screen, showing the term and its full definition without navigating anywhere at all, closed by its own X, or by tapping anywhere outside the card -- confirmed that tapping the card itself does not close it by mistake, only those two ways do. Confirmed this works identically whether the term appears during live quiz feedback or inside the end-of-session recap built earlier, and that the quiz sitting behind it is completely unaffected by opening or closing it.
Checking that things actually move the way they're supposed to, not just that the code reads fineWent through every animation and transition in the app one by one, triggering the real moment each one is meant to fire rather than only reading the styling that defines it -- a tab switching in, a study guide section opening, a decision tree step appearing, the coach's own thinking indicator, the new definition card's own entrance. All of them fired correctly. Checking every single button and effect in an app this size one at a time isn't realistic, so instead compared the two timed practice-exam modes directly against each other, since they're supposed to behave alike. They didn't: the shorter practice exam had never received the same stark, distraction-free visual treatment the full 170-question exam switches into, despite both being timed simulations of the same real test experience -- a real, standing inconsistency, now fixed, along with making sure the appearance correctly reverts afterward whether that shorter exam is finished normally or quit early, the same way the longer one already did. One thing looked like a second problem and wasn't: the calculator's own message line stayed blank right at the exact moment a problem was solved, which turned out to be correct, deliberate behavior once checked properly -- that line's job is guiding entry of the known values beforehand, while the genuine confirmation of a correct answer shows up elsewhere, in the solved value's own highlighted display and the full worked solution beneath it, both of which were confirmed to display correctly.
A gap hiding inside a calculation that already looked coveredReviewed the source documents once more for anything still genuinely missing, including a wider sweep of files beyond the core study PDFs -- confirmed a long list of image files scattered across this project's history were screenshots and bug reports from past development sessions, not study material, and set those aside. One real document gap turned up in a source teaching a specific three-part method for sizing annual college savings, built around a precise formula for blending an investment return with a rising cost into one combined rate. The app already covered a simpler, approximate version of that same idea elsewhere, close enough that a first pass could easily have called it covered -- but the exact version is a meaningfully different calculation, and only the simple one existed anywhere in the app. Added the precise formula to the guide's own explanation and a dedicated question built around it, with the simple version included deliberately as one of the wrong answers, since mixing the two up is exactly the kind of near-miss this gap could otherwise have produced on the real exam. Worth being transparent about the process here too: getting this question into the question bank took three attempts. The first two edits looked identical on screen but kept silently failing to match the file's actual text, eventually traced to an escaped character the file uses that a plain visual read doesn't reveal, and a locked-in habit of editing by matching a known string rather than questioning that the match itself was already broken. Switched to editing by exact position once the pattern repeated a second time, which surfaced a placement bug immediately rather than silently -- a syntax check at each step is what caught every one of these before anything reached the actual file.
A bug invisible to every check except the one that actually looksThe new definition card someone taps a highlighted term to open had a real, visible problem: its background rendered see-through instead of solid, leaving the quiz text sitting underneath bleeding straight through it and making the card's own words nearly unreadable, exactly as shown in a screenshot of the actual broken behavior. The root cause was a styling reference pointing at a color that was never actually defined anywhere in the file -- when a stylesheet reference like that resolves to nothing, a background specifically falls back to fully transparent rather than failing loudly, so nothing about this would have shown up in a syntax check, a structural check, or any of the automated testing used throughout this project, all of which confirm code runs rather than confirm it looks right. Corrected it to the same solid background color every other card in the app already uses correctly, confirmed solid and properly colored in both the light and dark theme, and checked the rest of the stylesheet directly for this exact same mistake -- a style pointing at a color name that was never actually defined -- confirming nothing else shares it.
A second look at the same card, after being told it wasn't actually fixedTold directly that the previous fix hadn't fully solved it, and given a new screenshot to work from. The card itself was genuinely solid and readable this time, which confirmed the background fix held -- but two real problems were still there. The card had no limit on its own height, so a longer definition would run off the bottom of the screen with no way to reach the rest of it, fixed by letting the card scroll its own content once it grows past a reasonable size. And opening it never followed the same discipline every other full-screen panel in the app already follows, of deliberately holding the page still underneath it, so a definition opened from the results screen could have left the page behind it free to drift while the card stayed fixed in place -- fixed by adopting that same discipline, and specifically only releasing it again if this card was the one that put the hold in place to begin with, so closing it can never undo a hold a quiz screen already had for its own reasons. A third thing in the screenshot looked like a bug and, on direct testing, genuinely wasn't: the dim, doubled-up look across the whole screen traced to the quiz view's own brief entrance animation, present since long before this feature existed, caught mid-motion at the exact instant a screenshot was taken rather than any lasting flaw -- confirmed by reproducing the same capture and then simply waiting the animation out, after which everything settled and read cleanly. Removed the separate, shorter entrance animation this card had been using on its own regardless, since a quick lookup like this has no real need for one and removing it closes off that narrow window entirely rather than just shortening it.
Confirmed on a real device, not explained awayChecked once more, directly on their own phone rather than through a screenshot, and it was still genuinely happening there -- which ruled out the earlier explanation completely and meant this needed to be treated as a real, unresolved bug rather than something already settled. The testing used throughout this entire project runs on a desktop browser, which handles one specific situation differently than an iPhone's own browser does: this card is the only thing in the whole app that ever has to appear on top of another already-open full-screen layer, since every other panel in the app replaces the screen under it rather than stacking above something still open. That specific setup -- one fixed layer opening on top of another one already there -- is a well-documented source of a rendering glitch unique to iPhones and iPads, where the new layer on top occasionally fails to paint itself in solid and correctly and instead sits there partially see-through, exactly matching what kept showing up. Applied the two standard, well-established fixes for exactly this situation: a hint that tells the browser to treat this card as its own independent layer from the moment it appears, and a forced, immediate repaint the instant it opens rather than leaving the browser to get to it whenever it gets around to it. Worth being direct about the limits here: the tools used throughout this project to verify every other fix this session genuinely cannot reproduce an iPhone's own browser behavior, so this specific fix cannot be confirmed solved the same thorough way everything else in this file has been -- it rests on a well-known, standard pattern for this exact class of problem rather than a direct before-and-after test, and is worth confirming on the actual device once more.
The actual answer, found by comparing what worked against what didn'tTwo new screenshots made the real problem genuinely visible for the first time: in both the light and dark version of this card, the definition's own heading read perfectly clearly, while the sentence underneath it was nearly invisible against its own card in both cases -- a pattern specific enough to point directly at that one piece of text rather than at the card's background again. The color that sentence was told to use turned out to be a value this app already uses for something else entirely: not a simple color meant to invert between light and dark, but the fixed, always-dark background behind the main quiz screen specifically, regardless of which theme is active -- which is exactly why it came out light in light mode and dark in dark mode: backwards both times, in precisely the way that would make text disappear into whatever sits behind it rather than stand out against it. The genuinely correct value is a different one already in use everywhere else -- set once, high up, and left for every regular piece of text in the entire app to pick up on its own, which is exactly why nothing else in this app ever had this problem: everything else was already quietly doing the right thing by doing nothing at all and simply inheriting it, while this one piece explicitly, deliberately set itself to the wrong value instead. Switched it to match, and checked this time with an actual measurement of the difference between the text and its own background in both themes, rather than trusting it to look right by eye -- confirmed strongly readable in both, with the heading above it left untouched since it was already using a correct, separate color the whole time.
Measuring thinness instead of guessing at itAsked to check broadly for any subject or concept still genuinely missing. Rather than reviewing the syllabus by eye, measured it directly: how many questions actually exist for each of the official topics making up each of the eight domains, not just how many sit in the domain as a whole. One topic inside estate planning -- where an estate actually gets the cash to pay its own taxes when most of its value is tied up in a business -- had exactly one question, and that question covered only life insurance trusts specifically, leaving out the two other standard techniques entirely: a specific tax provision letting a family business redeem a deceased owner's stock without it counting as a taxable payout, and a separate provision letting the estate pay those taxes in installments instead of all at once. A second topic, planning for a dependent with special needs, also had exactly one question, covering only the trust-based approach and leaving out a newer, simpler savings account built for exactly this situation. A third gap turned up in a different domain entirely: how to actually evaluate and choose between insurance companies had no coverage anywhere in the app, despite being its own named, official topic. Added three new questions closing these three real gaps. A real mistake surfaced immediately while doing this: the first two new questions were accidentally given ID numbers already in use by two older, unrelated questions already in the bank -- confirmed by directly counting how many entries now shared each ID, found exactly two of each, and corrected by renumbering only the two new ones, leaving the originals completely untouched. Two other topics that looked thin by the numbers turned out to be reasonably covered on closer look, each already testing two distinct, commonly-tested techniques rather than one narrow slice of a broader idea the way the three genuine gaps did, and were left as they already stood.
Continuing the same measurement into the rest of the syllabusCarried the same approach into the remaining domains rather than stopping at the two already checked. One more official topic came back with zero questions anywhere in the bank: the set of consumer protection laws governing how a planner is required to handle a client's own financial information, a named topic in its own right and a genuinely different thing from the ethics and fiduciary-duty material already covered elsewhere. Added a question built around the law most directly relevant to a planner's own day-to-day obligations here -- the specific federal law requiring a privacy notice and requiring client information to be safeguarded from unauthorized disclosure. Checked the remaining two domains the same way afterward and found nothing else missing entirely, though two individual topics turned up with only a single question each; both, on closer reading, turned out to already be broad enough on their own and already supported by other closely related material already sitting elsewhere in the bank, so neither genuinely needed more.
Turning a manual process into something that doesn't need me to run it by handAsked whether this same kind of check -- how many questions genuinely exist for each official topic -- could live in the app itself instead of being redone by hand each time. The part of it that's genuinely mechanical, counting matches against a set of search terms per topic, can live there; the part that actually requires reading a question and judging whether it's really testing a given idea can't, so what got built is a measurement tool, not a replacement for the judgment itself. Running it on a fixed schedule in the background was considered and set aside, since the result here only changes when the question bank itself changes -- never during ordinary use of the app -- so a repeating timer would just recompute the identical answer over and over for no reason; an on-demand button next to the existing content-quality check, doing nothing until someone actually asks for it, fits how this information actually behaves. Found one more genuinely uncovered topic while assembling the full set of search terms needed to cover the syllabus completely: how a business actually decides which type of retirement plan fits it, a named topic with no matching question anywhere in the bank. Added one, with wrong answers built around real misconceptions a planner might actually hold rather than obviously-wrong filler. Confirmed the new check's own output lines up with everything found by hand this session and last -- the handful of topics just given their first question all correctly show one now, up from zero.
Checking whether the thing built last time could quietly go wrong on its ownAsked to check broadly again that everything stays genuinely connected, with the newest feature the obvious place to look first. The new syllabus check works by reading the official topic list the rest of the app already uses, but its own search terms for recognizing each topic are a separate list sitting next to it rather than something pulled from that official list automatically -- which means the two could genuinely drift apart from each other over time without anything ever saying so. Tested this directly by deliberately adding an extra topic to the official list without touching the search-term list to match, the exact kind of accidental mismatch a future change could cause -- and it went by in total silence, the feature still cheerfully reporting that it had checked everything while quietly skipping the one topic nothing had been written to recognize yet. Fixed it so the check now compares those two lists directly against each other before doing anything else, and if it ever finds a mismatch again, says so plainly and names exactly which topic area is affected and how many of its topics genuinely have search terms versus how many should, rather than letting a silent gap stand in for a clean result. Confirmed this fires correctly when a mismatch is deliberately forced, and confirmed it stays silent and reports normally the rest of the time, when there's genuinely nothing to report.
Actually reading the full list the new tool produces, not just the shortened view of itPulled the complete, unshortened output from the new coverage check rather than only the first several rows most people would normally see, specifically to make sure nothing worth noticing was sitting further down where a shorter view wouldn't reach. One topic that had shown a single matching question turned out, on actually opening that question, to not be about the topic at all -- a mismatch in the tool's own search terms matched it to a trust-taxation question when the question was genuinely about a different kind of business entirely, meaning that topic had no real coverage rather than the thin-but-present coverage it appeared to have. A second topic's one matching question turned out to only mention its own subject in passing, as one item in a short list of unrelated examples, without actually teaching the more specific, commonly-tested technique belonging to it. Added one new question for each. A third topic that looked equally thin turned out to be a false alarm in the other direction: both of its real, distinct techniques already existed as their own separate questions, just credited to a different topic than the one actually asking about them, because the tool's own search terms hadn't been written broadly enough to catch both phrasings. Corrected those search terms directly instead of writing a question that would have genuinely duplicated material already there.
A direct report that the same material was genuinely repeating, taken seriously rather than explained awayTold directly that the same questions and scenarios were showing up again, with a clear expectation that this should never happen. Traced the actual, confirmed mechanism behind it rather than assuming it was already working as intended: a question missed is deliberately scheduled to come back up for review immediately, by design, on the reasoning that something just gotten wrong is exactly the thing worth seeing again soon -- and separately, this app can reword a repeating question on the fly using AI, specifically so a second look tests the underlying idea rather than a memorized sentence. Both of those are genuinely correct, deliberate design -- but traced the second piece all the way through its own logic and found a real, silent gap: when no AI connection is set up, that rewording step was written to just quietly stop and return, before ever putting anything on screen explaining why. The student sees the identical question again with nothing to indicate that was expected or why, which is indistinguishable from an actual bug from where they're sitting. Fixed it so a repeat without that connection now says so plainly instead of staying silent, confirmed it correctly shows only for a question genuinely seen before and never for a brand new one, and confirmed it sits correctly alongside the existing badge explaining why a question was chosen, since both now share that same small space without one breaking the other.
A photo of the actual screen, worth more than any amount of re-reading the stylingShown a real screenshot of the end-of-session recap, with the heading and each question inside it sitting barely visible against their own dark card. The styling itself read as perfectly reasonable on its own -- a specific color was named for the text, a different one for the background behind it -- so nothing about it would have looked wrong without actually seeing it rendered. The color named for the text turned out to be the same dual-purpose value already identified earlier this session as the one reserved for a fixed dark overlay background elsewhere in the app, not body text, which is exactly the same mistake in the same family as the one already caught and fixed in the definition pop-up card. It had just been quietly sitting in two more places this whole time, both in the one section built specifically to give a student one last honest look at what they missed. Corrected both to the one color every other normal line of text in the app already uses correctly, confirmed actually readable with a real measured color check in both the dark and light version rather than trusting it by eye, and checked the rest of the file specifically for this same mistake once more -- confirming nothing else shares it.
A silent download that was never asked for, removed at the plain request that it stopTold directly that a page kept popping up after finishing a quiz offering something to download, and that it was an old leftover behavior that was no longer wanted. The app had been quietly saving a full backup of all progress to the device's own downloads on its own, with no tap or request needed, once enough new questions had piled up since the last one -- and on this particular kind of device, a download that starts itself doesn't save quietly in the background the way it might elsewhere; it opens its own full-screen page asking what to do with the file, every single time. A comment left on this code at the time it was built claimed it had deliberately been kept away from firing during active answering, specifically because of this same disruption -- but a second, separate trigger for the exact same automatic save turned out to exist anyway, firing after literally every single question answered rather than only at a natural pause, quietly contradicting what that comment claimed. Removed both triggers entirely, along with the now-unused function they both called, while leaving the actual backup capability itself untouched for the one place it still belongs -- the button in Settings someone taps on purpose when they actually want a backup made. Confirmed no download fires at all across a full run through every section of the app with nothing but ordinary answering, and separately confirmed that button still saves a backup correctly when someone genuinely asks for one.
Going back to the source material itself, rather than only auditing against a syllabus outlineAsked to make sure everything in the uploaded source documents was genuinely reflected in the question bank, rather than relying only on the official topic outline used so far. Read through two of those documents closely: a detailed breakdown of the actual duties and rules a planner owes to clients, firm, and CFP Board, and a cheat sheet naming twenty-two specific, named behavioral-finance biases. The first surfaced several precise, easily-confused details worth testing directly -- the exact menu of what a planner may do when a client refuses needed planning, the rule that advice-only disclosures may be verbal while full planning disclosures must be written, and the genuinely separate 90-day and 30-day self-reporting windows that a careless reader could mix up. The second surfaced three of the twenty-two named biases with no question anywhere testing them at all, each written carefully against its closest neighboring concept so the correct answer depends on knowing its specific definition rather than just recognizing bias-related language in general. While adding the new psychology questions, caught a real collision before it could do any damage: the identifiers chosen for them happened to already belong to three unrelated, pre-existing questions in a completely different section, because that particular identifier style turns out to be shared globally across every section rather than restarting fresh within each one the way most others do. Found the true highest number in use everywhere before renaming, confirmed the original three questions were completely untouched, and confirmed no identifier anywhere repeats. Separately, the tool built earlier in this project to check answer-choice wording caught one of the new questions on its own, flagging that all three wrong answers leaned on the same telling word -- a real, fair catch, not a false alarm -- and that question was rewritten to remove the pattern before finishing.
A one-page diagram with no numbers on it, and a copy-paste mistake caught by actually reading the result backContinued working through the uploaded source material with a one-page flowchart about whether a traditional IRA contribution can actually be deducted. Confirmed there were no hidden figures sitting in an image or graphic that a plain text read might have missed, by rendering the page itself and looking at it directly rather than trusting the extracted text alone. What the diagram actually turned on wasn't a number at all but a definition: being covered by a workplace retirement plan specifically means money was actually put into an account for you that year, which is a narrower and easily-confused stand-in for simply being allowed to participate, and a spouse who isn't personally covered still gets their own, separate, more generous range based on the working spouse's plan rather than sharing it. Neither distinction had a single question testing it anywhere in the bank, so two were added. While writing one of them, a dollar sign meant to appear in the text came out the other side of a copy step as a single stray backslash with nothing after it -- an easy, invisible-looking mistake to introduce and just as easy to miss without reading the saved result back afterward, rather than trusting that what was typed is what landed. Caught it by reading the actual saved text rather than assuming the edit had gone through as written, found it in two separate places phrased slightly differently from each other, and fixed each individually.
A panel that only ever closed itself as a side effect of something elseAsked to make sure the worked-out calculator steps shown for a missed question actually close when moving on or leaving entirely, rather than assuming it already did. Traced where that panel genuinely gets closed and found it only ever happened as a side effect of answering the next question -- there was no moment where simply leaving a question behind, on its own, closed anything. Confirmed directly that advancing to the next question within the same session already worked correctly regardless, since answering is exactly the moment that reset fires. But stepping away entirely -- opening the panel, then leaving the session altogether without answering anything further first -- left it exactly as it was: still open, still showing the previous question's own worked steps, sitting untouched in the background. Started a fresh session afterward and confirmed directly that the stale panel was still there, fully intact, underneath a brand new question that had nothing to do with it and wasn't even the kind of question that panel applies to. Moved the reset to the one place a new question is always, genuinely about to appear on screen, rather than depending on whatever the student happens to do next, and confirmed both paths now behave correctly -- the already-working case stayed working, and the one that was silently stale before is now reliably closed and empty every single time, with nothing left over from whatever came before it.
A dense comparison table, read for what each column trades away, not just what it's calledReturned to working through the uploaded source material with a single compact page comparing four kinds of marital trusts side by side. Reading it for what it actually says, rather than just the four names across the top, surfaced two genuinely distinct, easily confused points. One trust type gives up a second, later step-up in basis in exchange for keeping those assets out of the surviving spouse's own taxable estate -- a real, named trade-off, not an incidental detail, and nothing in the bank tested it before. Another exists specifically to solve a problem outright inheritance can't: letting a surviving spouse keep income for life while making sure a first marriage's children still receive what's left afterward, regardless of whatever the surviving spouse might otherwise decide once in control of it. Both are the kind of distinction that rewards actually understanding why someone would choose one structure over another, not just recognizing a name, and that's the version each new question was written to test.
Told plainly, a second time, that the problem wasn't actually fixed -- and taking that at face value rather than re-explaining the earlier noticeHeard again, more directly this time, that the same exact material was still showing up, with a clear request that a repeated concept should at least come back reworded rather than word-for-word identical. Checked what the earlier fix had actually accomplished versus what it hadn't: it explained why a repeat happens with no AI connection in place, but explaining a limitation honestly is not the same thing as removing it, and this person was saying plainly that the explanation alone wasn't enough. Confirmed directly that reaching the one setting that actually solves this means leaving the app entirely to go sign up for a developer account elsewhere first -- a real, meaningful barrier for someone who just wants to study, not a small inconvenience. Also checked a second, unrelated theory before ruling it out: whether several questions sharing one long scenario might be clustering together and creating a different kind of repetition. Simulated fifteen consecutive sessions to check, and scenario questions barely appeared at all, let alone clustered -- that theory didn't hold up, and was dropped rather than chased further. Made the one remaining fix that was honestly possible without the AI connection: the explanation shown for a repeat is now something to tap directly, jumping straight to the exact field that needs filling in rather than just naming where to go looking for it, cutting what used to be a multi-step search down to one motion. Also checked, honestly, what a version of this that worked without any AI connection at all would actually take: of everything in the bank, only a small slice is built from numbers that could safely be swapped out and rechecked by a machine; nearly everything else is conceptual, and reliably rewriting a concept's own wording isn't something that can be done safely by a fixed set of rules -- a genuine limitation worth naming honestly rather than quietly working around with something that only looks like a fix.
A correction that mattered: the key genuinely was connected, and an entire theory had to be thrown out as a resultTold directly, plainly, that the key actually was connected when the repeats kept happening -- which meant the whole explanation given the turn before, built entirely on the opposite assumption, was simply wrong. That assumption was never something to have made without a way to check it, and it shaped an entire response that turned out to be solving the wrong problem. Went back into the actual rewording logic with that corrected fact in hand, and found a second, separate silent gap sitting right next to the first one already fixed: the explanatory note added earlier only ever shows up when no key is connected at all, so a person who did everything right and connected one correctly gets no such notice when an attempt is made and genuinely fails -- a network hiccup, a response that didn't parse, a rewritten question whose wrong answers happened to fail the same wording check applied throughout this whole project. Confirmed this precisely by forcing a failure on purpose with a key marked as connected, and watched the old explanation correctly stay silent while nothing else said anything either -- exactly the experience being described. Added a second, distinct notice for that exact case, and separately noticed something otherwise easy to miss entirely: genuine network failures already get retried automatically, but a response that comes back fine and simply fails its own quality check never got a second attempt at all -- one bad response ended things outright. Gave that specific case one retry of its own before falling back to the honest notice, confirmed a first failed attempt can now be rescued by a clean second one, and confirmed two failures in a row still stop there rather than retrying forever.
Checking the fix from the last turn for the same class of problem elsewhere, rather than assuming it was the only oneAsked to take another broad pass and make sure everything built recently genuinely holds together, not just works in the moment it was tested. Started with the two new honest notices added last turn for a repeat question that couldn't be freshened, since they sit in the same screen area a much earlier, real bug once lived in -- a leftover calculator walkthrough that stayed visible across an entirely new question until someone actually answered something. Deliberately tried to reproduce that exact pattern here too: triggered a notice, then moved to a new question both by advancing normally and by leaving the session and starting an entirely different one. Both came back clean -- confirmed this area rebuilds itself completely each time rather than leaving old pieces sitting underneath, so nothing stale carries forward. Also watched the loading message through both attempts of the new two-try system, confirming it stays steady the whole time rather than flashing the original question in between. Then stepped back and asked a broader question: does any other place in this app that talks to the AI have this same blind spot, where a real key is connected but the attempt itself quietly fails with nothing shown? Checked every other such place in the app one by one. Every single one already had its own clear, specific message for exactly that situation, confirming the earlier gap was a true one-off rather than a pattern copied in several places -- which means that fix closed the actual problem rather than papering over one visible symptom of a wider one.
A screenshot of the exact moment it kept happening, and a budget that was quietly too small for one specific kind of questionShown a photo of the honest failure notice firing in person, on a calculator-style question specifically, with a plain statement that this kept happening rather than being a one-off. Took that at face value and went looking for why this exact kind of question, rather than any question at random, might be failing more often than the rest. The rewording request for every repeat question was given the same fixed amount of room to respond in, regardless of what kind of question it actually was -- but this particular question's original version needed eight separate, fairly detailed steps just to walk through its own calculator process, on top of the question itself, its answer choices, and the reasoning behind each one. A genuine rewrite of this question would need to produce all of that over again, and the fixed amount of room given for it was tighter than the amount this same app already gives itself, per question, when writing entirely new calculator-based questions elsewhere -- a real, measurable gap between two numbers that should have been treated the same way. Deliberately built a response cut off at exactly that tighter limit, mid-step, to see what happens, and confirmed it fails to come through as anything usable at all, not even partially -- a response like that doesn't trail off gracefully, it just stops becoming valid. Gave calculator-based questions specifically the same amount of room already proven to work elsewhere in this app for the same kind of content, left every other kind of question exactly as it was, and confirmed a full, realistic response of that length and shape now comes through cleanly where the old limit would have cut it off.
A second photo, same message, and proof the last fix was only ever part of the answerShown a second screenshot of the same honest failure notice, firing again -- but this time on a plain conceptual question with no calculator walkthrough involved at all, nothing like the kind of question the length-based explanation from before was actually about. That alone ruled the previous theory out as the full story: a question this short was never going to run short on room to respond in, so whatever was happening here had to be something else entirely. Rather than guess again at a specific cause with no way to check it, went after visibility instead: the moment something fails, there's already a part of this app, used everywhere else an AI request can fail, that turns a raw error into a plain-language reason -- rate limited, a rejected key, a timeout, a problem on the other end. That reason was already being quietly captured here and then never actually used, sitting unread right next to the message that kept saying nothing more specific than "did not come through." Wired it in so the real reason shows up directly in the notice itself from now on, with the honest, general phrasing kept in reserve for the one case where there genuinely isn't a specific reason to give -- a response that came back fine but didn't take a usable shape. The next time this happens, whatever shows up in that message is the actual thing to go act on, not another guess.
Asked to compare two study modes side by side, feature by feature, rather than assuming they matchedAsked to make sure a domain drill genuinely carries every feature the main adaptive study mode has, rather than trusting that they already lined up. Went through every single place in the code where a feature decides which modes it's allowed to appear in, and compared each one against the others, since that's exactly where a quiet mismatch would hide. Most of them already agreed with each other. Three didn't. A worked calculator walkthrough for a missed question was written to appear only in the main adaptive mode, leaving a student who missed the same kind of question during a plain domain drill with no walkthrough at all, for no real reason tied to how a drill is any different from adaptive in that moment. A short recall exercise shown at the end of a session carried a comment claiming it matched another feature's own rules exactly -- except that other feature's actual rules were already broader than what this one followed, which was the real tell that this one had drifted from what it was supposed to match rather than being written that way on purpose. And separately, the running memory of which questions were shown most recently, kept specifically to avoid resurfacing something too soon, was only ever being filled in by the main adaptive mode's own picks -- so a domain drill's questions were invisible to it entirely, meaning a session started right after a drill had no way of knowing to avoid repeating what someone had just finished seeing. Fixed all three to follow the same shared rule the rest of the app already settled on. While confirming the fixes, ran into a separate, revealing problem in the testing itself: answers appeared to land correctly only some of the time, seemingly at random, which pointed first toward the app rather than the check. Tracing it down to its root showed the real issue was a stale answer key being reused after the app had already, correctly, shuffled the order of the choices on its own -- the test was still comparing against where the right answer used to sit, not where it had moved to. Once corrected to always check the live, current position instead, the same test passed consistently, every single time, confirming the actual fixes had been solid from the start and the inconsistency belonged to how they were being checked, not to the fixes themselves.
Making the tutor actually see the whole picture, act on more of it directly, and teach the way the research says actually worksAsked to make sure the built-in tutor genuinely draws on everything the app already tracks about a student and feels more like real tutoring, grounded in how people actually learn rather than just sounding encouraging. Went through everything the tutor could already see and do, and found it was already carrying a real, substantial amount of context -- but in several places it was working from less than the app itself already knew. It could only ever see a single weakest subject, never the full standing across every area, even though that fuller picture was already being computed elsewhere in the app for other screens. It had no visibility into which specific named topics, out of all seventy official ones, a student had personally marked as reviewed versus not -- meaning it could only ever speak in generalities about a weak area instead of naming the exact piece still worth covering. It could start a general mixed session or a single-topic one, but had no way to start a focused review of specifically what someone had gotten wrong, even though that exact mode already existed elsewhere in the app. It could tell a student to go try one of the six interactive decision tools by name, but could only ever drop them on the general tools page and leave them to go find the right one themselves. And it had no way at all to close the loop after actually teaching something -- no way to mark a topic reviewed once it had genuinely been covered, leaving that step sitting entirely on the student to go do manually afterward, elsewhere. Fixed all five: a full subject-by-subject standing now available to draw on, specific unreviewed topic names in a student's weaker areas, a direct review-session trigger, a true one-tap jump straight into the specific tool being discussed, and a way to check a topic off together once it's actually been taught and the student agrees -- never on its own. Separately, rewrote the core instruction behind how it teaches, grounded in one of the better-established findings in how people actually learn: producing an answer yourself, even a wrong one, cements it more than simply being told. The tutor now defaults toward asking before explaining, connects new material to a student's own real mistakes rather than teaching in the abstract, and checks that something landed before moving on, rather than just being told once to "be encouraging" and left to interpret that alone.
Five photos of the same honest message, and finally a fix aimed at why it keeps firing instead of just explaining it betterShown five separate photos of the same repeat-question notice firing across very different topics -- a workers' comp question, two different tax-deadline questions, a Social Security scenario, and a college-funding scenario -- with a plain statement that this keeps happening. That spread across unrelated subjects was the real clue: whatever was wrong wasn't tied to one topic, which meant the honest explanations added in earlier turns, however accurate each one was in the moment, were still just describing the symptom every time rather than making it happen less. Went looking specifically for why a rewritten version of a question would fail more often than a question written from scratch, and found a genuine, structural reason: the task of rewriting an existing question necessarily starts from that question's own four answer choices, and quietly carries their patterns forward -- the same distinctive word turning up in more than one wrong answer, say -- in a way a freshly written question wouldn't be as prone to. That exact failure had already been caught by hand earlier in this project, on a question written manually rather than by AI, and the same quality check built from that experience was almost certainly rejecting a meaningful share of rewritten questions for exactly that reason. Added explicit guidance into the rewriting request itself, spelling out the two specific patterns to avoid, aimed at making each individual attempt less likely to fail this way in the first place -- a fix at the source, not another layer of retrying after the fact. Gave failures one additional retry on top of that regardless, since a stricter bar genuinely does mean more attempts are worth making before giving up. Separately, noticed two of the photos showed an older, less specific version of this same message, from before a prior fix -- worth mentioning directly, since the newest version is the one that should be in use going forward.
Told to keep going and check every angle, and found a second, exact hit sitting right next to the first oneAsked to keep checking this same issue for anything else that could be causing it, rather than treating one fix as the end of the search. The clearest lead left was a fix made earlier this session for a completely different reason: a calculation-style question needs extra room to write out a full worked solution when rewritten, and the original fixed amount of room was too tight for that specific case. The same exact reasoning, examined properly this time, applied just as much to a second, separate kind of question that had been missed: ones built around a short client story at the top, which a genuine rewrite needs to replace with an equally detailed new one, not just a sentence or two of filler. Checked how long those client stories actually run throughout the question bank, and the single longest one, measured directly, turned out to be the exact same story already seen failing in one of the photos shared earlier -- not a similar case, the literal same one. Gave that same kind of question the same extra room already given to calculation questions, and a question that happens to need both gets more room still. Went on to rule out several other real possibilities directly rather than stopping there: whether answer choices were being compared to each other too strictly and catching close-but-different wording by mistake, and whether a rewritten question gets checked against the entire existing bank for being too similar to something else already in it. Neither turned out to be true -- the comparison logic only catches a close to word-for-word repeat, and that broader bank-wide check was confirmed to never run on a rewritten question in the first place, only on batches of brand new ones. The specific, direct hit was the one worth fixing; the rest were checked and genuinely ruled out rather than assumed fine.
Finding a question missed, then genuinely reaching for a second one about the same exact thing before moving onAsked to make the main study mode feel genuinely like being walked through material brick by brick, not just a well-calibrated difficulty curve reacting after the fact. Looked at what that selection logic already did closely, and it turned out to be more thoughtful than expected -- real research-backed reasoning behind difficulty, behind which topics get priority, behind catching a confident wrong answer soon after it happens. But none of that reached the one thing "brick by brick" is actually about: when something is missed, is the very next relevant thing genuinely about that same specific idea, or does the session just move on to whatever else happens to be due. Checked directly, and the entire selection process ran purely at the level of which of the eight broad subjects a question belonged to -- nothing finer than that existed anywhere, so there was no way for the system to know two particular questions were actually about the same narrow thing in the first place. A measurement tool built earlier in this project for an entirely different reason -- checking how well the syllabus itself was being covered -- turned out to already contain exactly the missing piece: a working way to guess which specific official topic a given question is actually testing. Reused that same matching logic for a new purpose here: when a question gets missed, immediately look for one other, different question testing that same narrow thing, and make sure it lands genuinely next to the missed one rather than being left to chance -- while keeping everything else about the session exactly as unpredictable and varied as it already was. The one real complication was that pairing two questions together only matters if they survive whatever comes after -- most importantly, the step that shuffles the whole session into its final order. Grouping each pair as a single unit before that shuffle runs, rather than shuffling every question individually, keeps a pair intact through it. Ran that exact scenario hundreds of times in a row to make sure it held up reliably rather than trusting it after a handful of clean runs, and one specific case genuinely failed about once in thirty: a missed question chosen by a completely different, earlier part of the process -- one that guarantees every subject area gets at least some representation -- was invisible to the new pairing step entirely, because that step had only ever looked at missed questions chosen a different way. Traced that down to its root and fixed it directly, then reran the same hundreds-of-times check clean. A small, honest label now shows directly on a question placed this way, so a student sees plainly that it's deliberately building on what they just got wrong, not a coincidence.
Two more photos, two more tax questions, and finally reacting to the actual evidence instead of guessing againShown two more photos of the same message, both tax questions this time, with the same plain statement that this was still happening. Checked first whether tax questions as a category were simply longer or more demanding to rewrite than other subjects, which would have pointed at another case like the last two fixes -- measured directly across the whole bank, and tax came back entirely ordinary, not even above the typical length. That ruled out a third case of the same specific pattern and meant the real cause was still something else entirely, not another subject-specific gap to patch individually. Went looking instead at the actual mechanical signature a cut-off response leaves behind: genuinely complete JSON always ends in a closing bracket or brace, and a response that got cut off simply handing back more detail than it had room for, rather than one with some other kind of problem, is the one case reliably missing that. Checked this directly in both directions before trusting it -- confirmed a deliberately cut-off response is correctly caught by this, and confirmed a response that was complete but simply wrong in some other way is correctly left alone and not mistaken for the same thing. Rather than continuing to hand-pick a separate fixed number for every individual kind of question that might need more room -- which is exactly what the last two fixes were, and exactly the kind of fix that keeps needing a new case added -- this reacts directly to that specific signature wherever it shows up and gives the next try real additional room on the spot, growing further still if it genuinely needs to a second time, rather than quietly repeating the same amount of room that may have been the actual problem in the first place.
A genuinely well-stocked coach that was never actually in the room, and a small fix to let it finally speak upAsked to make the main study flow itself feel more like being genuinely coached through the material, grounded in real, established learning science rather than just vibes. Went looking at what already existed before building anything new, and it turned out a quietly thorough coaching voice was already fully built -- real milestone recognition, real research-backed messages about testing effects and spacing and desirable difficulty, written out and ready to go. But tracing exactly when any of it actually spoke up revealed it only ever did so at the very edges of a session -- right as one ended, or right as the screen was left entirely. The whole time someone was actually answering questions, which is the one moment this would matter most, that voice was structurally somewhere else on the page, behind a different screen, never actually heard. The most direct fix wasn't writing new coaching content -- it already existed and was well written -- it was giving it an actual way to speak during the part that matters. Added a small, clearly set-apart spot that does two specific things: first, it directly and warmly calls out the moment a concept that was missed earlier gets successfully answered a few questions later, naming exactly why that moment matters rather than leaving it as a small unexplained label. Second, at a few natural spacing points through a session, it surfaces one of the research notes that were already sitting there unused. While confirming this worked, running it right before a timed practice exam surfaced a real, separate issue: that same new spot had no way of knowing a mode switch had happened, so it would keep showing something left over from whatever came right before it -- the same specific kind of leftover-state problem already caught and fixed in a few other corners of this app earlier on. Found and fixed that cleanly before calling it done, confirmed with the exact back-to-back sequence that exposed it in the first place.
Going back over the thing just built, by hand, from several directions, before calling it finishedAsked to keep refining and polishing the small coaching spot added just before this. Rather than treat the earlier work as finished, went back over it deliberately from several different directions: confirmed the quieter half of it -- the general research notes, as opposed to the one tied to a specific missed-then-recovered question -- genuinely also works in the other study modes, not only the main one it was first tested in, and confirmed a short session with too few questions for that to ever come up simply stays quiet rather than breaking. Confirmed the read-aloud button stays limited to the actual question and explanation and was never at risk of also reading this new coaching text out loud, which would have been an odd listening experience. Confirmed several of these moments happening back to back in one sitting each come through correctly rather than only the first one working. Took actual screenshots in both light and dark versions of the app to visually confirm this new spot and an existing, similarly-styled warning spot never land on screen at the same time in a way that would look cluttered, and confirmed the colors read clearly in both. Then found one more real, worthwhile gap while looking: a separate, existing moment -- correctly recovering a question that was previously answered wrong while feeling confident about it -- already had a warning shown the first time it went wrong, but nothing ever specifically marked the moment it was finally gotten right afterward, even though that pairing of being confidently wrong and then corrected is specifically called out elsewhere in this app as unusually effective for memory. Added that second, matching piece so succeeding there is now named and explained too, not just the original mistake.
A feature already there, examined closely rather than left alone, plus a precise hole found in a routine math checkAsked to keep going on the same refinement work. Looked closely at a separate, already-existing feature nearby -- a place to type out an explanation in one's own words and get real feedback on it, grounded in research on how producing an explanation yourself surfaces gaps that passive reading never does. It turned out to already be carefully built: handles an empty attempt, handles no key connected, correctly limited to the same study modes as everything else here, and already cleared out properly between questions the same deliberate way several other spots in this app were fixed to do earlier. Rather than touch something already working well, connected it instead to the newer sequencing work from a few turns back: when someone writes out an explanation for a question specifically placed right after one they'd just missed on the same idea, the feedback on what they wrote can now actually recognize that and speak to whether they've genuinely closed that particular gap, not just treat it as any other unconnected question. Also chased down a specific worry directly rather than letting it sit unverified: two different spots pull from the same small set of research notes using the same simple repeating counter, raising a real question of whether someone could see the exact same note twice in a row. Worked out the actual numbers by hand first, then ran the precise scenario to confirm directly rather than trust the arithmetic alone -- it turned out fine, built on a wrong headcount of how many notes exist in the first place. Separately, caught and corrected a small formatting slip from the write-up two turns back on the way through -- a closing tag that had been quietly squeezed onto the wrong line during an earlier edit, found by comparing what the raw file said against what a real screen actually rendered, not just by reading the text back.
Making the readiness number explain itself, and telling the coach to say what to do nextAsked to make the coaching area and the readiness gauge genuinely more useful and more polished. Started by looking at what they actually showed with realistic study history loaded: the gauge was just a bare number with no meaning attached, no sense of whether it was rising or falling, and no way to learn why it was what it was, while the coach area listed weak subjects but never said what to do about them. So the gauge now carries a plain-language label for where you stand, a small marker showing whether the score has moved over the past week (or since your very first session, labelled honestly when there is no week of history yet), and a tap-to-open explanation. That explanation shows, for each exam area, how many points it contributes out of how many it could, ordered by what is holding you back most, with a one-line reason that states both things that are true at once: how much of that area you have tried and how solid your recall is on what you have tried. If overconfidence is quietly costing points, it says so, with your own numbers, because that deduction used to be invisible. Every row is tappable and starts practice in that area. The coach area now opens with a single recommended next step and a button that starts it: a first session for newcomers, a short drill when one subject has been going badly, a blind spot you have never touched, reviews that have come due, a full simulation only when there are enough days left to learn from it, or a mock exam when everything looks strong. Below the usual weak-subject chips it adds a quick look at the last seven days, with questions, time and accuracy compared against the week before. The AI tutor now sees the same score breakdown and the same recommendation, so it never contradicts the screen. Along the way, fixed the row of four small numbers that left Day streak stranded alone on its own line on phones, and hid the two zero counters for AI-made questions when no key is connected and nothing has been made. Checked the arithmetic directly (the per-area points add up exactly to the raw score, and the leftover splits exactly into not-tried-enough versus not-solid-yet), walked every recommendation path including edge cases like a brand-new user and exam day approaching, and looked at it on a phone and a desktop in both light and dark. Testing also caught a real mistake in my own first draft: it would have suggested a six-hour simulation only three days before the exam, which leaves no time to act on what it shows, so that now requires at least five days.
Wiring the new score explanation and next-step coach into the rest of the appAsked to refine the readiness explanation and the coach recommendation just added, and to make sure they are fully woven into everything else rather than sitting on one screen. Went looking for every place where they were cut off, and found several.
