The end-of-session results screen said nothing about how the session had moved the score, so it now shows where the score started and where it ended, and offers the recommended next step right there so there is no dead end. A single session usually moves the score by a fraction of a point, which a whole-number gauge would hide behind a discouraging "24 to 24", so the change is shown to one decimal; if a session of misses does pull the score down, the screen says plainly why that is normal, because missed questions return to the start of the review schedule and come around sooner. The recommended step could also go stale: changing the exam date, reopening the app the next morning, or switching back to the study screen did not refresh it, so those now all do, and as a safety net, tapping a recommendation that has quietly gone out of date refreshes it and says so instead of launching something the student never saw the reasoning for. It now respects a half-finished session by offering to resume it, matching the resume banner instead of competing with it, and it notices flashcards that have genuinely come due, ignoring cards never yet seen since those are simply a fresh pool, not an obligation. The Exam Day screen gained a short readiness summary with the biggest gap and a link straight to the full explanation. The AI Tutor can now open that explanation when asked why the score is what it is. The coach line announces, once, when the score moves into a new range. Also added spoken labels and landmarks for screen readers, and made the scrolling respect the reduced-motion setting. Tested every one of these paths, including a genuine page reload to confirm a resumed session remembers the score it started from. A final look at tablet-sized screens also turned up the row of four small numbers sitting lopsided at the far right, so it now spreads evenly across its own row.
Making the score and coach move with you, and fixing a streak that reset every morningAsked to make the new score and coach truly live and connected. The readiness gauge now updates after every single answer instead of only when a session ends, and while you work through a quiz a small chip beside the progress bar shows how much this session has moved your score so far; it stays neutral in color when the score dips, since a dip is not a failure, and it is hidden during timed exams where nothing should distract you. A quiet timer refreshes the coach every minute and when you return to the app, so the recommendation and the countdown are right after midnight or after leaving the tab open all afternoon. The question-bank tiles now follow whether an AI key is set, and the tutor gained two shortcut chips, one asking why your score is what it is and one asking what to do next. While testing, a deeper problem turned up: study days were being recorded in universal time but compared against local midnight, so for anyone in an evening time zone the streak read zero every morning even after studying the day before. Study days are now recorded and compared as plain local calendar days, which I checked across several time zones and a daylight saving change. I also found that a session made entirely of correct answers can still dip the score slightly, because brand-new questions start on the first rung of the review schedule; the results screen, the live chip and the score explanation now say so honestly instead of blaming missed questions.
Showing whether your daily pace will get you through the material by exam dayAsked to keep adding value to the score explanation. A score tells you where you stand but not whether your current habits will get you where you need to be, so the explanation panel now has a short pace note when an exam date is set. It counts how many questions you have not yet tried before every domain reaches its coverage target, divides that by the days remaining, and compares it with how many questions a day you have actually been answering over the last two weeks. If you are keeping up it says so and tells you to keep the rhythm; if you are behind it says exactly how many more a day closes the gap; if you have not practiced in two weeks it says that plainly instead of dressing it up. Once everything is covered it switches to reminding you that the score now grows through spaced review. It is plain arithmetic rather than a prediction, so it never promises a score. Checked in light and dark themes on a phone-sized screen. A follow-up pass wired the pace note into the rest of the app: the Exam Day screen shows a one-line version, the AI Tutor knows your pace when you ask how you are doing, changing or clearing the exam date refreshes every one of those places at once, answering a new question shrinks the untried count live, and when no exam date is set the panel offers a button that jumps straight to the date field.
A full check-up of the app, looking for weak spots rather than adding featuresAsked to audit the whole app for anything overlooked. Ran automated checks on the question bank, on how the app copes with bad or missing saved data, on layout at four screen widths in both themes, on text contrast, and on keyboard use. The good news first: all 458 questions have a valid answer, four distinct choices, a written reason for every choice, and no duplicate numbers; the answer position is shuffled every session, so the heavy lean toward the first choice in the stored data never shows; and the app starts and works normally even when saved data is garbled, blocked by the browser, or full. A backup-and-restore round trip brought the score, the explanation panel and the recommendation back exactly. What needed fixing: on the narrowest phones the domain legend at the top of the study screen clipped its labels, so it now wraps; two small controls were too short to tap comfortably and were enlarged; a muted grey in dark mode was a hair under the readable minimum and was lightened; the big study-mode card on the home screen and the highlighted key terms inside questions could only be used by touch or mouse, so they now work from the keyboard too; the key-term popup now announces itself as a dialog, takes focus when it opens, closes with Escape and hands focus back; and the phone's browser bar now matches the chosen light or dark theme, with the usual add-to-home-screen settings in place. One thing I did not change because it is about the questions themselves: in 54 percent of the stored questions the correct choice is also the longest one, against 25 percent expected by chance, and in 38 questions it is at least 30 percent longer than the next. A sharp test-taker can learn to pick the longest answer, which would flatter the score. The questions the AI writes already avoid this; the stored ones would need their wrong choices rewritten. Followed up by doing exactly that: in 37 of those 38 questions the three wrong choices were lengthened or the correct one tightened so all four read at similar length, keeping every wrong choice clearly wrong, every right answer unchanged in meaning and position, and every written reason still accurate. The one left alone is a numeric answer where length means nothing. Questions where the correct choice is at least 30 percent longer than the next went from 38 to 1, and the average gap between right and wrong choices fell from about 14 percent to about 10 percent. A milder lean remains in roughly 57 more questions that are 20 percent or more longer, which a later pass could even out.
Checking speed and what happens when the AI connection failsKept going on the check-up with two more tests. On speed, the app opens in about a third of a second, recalculating the readiness score takes a fraction of a millisecond, starting a session and answering a question each take well under 30 milliseconds, and left idle it does no background work that slows the screen, so nothing needed changing. On the AI side, simulated a rejected key, too many requests, a server fault, a dropped connection and a garbled reply. Every case already ended cleanly: the typing indicator cleared, the send button came back, and the message said what to do. Two of the messages were still written for engineers, though. A dropped connection read "Failed to fetch" and a garbled reply showed a raw technical parsing complaint. Those now say "Could not reach the AI service, check your internet connection and try again" and "The AI sent back a reply this app could not read, this is usually a one-off", and the app still retries quietly in the background before showing either.
Putting the recommended next step where the eye lands firstAsked to keep improving the layout, so looked at the study screen as a whole on a large monitor and on a phone. Two things stood out. The recommended next step, the single most useful thing on the page, was buried in the coach card well below the fold, while a second gold button for the general adaptive session sat higher up and competed with it. The recommendation now sits directly under the readiness score and the one-line coach comment, before the domain chart, so the first screen answers what to do next. On phones the domain legend squeezed each long domain name into narrow half-width boxes that wrapped to four lines, so on narrow screens it is now a single clean column with the percentage on the right. Everything that used to refresh the recommendation still does, and the tests found it in its new place without changes.
Making two open windows share one set of progressAsked to make sure everything is optimized, dynamic and properly integrated, so checked whether every screen agrees with every other after studying, resetting and switching themes. They did: the readiness number, the Exam Day summary, the tutor and the stats row all matched after a session, and after a reset nothing stale was left behind. Two real gaps turned up, though. First, if the app was open in two windows at once, such as the installed app plus a browser tab, whichever window saved last silently erased the other's progress. Now, when one window saves, the other picks the new progress up straight away, stays on the screen it was showing, and says so in the coach line; a window in the middle of a quiz is left alone so nobody loses their place, and tests confirmed there is no back-and-forth loop between windows. Second, rating a flashcard updated the stats row but not the recommended next step, which counts flashcards that are due, so that recommendation could lag behind. It now refreshes after every rating.
Making the calculator practice part of every adaptive sessionAsked to make sure the calculator tool is excellent and a true value add, and to weave it into the adaptive session. Until now the calculator practice sat in its own corner with a fixed list of seventeen problems, so a diligent student would eventually see repeats, and nothing you did there touched your normal sessions. Now the tool can build fresh problems on demand in thirteen styles, from a simple lump sum up to monthly loan payments and payments due at the start of the period, with new amounts, rates and time spans each time, and once the fixed list has been seen it mixes in new ones. Every generated problem was checked by working the balance forward month by month, independently of the tool, across thousands of random draws, and the answer always closed to the penny. The bigger change is that once you have answered a couple of weeks of questions, an adaptive session now swaps in one or occasionally two real calculation questions at your calculator level, with answer choices built from the exact slips people make, such as forgetting to convert to monthly or leaving the calculator in the wrong mode. If you miss one, the step-by-step key-press walkthrough appears, with a button to practice a similar one on the calculator right there, and the quiz is still waiting when you close it. Those answers count toward your calculator level and your list of slips to watch, show up in a short card on the results screen, and are mentioned to the tutor, while staying out of your missed-question and spaced-review lists because they are made fresh each time. The calculator itself also gained a short status line showing your level and what is needed to move up, and its instructions fold away once you have solved a few problems. Tests covered the injection, answering, finishing, resuming a saved session and opening the calculator over a quiz, with no errors.
Tying the calculator into the coach and tidying its buttonsAsked to make sure the calculator work is properly integrated, dynamic and polished, so went back over every place it touches. One real gap: if calculation questions keep going wrong in your sessions, the coach had no way to say so. Now, when you have missed most of them and have not opened the calculator for a few days, the recommended next step becomes a short calculator practice, naming the slip that shows up most, and it steps aside as soon as you use the tool. It sits below the urgent items such as a half-finished session, an exam that is close, or a weak domain, so it never crowds them out. Also fixed on the phone: the two buttons under a missed calculation question were different sizes with text lined up differently, so they now stretch evenly and centre their labels, and the practice button has a shorter name. Checked in both light and dark, on the quiz and on the results screen, with no errors.
Fitting the app to a phone turned on its side or folded openAsked to make sure the layout is optimized when the phone rotates to landscape or changes posture. Tested the app at five sizes, a normal phone upright and sideways, a small phone sideways, a half-open foldable and a small tablet, across every tab, the quiz, the flashcards and the calculator. Nothing spilled off the side anywhere, but the app had no special handling for a screen that is wide and short, so the header alone used up most of a sideways phone and each quiz question needed a lot of scrolling. Now, on a short wide screen, the header shrinks, the tab bar stays pinned to the top so you can always switch sections, the quiz and flashcard cards use less padding, and the calculator sits beside its problem, staying put while you read, instead of far below it. The calculator instructions also start folded in that shape so the problem is visible right away. Edges now respect a camera notch or a fold hinge on either side. Rotating in the middle of a quiz question, or with the calculator open, keeps your place and your answer, and the calculator returns to a single column when you turn back upright. No errors appeared in any of these tests.
Making the right answer harder to spot by lengthPicked up the leftover from the earlier length check: questions where the correct choice was clearly longer than the others, which lets a test taker guess by eye without knowing the material. Of 55 such questions, 43 were evened out, mostly by trimming wordy correct answers down to what actually matters, and in a few cases by giving the shorter wrong answers a little more substance. No facts were changed and no new claims were added, only filler words and repeated qualifiers were removed. Twelve mild cases remain where the gap is small and natural, and one ethics question was left alone because its wording is unusual enough that it deserves a separate look. The app's own content check still reports no problems, and all tests pass.
Checking the screens nobody tests: tiny covers, keyboards and old backupsAsked to look at something not yet checked, so tried three things. First, the very narrow front screen of a folding phone, about 280 pixels wide. At 320 pixels everything was fine, but at 280 the Study, Flashcards and Exam Day screens could be dragged sideways because a few rows of stats and buttons refused to shrink. Those rows now wrap or stack, and all six tabs, the quiz and the calculator fit without sideways scrolling. Second, keyboard and screen-reader use of the calculator: opening it now moves focus into it, Escape closes it without leaving the quiz underneath, focus returns to the button you used, and it is announced as a dialog. Third, restoring a backup made before the calculator features existed: nothing broke, and the missing calculator records are now filled in on restore so the level, slips and stats start clean instead of empty. All earlier tests still pass.
Talking to the tutor about the question in front of youAsked to swap the "Explain it back to me" button for a way to ask the tutor about the question on screen and talk it through. Now, after you answer, an "Ask the tutor about this" button opens a chat right under the question. The tutor already knows the question, all four choices, which one you picked, the written explanations and, for calculation questions, the verified calculator steps, so you never have to retype anything. You can type any question you like, or tap a starter such as "Why is my pick wrong?", "Give me an example" or "Quiz me on this". The old explaining-it-back exercise is still there as a starter chip, which drops a sentence stem into the box so you can write your own explanation and get specific feedback on it. Replies are kept short and conversational, the tutor is told to correct mistakes rather than just agree, and it remembers the back and forth within that question. Moving to the next question starts a fresh chat, and an answer that arrives late is dropped instead of landing on the wrong question. Without an API key it says so kindly instead of failing. It is also wired into the rest of the app: the app keeps count of which questions you had to talk through, the results screen lists them with a button to revisit just those questions, the main tutor knows which topics you tend to need help on, calculation questions get a starter that walks through the key presses, and older backups restore cleanly. Tested on phone and landscape, with errors, slow replies and double taps all handled.
Checking the questions for stale facts and repeatsAsked to keep the quality of the questions very high, so audited them two ways. First, every question that depends on a dollar limit, an age or a tax rule was checked against current law: the 2026 limits for retirement accounts, health savings, gifts and the estate exemption were all right, and the arithmetic in every worked question came out correctly. One real gap turned up: the age when required withdrawals begin is 73 for people born 1951 through 1959 but 75 for anyone born in 1960 or later, and the question, the reference sheet and the flashcard only mentioned 73. All three now give both ages. Second, a similarity scan found fourteen pairs of questions that asked about the same concept with nearly the same answer, such as two on call options, two on price-to-earnings and two on the real estate distribution rule, which wasted slots in a session and made coverage look better than it was. One of each pair was replaced with a question on a topic the bank barely covered: inflation-protected Treasuries, savings bonds, alpha, covered calls, bond convexity, closed-end funds, the investment income tax, installment sales, the capital loss limit, donating appreciated stock, spousal IRAs, 457(b) plans, cash balance plans and net present value. Each new question was written with four plausible wrong answers, an explanation for every choice and balanced answer lengths, and passes the app's own quality check. While doing this a real bug appeared: if someone had missed one of the retired questions, a review of missed questions could fail to start. The app now quietly drops retired questions from saved progress when it opens and when a backup is restored, and a review with nothing left to show simply does nothing. A last lint pass over all 458 questions for structure found every answer key lining up with its explanation and no stray typos; the only fixes needed were five wrong-answer explanations on two calculation questions that said little more than too high or too low, which now say exactly which slip produces each wrong number. The flashcards got the same treatment: three cards that repeated another card (full retirement age, endowment effect and the back-end ratio were each defined twice) were swapped out, and six new cards were added for topics the new questions cover, such as covered calls, inflation-protected Treasuries, 457(b) plans, installment sales, the investment income tax and the Crummey power, plus spousal IRAs, status quo bias and net present value. The count is now 205, and saved flashcard ratings for retired cards are dropped quietly. The same bar now applies to questions the app writes with AI: a new question is rejected if its correct answer is clearly the longest, if any choice is an all-of-the-above style option, if its explanations do not agree with the answer key, or if it reads like a question already in the bank for that domain. Reworded versions of a question you have already seen are exempt from the repeat check, since being on the same concept is their purpose, and both AI instructions now ask for explanations that begin with Correct or Wrong so the check has something to verify. A last pass looked at wording rather than facts: in a dozen questions the right answer was the only one phrased in a different grammatical shape from the others, which let you spot it without knowing the material, so those wrong answers were rewritten to match.
Practising with a whole client case, the way the exam presents itMost questions on the real exam are not stand-alone: they arrive wrapped in a paragraph about one client, followed by several questions that each reach into a different subject. The app had only three such cases and no way to work one from start to finish, so this was the thinnest part of the practice. There is now a Case studies card on the study screen. Pick a client and you answer all of their questions in order with the same facts pinned above every question, so you practise pulling the numbers and details out of a story rather than answering from memory. Three new cases were written, a physician couple with a concentrated stock holding, a retired couple deciding when to claim Social Security and how to leave money to children and charity, and a dental practice owner planning a sale, and the divorce case was extended, for six cases and 38 questions in all. Each case ends with its own score, shows your best result on the picker, can be resumed if you stop partway, and is offered by the coach once you have answered enough questions to benefit. Case questions never get swapped for AI rewordings, because a reworded question could drift away from the facts printed above it. When a case ends you get a question-by-question recap with the subject of each, a comparison with your previous best, and a button straight to the next case. The study card keeps a running tally of how many cases you have tried, and the AI tutor can start one for you if you ask for exam-style practice. Your case scores are included in backups. With an API key connected, a button on the case picker has the AI write a brand-new case on demand, aimed at your weaker areas; it has to pass the same checks as other AI questions (a right answer that is not the longest, no giveaway wording, no repeats of the existing bank) or it is thrown away, and you can remove any you do not want.
Practising the exam's formulas with fresh numbersTime-value-of-money had a hands-on practice tool, but the other fifteen formulas the exam provides (expected return, the Sharpe ratio, required minimum distributions, taxable-equivalent yield, a like-kind exchange and the rest) were only printed in a list, and recognising a formula is not the same as being able to use it. Formula drills writes a new problem for each of them every time, with a number you type in rather than a choice to pick, so there is nothing to guess from. Afterwards it shows the working one line at a time and, when your answer is wrong, checks it against the slips people most often make, such as applying beta to the whole market return instead of the premium over the risk-free rate, or compressing the real-return formula into a simple subtraction, and names the one you made. Formulas you get wrong come up more often, each formula in the Reference list has a Practise button and a running score, the coach suggests a formula that keeps going wrong, and the AI tutor can open the drills for you.
Knowing whether you are fast enoughThe exam gives about two minutes a question, 85 in each three-hour section with no time carried between sections, and until now the timed practice only showed a countdown, so you could finish a mock and still not know whether the pace was the problem. Every question is now timed (only while you are actually looking at it, so a phone call in the middle does not count). During a mock or the full exam a small chip beside the clock says whether you are on pace, ahead or behind where you would be by now, in amber rather than red, and its tooltip gives the figures. The results screen shows your average against the budget and lists the three slowest questions with how much of your time they took and whether you got them right, which is usually where time is being lost for no gain. The Exam Day tab has a new Pacing card with the checkpoint numbers to aim for, such as question 28 by the one-hour mark, and your own averages by kind of question and by subject.
Checking the app against the official exam outlineI compared every topic in the app with the official list of 70 exam topics across the eight domains, and the lists matched. Then I searched the questions and flashcards for the specific ideas under each topic and found thin spots: consumer protection laws, education funding, annuities, reverse mortgages, trust taxation, stock-based pay, charitable and generation-skipping trusts, and how to talk with clients through grief or stress. I added 73 questions and 17 flashcards for those, then ran a second pass on named laws and rules that still had only one question (FATCA, Medicare surcharges, portability of a spouse's estate exemption, the home-sale exclusion, wash sales, and how to handle transference and motivational interviewing) and added 32 more. Finally I checked the glossary itself against a list of about 500 exam terms and found that many everyday ones, such as mutual fund, balance sheet, COBRA, probate and stock options, had no definition at all. I wrote definitions for the missing terms, which took the glossary from 222 to 598 entries. Last, I counted questions under each of the 70 official topics and added 38 more where the count was lowest: charitable and gift tax strategies, market cycles, crises such as job loss or a spouse's death, the steps of the planning process, trust taxation, family business transfers, divorce and special-needs planning. A final pass went concept by concept through about 540 ideas that can appear on the exam, from plan-administration rules and Medicaid look-backs to bond tax rules, insurance forms, SEC advertising and privacy rules, and present-value and return arithmetic. Wherever an idea had zero or one question, I added 98 more questions, after removing any that repeated a question already in the app, and rebalanced the answer choices so the correct one is not simply the longest. The app's own topic-coverage check then showed six topics still thinly covered (fiduciary standard, education funding, risk exposures, choosing an insurer, picking a business retirement plan, and planning after a death), so I added 14 more questions for them. I then compared the app with what the big review companies (Kaplan, Dalton, College for Financial Planning) and the published CFP formula sheets list, and found that the theories of why interest rates differ by maturity, the bond price-change math from duration, two-stock portfolio risk, correlation and forward rates were missing, so I added 12 questions and 8 glossary terms for them. Finally I went through the files you uploaded: the Investment Planning one-pager was already well covered, but the ideas it leans on that had only one or two questions (core and satellite investing, sector rotation, the weak form of market efficiency, which risk measure fits a given R-squared, which bonds get called, and how rental income and suspended losses work) got new ones. Your screenshots turned up two more things: the rules for how long the IRS can assess tax and how long you have to claim a refund had no questions at all, so I added those along with the order of loss limits for S corporation owners and the 10-year rule for inherited IRAs, and the pop-up that explains a highlighted term was drawing faintly on an iPhone, so it is now built to be fully painted before it appears. The formula sheet and its practice drills grew from 15 to 31 formulas (Treynor, Jensen's alpha, information ratio, effective annual rate, geometric mean, two-stock portfolio risk, correlation, modified duration and price change, forward rates, cap rate, coinsurance, and the balance-sheet ratios), each with fresh numbers, step-by-step working and a warning about the usual slip. One more gap turned up when checking what gets saved: when you meet a question a second time and the AI writes a fresh version of it, that new version used to vanish when the session ended. Each accepted rewrite is now kept with your other generated questions (up to three per original), so it is saved on the device, included in the backup file, and comes back later as a new question; a backup made by an older version of the app is also topped up with any newer fields it lacks when you restore it. The legal and tax figures were written from memory, so check them against current rules before relying on them.
Catching look-alike concepts before they become a habitA lot of exam misses are not missing knowledge but two things swapped: a Roth and a traditional IRA, Section 1245 and 1250 property, a charitable remainder and a charitable lead trust, the Sharpe and Treynor ratios, an occurrence and a claims-made policy. The app now knows about twenty-nine such pairs. When the answer you picked belongs to one half of a pair and the right answer belongs to the other, the two-line contrast appears right under the feedback, because correcting a confusion while it is fresh works best. The swap is counted; once the same pair has been mixed up twice, a note on the Study tab spells out the difference and a couple of questions on that pair are guaranteed a slot in your next adaptive sessions, until correct answers on it wear the count back down. Checking the question bank against these pairs showed several had almost no practice questions (claims-made policies, homeowners forms, nonqualified annuities, incentive versus nonqualified options), so thirty contrast questions were written for them. The tutor now knows your miss pattern and your current mix-ups too, and offers a one-tap chip to untangle the pair, so its answers start from what is actually going wrong for you. Honest limit: detection is by wording, so an unusually phrased question can be missed, and the pair list is a curated starting set, not every possible confusion.
Sorting every miss by why it happened, and forecasting your paceTwo additions that work without being asked. First, every wrong answer is now quietly sorted into a kind of error: misreading the question (a NOT, EXCEPT or LEAST that was skimmed past), a calculation or setup slip, overconfidence (you marked it confident), answering too fast, a gap you have hit before, or a plain knowledge gap. This follows the idea behind the error log in the shared study folder, but is filled in for you. The label and a one-line fix appear right under the feedback, the Detailed Diagnosis card shows your mix, and when one pattern clearly dominates the coach says so, because the cure for misreading is a technique and the cure for a gap is more study. Qualifier words in questions are also marked in study sessions, and left plain in mock exams where the real test gives no help. Second, once you have set an exam date, the study plan compares how many questions are still unseen with your pace over the last two weeks and says whether you will get through everything before exam day, or how many a day you would need. Honest limits: the error labels are rules of thumb based on wording, timing and your confidence rating, not a verdict, and the forecast counts first passes only.
Looking for the same failure everywhere elseAfter the repeat-question problem was traced to one overly strict length rule, every other automatic generator was checked for the same family of trouble. Three things turned up. First, failures were retried without any brake: a refresh that could not pass the checks was attempted again every session, and bulk generation could try again every few answers. All automatic generation now shares one brake that pauses for one, two, four, eight and then fifteen minutes after a failure and clears on the first success, and a repeat question that could not be refreshed is remembered for three days (ten minutes if the cause was a network error) rather than retried each time. Second, the case-study generator was still a manual "write a new case" button using the strictest checks on every question, so it now writes new cases by itself once only one is left untried, at most one every twelve hours, and quietly accepts a slightly looser answer-length balance on its last try. Third, its failure message told you to try again by hand; it now says it will try again on its own. What was checked and found fine: the question bank itself passes every generation rule except four older questions, so the rules match the standard the bank was built to, and the other AI features only show an error when you asked for something directly.
Why a repeat question sometimes stayed word-for-word the sameWhen you meet a question again, the app asks the AI for a fresh version and checks it before showing it. One check rejects answers that are much longer than the wrong choices, since a long right answer is a giveaway. That rule was a pure ratio, which is harsh on questions whose choices are short names, such as "Active listening" beside "The primacy and recency effects": the ratio looks big but the difference is a handful of characters and tells nobody anything. Three attempts could fail on that alone, and the original wording was shown with a long apologetic tag. The rule now also requires a real difference in length (sixteen characters or more) before it counts as a giveaway, so those variants come through, while padded sentence-length answers are still rejected. The tag is now just "repeat", with the detail left in a tooltip.
Taking buttons away that the app should press for youThe "Expand weak areas now" button was not doing its job, and it was also the wrong idea: the app already watches how many fresh questions are left and writes more, ahead of running low, so asking a person to trigger it by hand put the work on the wrong side. It is gone, along with the manual "Generate more flashcards" card and the tutor shortcut for generating practice. A failed generation now retries by itself within a few answers rather than telling you to try again. The two quality checks in Settings (content and syllabus coverage) used to wait for a click; they now run every time Settings opens. Podcast episodes are written automatically when you pick one that does not exist yet, after a short pause so flicking through the menus does not spend a generation on every stop; the button only remains to rewrite an episode. What was kept on purpose are things that are genuinely your choice, such as shuffling cards, picking a session, or asking the tutor a question.
Going back through the shared study folder for what was still missingRead every remaining file in the AdviseWise folder and checked each against the app instead of assuming the earlier passes had caught it all. Most of it was already here: the twenty-two behavioral finance biases, the tax topics and the conflict-of-interest steps. What was genuinely absent was the exam-day logistics list (practice drive, calculator memory and preferences reset, clothing, food), so it is now a tick-off checklist on the Exam Day tab that saves with your progress and backups. Eight flashcards were added for the Social Security survivor, disability and divorced-spouse eligibility rules, the claiming-timing exception, the 90-day and 30-day self-reporting windows, the three duty groups, the three conflict steps and what counts as financial advice. A follow-up pass then compared the app against CFP Board's official list of seventy exam topics: all seventy are present. Counting questions per topic showed General Principles running a little light against its fifteen percent exam weight and a handful of topics thin, so thirty-six new questions went to education needs analysis (the growth-adjusted rate and three-step method from the folder), gift basis and the kiddie tax, the planning process, financial ratios, insurance principles and company ratings, money scripts and grief, retirement needs, Medicare and Medicaid rules, the investment policy statement, charitable limits, installment payment of estate tax, disclaimers and special needs trusts. Honest limit: the provider comparison and the error-log template are study-planning material rather than exam content, so they were noted but not copied in; the app already logs every miss with its category automatically.
Making the readiness number a real estimateAsked to make sure the readiness meter is accurate, live and tied into everything else. Looking at how it was built showed several problems: it only counted how many times in a row you had answered a question correctly, so someone getting nearly everything right still scored low for weeks; it ignored how long it had been since you last saw something, so a score would stay high while you forgot things; it counted 40 percent of a subject as full coverage; and it ignored flashcards, formula practice and mock exams entirely. It now estimates your chance of getting a typical exam question right in each subject, and shows the score as how far above guessing that puts you, weighted by each subject's share of the exam. The estimate uses how you did the first time you met each question (the best guide to questions you have not seen), how well answered questions have stuck in review, a gradual fade for anything overdue, your flashcards, your formula drills, and your recent timed mock exams, which pull the estimate toward what actually happened under time pressure. It starts at zero with no data, never claims more than the evidence supports, and shows a likely range that narrows as you answer more. The gauge itself also shows the estimated exam accuracy under the score (marked as an early estimate until enough questions are tried), and the ring, number and estimate refresh when you come back to the app, so a score that has faded while you were away is never shown stale. The breakdown now states the implied exam accuracy, each subject shows its own expected accuracy, the tutor and the Exam Day tab quote the same numbers, and scores saved under the old method are left out of the weekly trend so the two are never compared. It is still an estimate, not a prediction of passing, because the real passing score is not published.
Tutor help on more screensAsked to keep the tutor useful everywhere. Flashcards now have an "Explain it with an example" button next to the memory trick: it gives a short worked example and says how the exam tends to test the idea. The Exam Day tab has a "Talk it through with your tutor" row whose buttons change with how many days you have left (a plan for the days remaining, an eve-of-exam walkthrough, pacing for the 170 questions), and the Tools tab has buttons for choosing a tool and practising a TVM problem. These open the Tutor tab and send the question for you, so the tutor already knows where you were. The tutor still only knows what the app tells it, and it can be wrong, so check figures against the official sources.
Fewer repeated questionsReported that questions you have already seen kept showing up with a "repeat" tag. That tag means the app tried to reword the question and the attempt failed. Three changes: the app now tries the newest AI model first and falls back to the older one if the service does not recognise it, a fourth and final try accepts a reworded question that is slightly uneven in answer length rather than showing the identical one, and a failed reword is retried after an hour instead of three days. Tapping the tag now shows what went wrong. I could not see your phone's real error, so I cannot be sure which of these was the cause; if the tag keeps appearing, tap it and tell me what it says.
Checking the app against the official exam handbookAsked to make sure everything needed to pass is covered. The October 2026 CFP Board candidate handbook confirms the eight domains and their weights, the 170-question format, the approved calculators (the HP 10bII+ is on the list), and that exams through the October 2026 window test 2026 tax law, so those parts already matched. What was missing were 2026 figures the exam commonly uses. Added to Key Numbers, and to questions and flashcards, were the SIMPLE IRA limit, the defined contribution and defined benefit limits, the pay thresholds for highly compensated and key employees, the Roth and traditional IRA phase-out ranges, the Social Security taxable maximum, earnings test and credit amount, the Medicare Part A and Part B figures, the FSA limits and the QLAC limit. The retirement-plan figures come from the IRS notice and release, and the Social Security taxable maximum from ssa.gov. The Medicare and FSA figures come from summaries of the official announcements, and the credit amount and earnings test limits from one secondary source, so check those against ssa.gov and cms.gov. The results line on the Exam Day tab was also corrected.
Drilling one topic at a timeAsked to keep making the app powerful enough to pass. The Syllabus checklist now shows, under each of the 70 official topics, how many matching questions you have seen and how you are doing on them, with a Drill button that starts 12 questions on that topic, missed ones first. The match between questions and topics is by keywords, so it is approximate. The coach now suggests drilling a topic where you are under 65% across at least six attempts, the tutor is told your three shakiest topics, and on the day before and the day of the exam the coach tells you to keep it light instead of starting another session.
A plan for today, and a tutor that can run itAsked to make sure the tutor can say what to do step by step and what the best use of time is. The Study tab now has a Today's plan card: an ordered list built from how many days you have left, what is due for review, which topics are weak, what you have missed, and what you have already done today, sized to the time you pick (20, 45 or 90 minutes). The order changes with the countdown: build coverage and review early, repair weak spots and rehearse the full exam in the last two weeks, consolidate in the last few days, and keep the last day light. The tutor can build the same plan, explain each step in plain language, and start a step when you say yes. The reasons given are the better-supported study methods: testing yourself, spacing reviews, mixing topics, going back over mistakes, and explaining concepts in your own words. The time estimates are rough, and the plan only knows what the app can see.
Bigger, smoother buttonsThe Start buttons on Today's plan, the 20/45/90 minute choices and the topic Drill buttons are now at least finger-sized (44 pixels) and respond when you hover or press them, matching the rest of the app.
Fixing blank AI answersSome AI requests came back with nothing to show, which is what produced "no usable text" on the flashcard example button. The app now tells the AI not to spend its budget on hidden thinking, retries with more room if a reply still comes back empty, and says why when it fails.
Checking us against the test-prep providers' public topic listsCompared our coverage with CFP Board's published topic list and what the major prep companies and recent candidates publicly say matters. The big structure matched, and the real gap was the 2025 tax law changes (no tax on tips, overtime and new-car loan interest, Trump accounts, the new small-business-stock tiers, HSA and SALT changes), plus a few small items (Forms 2848 and 8821, the tax-preparer disclosure rule, and §1244 stock). Added 15 original practice questions, 10 flashcards and 6 key numbers for them. No provider's paid or leaked material was used; everything is written from public sources and checked against them.
Fact-checking the numbers against the government sourcesRechecked the 2026 limits against the IRS notices (retirement plan limits, the inflation adjustments), the Social Security Administration (taxable maximum, earnings test, credit amount) and Medicare. Everything matched. Filled in numbers that were missing: the 2026 tax brackets, kiddie tax, AMT exemption, charitable IRA gift limit and adoption credit, and spelled out the SALT cap by year.
Connecting every question to its syllabus topicAbout three in ten questions were not linked to any official topic, so they never counted toward your per-topic accuracy or showed up in a topic drill. Widened the matching (options, Medicare, home and auto insurance, behavioral finance, consumer-credit laws, savings bonds, the new 2025 tax-law items and more) so all but one are now linked. Your weak-topic suggestions and the Study plan now draw on the whole question bank.
Making each study mode earn its placeThe 24-question mock was timed at 35 minutes, which is about 1.5 times faster than the real exam's pace, so it overstated how rushed the real exam is. It is now a timed checkpoint at the real pace (about 51 minutes) and its score still counts toward your readiness. Every mode now says when to use it and shows when you last did it and how you scored. The checkpoint also appears in Today's plan about once a week, and the tutor can start it for you.
Training how to read a case, not just answer itMost of a case-study question is a reading task: find the two or three facts that decide it, ignore the ones that only look relevant, and notice what is really being asked. Case text now color-codes figures, goals, red flags and accounts; you can tap the sentences you would circle before answering; and afterward the app shows which facts decided the answer, which only looked relevant, and how many you caught. A short line under each question also decodes words like "most", "if", "first" and "not". The same aids show on other scenario questions, and switch off in the timed exam modes so those stay realistic. Every case question has its deciding facts written out, and AI-written cases include them too.
Wiring case reading into the rest of the appMissing a case question after you circled the wrong facts is now sorted as "missed a deciding fact" instead of a generic knowledge gap, so your miss pattern and the tutor can tell reading problems from knowledge problems. The tutor knows which facts decide a question and which sentences you circled, and offers a "Which facts mattered?" button after you answer. Each case now shows how many of its deciding facts you caught, and the plan shown before a case explains the circle-then-check routine.
A calculator reminder that fits the problem in front of youThe pre-answer calculator check used to be the same paragraph on every time-value-of-money question. It now reads the question itself and says what matters for that one: which key you are solving for, whether it is a monthly or annual problem, whether payments start at the beginning or end of the period (or there are none), and which numbers need the negative sign. Your personal slip reminder only appears when it applies to this problem, so a monthly-conversion tip no longer shows on an annual question.
Waiting for an AI answer should look like waitingWhen the tutor is writing an explanation, a memory trick, a glossary example or a podcast episode, the box used to just go a bit dim, which looks the same as "broken". Each one now shows a slim moving bar, and if the wait runs past ten seconds a line appears saying it is still working and can take up to a minute. Screen readers are told when something is loading and when the answer lands, and the tutor's typing dots now say "Tutor is typing". Along the way, a plain fact question about a dollar limit was being labelled a calculator slip; those misses are now labelled by what they were, and the calculator tip only mentions BEGIN/END when the question actually has payments.
Plans for real study days, not 20-minute scrapsWith the exam about two weeks out, the 20, 45 and 90 minute choices on Today's plan no longer matched how you actually study. The choices are now 2 hours, 2.5 hours and 3 hours, and a longer day gets a longer plan: a second adaptive round, extra drills on your next-weakest topics, and a reminder to take a break halfway. A shorter number saved from before is treated as 2.5 hours.
The plan learns how long you actually studyUntil you pick 2, 2.5 or 3 hours, Today's plan now follows your last week of real study time instead of a fixed guess. The header shows how much of the plan is still left today, and if it is evening and the rest would run past bedtime, it suggests finishing tomorrow rather than cutting sleep.
A tutor that teaches the way the research says to, and adapts to the momentThe tutor already used retrieval practice and spacing. It now also follows a short list of well-supported teaching moves: ask before explaining something new (pretesting), give small hints before the answer, show one worked example and then fade the help for topics you are new to, skip the basics for topics you are strong in, have you explain why in your own words, compare look-alike ideas side by side, change the numbers to check you can transfer an idea, and end by naming what to retest in a couple of days. In the chat after each question it picks the one move that fits that moment: sure-and-wrong gets a precise correction you restate, wrong-and-unsure gets a hint first, right-but-unsure gets reinforced, right-and-confident gets a harder variation. The evidence behind these is real but varies in strength, and the tutor is told not to overstate it.
Balancing the question bank to the exam's weightsComparing how many questions each exam area has against how much of the exam it is worth showed General Principles of Financial Planning running about twenty questions short, with Retirement and Investments slightly behind. Several narrow topics had only six or seven questions each: insurance needs analysis, postmortem estate planning, special needs planning, annuities, eldercare, nonqualified plans and the income tax of trusts. Ninety-four new questions were added, aimed at exactly those spots (a later duplicate check removed the ones that turned out to repeat an existing question), along with eight flashcards for ideas those questions introduced, with the 2026 figures checked against IRS and CFP Board sources.
Never asking the same thing twiceA check of the whole question bank found no identical questions, but about a hundred that tested the same fact as another with different wording, such as two separate questions on the 30-day wash sale window, or on how long a disclaimer can wait. Seeing the same idea twice makes you feel more ready than you are, and it wastes minutes you could spend on something new, so the repeats were removed and whatever you had already answered on them carries over to the one that stays. The app now also checks every practice set before it starts, so two questions that ask the same thing can never land in the same session, and a replacement from the same topic is used instead. New questions the AI writes are compared with everything already in the bank before they are saved, and any that repeat an existing idea are dropped. When you miss a question, the reworded retry that follows it is still shown on purpose, because being able to answer the same idea in new words is a better sign of learning than recognizing one wording.
Ideas come back as new questions, not the same onesWhen a question is due to return, or you missed it, the app now picks a question you have not seen on the same topic instead of showing the old one again. Get the new one right and the old one counts as reviewed on schedule; get it wrong and it goes back to the start. This is on purpose: seeing the same question again mostly tests whether you remember that question, and the real exam will not use any of these questions. Research on test-enhanced learning (Butler, 2010) found that practice retrieving an idea carried over to new questions on it, and a recent Carnegie Mellon study (still a preprint) found that people who answered different questions on an idea did better on unseen ones than people who repeated the same questions, even though repeating helped on the repeated ones. New questions are limited, though: at two to three hours a day you would use roughly nine hundred to fourteen hundred before the exam (an estimate), and the bank has about nine hundred. So the plan now shows how many are still new to you, and when a topic has none left the app uses a reworded copy if you have an AI key. Without one it hides the choices until you have answered in your own head, because pulling an answer out of memory beats spotting it in a list (Rowland, 2014).
The tutor decides when you need a question written just for youAnother question from the bank is a good retest when it covers the same part of the idea. It is a poor one when you keep choosing the same wrong answer, when you were sure and wrong, or when no unseen question tests the same point. In those cases the app now writes a new question on the same idea, built around the mistake you actually make, and keeps the bank question as a fallback if the writing fails. In the chat after a question, the tutor makes the same call: it can write a new question and put it next, and it is told not to do that for a careless slip, for something you have not been taught yet, or for a 2026 figure it is not sure of. Written questions are not as carefully checked as the built-in ones, so the app uses only the checked ones in the last two days before the exam.
Flashcards now follow your gapsThe deck used to be ordered by review timing and how weak each whole domain is. Now it also looks at the questions you missed, or were sure about and got wrong, and moves up the cards that cover those same ideas, even if the card was not due yet. Cards in your weak official subtopics move up too. A card you have missed three or more times gets a worked example automatically and asks you to say it in your own words before you flip it. Each card shows a short "why now" line, and the top of the deck says what is coming next. Domains are mixed so you do not get a long run of one topic, and mixed practice has beaten one-topic-at-a-time practice on later tests in studies of interleaving (for example Rohrer and Taylor, 2007, which used math problems, so how far it carries to flashcards is less certain). Within a week of the exam, new cards are held back so review comes first. If you have an AI key, the app also writes a few new cards aimed at your weakest subtopic when it has few cards. A "Cards on what I missed" button starts a set of just those cards, today's plan can start the same set, and the tutor can start it for you when you ask. Which signals count most, and the cutoffs, are my judgment, not tested numbers.
Today's plan can now run as one guided sessionBefore, the plan was a list of separate Start buttons, and each one ended on its own. Now "Start my session" in Today's plan (or asking the tutor to run your study time) opens a short briefing, then takes you through each part in order. Before each part there is one line on how to do it well, for example to answer in your head before you look at the choices. After each part you get a quick debrief (your score, or how many cards you knew) and what is next, and the next part is chosen again from what you just did, so a drill that turns up misses can add a review. You can skip a part, stop early, or come back through the small "Session" button, and the session ends with a short summary and what to start with next time. This part does not use the AI at all, so it works without a key. The coaching lines are based on retrieval practice (trying to answer before seeing options), which is among the best-supported study methods; the exact wording and the "stop when the time is used" rule are my choices, not tested. While a session is running, the tutor (and the chat on each question) knows which part you are on and what is next, the Study tab's next-best-step points back to the session, and changing your time for the day changes the running session.
Sturdier: bad data, offline use, and wrong answers that gave themselves awayI tried loading the app from twenty-two kinds of damaged saved data. One broke a screen: a single badly formed AI-written card could stop the Reference tab from opening. Saved data and restored backups now drop malformed written questions and cards, and always have a record for every exam domain. The app can now be opened without a connection from the last copy it saw (the AI features still need one) and can be added to a phone's home screen with an icon; the page is still fetched fresh whenever you are online, so updates show up on the next open. It also asks the browser to keep your progress when space runs low, says in Settings whether the browser agreed, and, if something unexpected goes wrong on a screen, tells you your progress is saved instead of failing silently. In the question bank, 61 wrong answers used words like "always", "never" and "guaranteed", which let a test-wise student rule them out without knowing the material, so I rewrote them to be wrong on substance. Fourteen correct answers were much longer than the other choices, so I lengthened the others. Ninety wrong answers still contain the word "only", which I left because it is often a legitimate part of a wrong statement. Answer positions in the raw bank lean toward A, but every session shuffles the choices, and I checked that in each mode.
Every screen now lands where you would expectSwitching tabs used to carry over the scroll position of the tab you left, so Flashcards could open with its heading cut off and Tutor or Reference could open halfway down. Each tab now remembers where you were: tapping it in the bar returns you to that spot, opening it from a button inside the app starts at the top, and tapping the tab you are already on scrolls it to the top. The tutor opens at its latest message, and Settings and the study guide open at the top every time. In a quiz, each new question already started at the top, but after answering you often had to scroll to find Next question; that bar now stays at the bottom of the screen, and the feedback is scrolled to sit just above it. The flashcard stays on screen as you go through the deck. I measured these by scripting each move on a phone-sized screen, not on a real phone.
Less scrolling, tuned separately for sideways and uprightI measured how far you had to scroll on phones and tablets held both ways, then fixed the worst spots. Held sideways (and on wide screens), a practice question now sits on the left and its answers on the right, so the question stays in view while you read the explanations, and a new question fits on one screen without any scrolling. Held upright, spacing is tighter, the "how sure are you" row shrinks once you have answered, and the page title no longer wastes space on a long tagline. Flashcards now open on the card itself, with the explanation and filters underneath instead of above. The tutor puts the conversation and the message box at the top, and once you start talking the intro and idea buttons fold away. On a sideways phone the tab bar becomes a slim strip down the left edge so you keep the full height of the screen. On the Study tab, the session picker now comes right after today's plan, and on phones each option is trimmed to a title and a "use it when" line. The results screen keeps its buttons pinned at the bottom. I measured all of this in a desktop browser at phone and tablet sizes, not on a real phone.
The right answer is no longer usually "A"A check of the question bank found the correct answer sat in position A for about 35% of questions and in C or D for only about 19% each. On a real exam the answer is spread evenly, so practicing on a lopsided bank could quietly teach you to lean toward A when unsure. The correct answers are now spread evenly across A, B, C and D (about 22% each). Questions whose wording points at other choices by letter, such as "both A and B", or whose choices are ordered numbers were left exactly as they were. Your saved record of which wrong answers you tend to pick was moved to the new positions automatically, so nothing you built up is lost; a practice session that was half finished before this change will start fresh.
Less to scroll past: long cards now fold upThe Tools tab stacked six decision tools, each over 500 pixels tall, though you only use one at a time. Each now shows its title and a one-line summary and opens when tapped. The same goes for the exam format, calculator policy and what-to-bring cards on the Exam Day tab, and for the podcast card on the Reference tab. Nothing was removed. Anything in the app that points you to one of them opens it for you. Today's plan shows its first four steps with the rest one tap away. Together this cuts the Tools tab by about 60% and the Exam Day tab by about 45%.
The tutor can tell you what to do next, even without an AI keyAsking the tutor "what should I do next?" used to need an API key, even though the app already knows your next step, today's plan, your weak topics and what you have missed. Now the tutor answers those questions straight from your own progress, in the chat, with buttons that do the thing: start the step, run your whole session, drill your weakest domain, review what you missed, open the calculator or the study guide, or show you where something is on screen. With a key connected, the full AI tutor still handles explanations and follow-up questions. Explaining a concept or writing a new question still needs the key, and the tutor says so.
The tutor remembers what you asked itThe tutor now keeps a short list of the questions you have typed to it, for about two weeks. When you come back it mentions your latest one and offers a "Pick that up" button, and with an AI key it also uses that history so it can build on earlier answers instead of starting cold. Your list lives only in this browser.
The Next button bar no longer lets questions show underneathDuring a quiz, a thin strip below the Exit and Next buttons let answer text scroll through behind it. The bar now sits flush with the bottom of the screen in both portrait and landscape, so there is a little more room for the question and nothing peeking out beneath the buttons.
Tutor tab and buttons tidied on phonesThe bottom tab bar now always fits all six tabs, so the highlighted Tutor tab no longer pokes past the right edge. The "what you can ask me to do" buttons now match the dark theme instead of showing as light grey, and the tutor's greeting now points to the suggestions below it and phrases the next step more naturally.
Readiness text stays inside its columnOn a sideways phone, the line under the readiness ring ("about 66% on exam-style questions") and the trend pill could spill past the column and touch the tab rail. They now wrap within the column and the column sizes to fit its text.
A softer Next button barThe Exit and Next bar under each question used to carry a hard line and a shadow, which showed up as a stray smudge under the card on short questions. It now blends in, and only fades slightly over the answers when they scroll beneath it.
Content no longer touches the side tab barOn phones held sideways, the page content started exactly at the edge of the side tab bar because the notch area was counted as part of the gap. A proper margin now always separates them.
Tighter spacing on the recommended session cardOn phones, the recommended Adaptive Session card had a wide empty band above its status line and cut its description short. The gaps are tighter and more of the description now shows. A check of the other tabs in portrait, sideways and tablet sizes found their spacing already even.
Readiness ring and countdown sit side by side againOn an upright phone, the longer readiness lines pushed the exam countdown card below the ring and left a blank area beside it. The readiness block is now a fixed narrow width so the countdown sits next to it, and the page tagline fits on one line instead of three.
Your progress is saved on this device (in this browser) — nothing is sent to a server. Blueprint sourced from CFP Board's official topic outline (cfp.net) — practice questions are original, not from a real exam, and this tool is not affiliated with or endorsed by CFP Board.

Decision tools

tap through, or see the whole map at once

Six tools built from the study guide's own knowledge — four walk you through one question at a time to a recommendation, two are built for exploring rather than following a single path.

Which trust fits?

Tap through the questions to reach a recommendation — not a substitute for the specifics in the estate planning section of the study guide.

Which business entity fits?

Tap through the questions to reach a recommendation. Watch for "LLC" as an answer choice on a tax-treatment question — it's a legal structure, not a tax election, and defaults to being taxed as a sole proprietorship or partnership unless it elects otherwise.

Is a traditional IRA contribution deductible?

Anyone can contribute to a traditional IRA — this only decides whether the contribution is deductible.

When should Social Security be claimed?

Not a single "right age" — the client's own income need, work status, spousal situation, and longevity expectations each point in different directions.

Options matrix

Four positions, four different risk profiles — buying caps the loss at the premium; selling doesn't. Tap each one for more detail.

Qualified plan family tree

Where each specific plan name actually sits in the bigger picture. Tap each branch for more detail.

search all terms

Every term from your flashcards, always visible for quick lookup — no flipping, no rating, just a fast way to check a definition while you're reading something else.

Syllabus checklist

all 70 official subtopics — reordered weakest-first

Straight from CFP Board's Principal Knowledge Topics, sorted by your current quiz performance — your weakest domain(s) always float to the top, tagged "Focus first." Checkboxes track your own review, separately from quiz mastery. Under each topic is your accuracy on its matching questions (matched by keywords, so approximate) and a Drill button. The study guide has a fixed, printable snapshot of the same syllabus.

Flashcards

tap the card to flip

Ordered live by what you need most: your weakest domains and anything marked "still learning" surface first. how the ordering actually works — tap to expand ▾

Underneath, a Leitner-style spaced-repetition system tracks each card separately. A correct answer pushes the card further out (a day, then three, then a week, up to a month); a miss brings it back right away. Growing gaps between repeats are what make it stick. On top of that, cards that match ideas in questions you missed move up, so do cards in your weak subtopics, and a card you keep missing gets an automatic worked example. Close to the exam, new cards wait so review comes first.

Talk it through with your tutor

Pacing

about two minutes a question

Exam format

source: cfp.net
Total questions170 multiple-choice, in stand-alone items, short scenarios, and longer case histories.
StructureTwo 3-hour sections, each split into two subsections (43 + 42 questions), for four subsections total.
TimingEach 3-hour section has one shared, pooled timer across its two subsections — unused time doesn't carry to the next section.
BreaksOne optional break after the first subsection of each section, plus a scheduled 40-minute break between the two sections that you can skip. The clock keeps running during the optional breaks.
No going backOnce you submit a subsection, you cannot return to it — including after the 40-minute break.
Check-in securityExpect a fingerprint scan and photo capture at check-in, repeated every time you leave and re-enter the room (including after breaks), plus a pocket check and a security wand scan.
ResultsPrometric emails a preliminary result shortly after the exam. Official results follow by email, typically four to six weeks after the testing window closes.
Tax law testedExams in the July 2026, October 2026 and March 2027 windows test 2026 tax law, so use the 2026 figures in this app. The October 2026 window runs October 29 to November 5.
Appointment lengthThe appointment is 7 hours, including 6 hours of testing, plus a 2-minute nondisclosure agreement, a 5-minute tutorial and a 5-minute survey. Clear your calculator's memory before each section; the proctor will not do it for you.
Pass rateRecent administrations have run roughly 62–68%, averaging around 65% over the last several years; first-time takers pass at a noticeably higher rate than repeaters.
If you don't passYou'll receive a diagnostic report showing your performance across the Principal Knowledge Topics to help target a retake.

Calculator policy

source: cfp.net

You must bring your own battery-powered, non-programmable, dedicated financial calculator — CFP Board does not provide one. Only these models are allowed into the testing room:

HP 10BHP 10BIIHP 10BII+ HP 12CHP 12C PlatinumHP 17BII+ TI BA II PlusTI BA II Plus Professional Sharp EL-733Sharp EL-733ASharp EL-738

You clear your calculator's memory yourself before each section (staff inspect it first, but don't clear it for you), then reset your settings. On the HP 10bII+ that means checking P/YR (the default is 12) and END mode. Cover any printed formulas or notes on the calculator with solid tape.

Exam-week checklist

What to bring

source: cfp.net
ArrivalPlan to begin check-in 30 minutes before your scheduled time. Arriving late means being turned away and forfeiting the exam fee entirely — there's no grace period.
RequiredValid, unexpired government-issued photo ID matching your registration name.
CalculatorOne or more approved models (see above). Backups allowed.
WaterOne clear bottle with all labels removed is allowed in the exam room.
Food & notesNot allowed in the exam room, but you may store them in your locker to use during the scheduled 40-minute break.
ElectronicsNo phones, smartwatches, or other electronic devices are accessible once testing begins — they stay locked away until you finish.

AI connection

Run as a downloaded file, the tutor, AI-generated practice, podcasts and other AI tools need your own API key (console.anthropic.com). It's stored only in this browser and sent straight to Anthropic, never through another server. Don't share this file once a key is saved in it.

AI token usage

Counts the tokens used by this app's own AI requests. It is not your account balance, which no app can read; check billing at console.anthropic.com.

Display

evening warm tone

Voice

The device voice that reads flashcards, rationales and podcasts aloud. Auto picks the most natural-sounding one available. The two podcast hosts use two different voices, and if you choose only one, the other is filled in automatically.

Backup & restore

Progress is saved to this browser automatically, but that save isn't fully reliable in every environment — even a page refresh can occasionally lose it, not just an update to this app. The only guaranteed-safe copy is one you export yourself. Download a backup regularly, especially before refreshing or closing the app.

A backup file just downloaded automatically to your device (this doesn't depend on this app's storage at all, so it survives no matter what). Need another copy?
Or select all the text below and copy it somewhere safe (notes app, email to yourself, etc.):
Have a downloaded backup file? It'll be named something like "cfp-blueprint-backup-2026-08-31-...txt" in your downloads folder — select it here:
Or paste your previously backed-up text below:

Content quality check

Checks everything in your bank, including AI-generated content, for duplicates, lopsided answer choices, malformed entries and TVM problems that don't solve. It checks structure, not factual accuracy. Worth running now and then after a lot of AI-generated content builds up.

Syllabus coverage check

Estimates how many questions cover each of the 70 official CFP Board subtopics and lists the thinnest first. Questions aren't tagged by subtopic, so the counts come from matching key terms and are rough. A low number is a pointer, not proof of a gap.

Reset

Clears all saved progress on this device — mastery stats, session history, missed questions, syllabus checklist, flashcard ratings, AI-generated content, and your tutor conversation. Your exam date and light/dark theme choice are kept. This cannot be undone; back up first if you want to keep a copy.
